paragraphs.text: Beginning with the conjunction "and" shows that the Book of Judges is a continuation of the Book of Joshua. Joshua had divided the Promised Land among the tribes, but the whole land had not yet been cleared of its pagan inhabitants, and this was left for the tribes to carry out. So after the death of Joshua, the children of Israel asked which of the tribes should begin the fight against the Canaanites, the original inhabitants of the land, who were still living in some regions and had recovered some parts of what the children of Israel had possessed. The inquiry of God was made through the high priest in the tabernacle of meeting.

God answered by choosing the tribe of Judah to begin fighting the Canaanites. The reason for choosing this tribe is that it was the most numerous of the tribes, and also that from it would come Christ, who overcomes Satan and binds him by the Cross.

The tribe of Judah asked the tribe of Simeon to go out with it to fight the Canaanites, on the condition that Judah would go out and take part with Simeon in its coming wars against the Canaanites, for the following reasons:
1- The tribe of Simeon lived next to the tribe of Judah.
2- Simeon and Judah were both sons of Leah.

3- Simeon was a small tribe, so that it would not feel its weakness, Judah included it in the war with him, and afterward the great tribe of Judah would share with its brother in its wars to help it win the war. This is a kind of encouragement for the smaller and the weaker. The tribe of Simeon agreed to take part with the tribe of Judah in the war.

How beautiful it is that you encourage the small of soul and include them in the work with you, even in a small way, to commend and honor them, just as God includes you in His service and blesses you and glorifies you.
The Perizzites: one of the original inhabitants of the land. They were the dwellers of villages, for the meaning of their name is villagers.
Bezek: a city in the tribe of Judah, about 24 km northwest of Jerusalem.
The tribes of Judah and Simeon advanced to the city of Bezek and fought the Canaanites and the Perizzites who lived there. They defeated them and killed ten thousand of them.
Adoni: a word meaning lord. So Adoni-bezek means the king or lord of the city of Bezek.
Thumbs: the plural of thumb, the big digit of the hand or the foot, which is regarded as essential for gripping weapons in war or for walking.

During the war of Judah and Simeon against Bezek, they seized its king, called Adoni-bezek, who was famous for humiliating the kings he defeated: he would cut off the thumbs of their hands so that they could not grip weapons, and the thumbs of their feet so that they could not run. So they did to him as he had done to the kings he had defeated before, and cut off the thumbs of his hands and feet, perhaps so that this might lead him to humility, repentance and faith.

Adoni-bezek remembered what he had done to the kings he had defeated during his life, who were seventy kings. This shows the extent of his strength in war, yet he was defeated before the power of God. It was a humiliation of those kings that he made them sit under his table like dogs while he ate, to throw them some food, and because of his injustice to them, God decided to take vengeance on him in the same way. The Jews brought him to Jerusalem, and he died there.

entries.section: (2) The capture of Jerusalem, Hebron and Debir

paragraphs.text: Joshua had captured Jerusalem, but it seems that some of its original, pagan inhabitants were able to retake it, so the tribe of Judah fought against it, captured it, and burned it with fire, together with the pagans in it, as a lesson to others so that the pagans would fear. It should be noted that the burning of the city was only partial, as is shown by the fact that they lived in it afterward and that some Jebusites also lived with them (v. 21). The tribe of Judah captured Jerusalem, but did not take the stronghold of Zion adjoining the city, in which the Jebusites remained; but King David was later able to capture the city and the stronghold and drive out the Jebusites completely (2 Sam 5:6, 7).

entries.section: (2) The capture of Jerusalem, Hebron and Debir

paragraphs.text: The mountain: the mountainous lands lying south of Jerusalem, including Bethlehem and Hebron. The south: the dry lands lying between the Dead Sea on the east and the Mediterranean on the west, and from Hebron on the north to the wilderness on the south, called the Negev desert (Josh 15:21) (Map 10). The valley: the valleys that are in the tribe of Judah.
After that Judah fought the Canaanites in various places in the mountains, the southern deserts and the valleys, and took possession of their lands.

entries.section: (2) The capture of Jerusalem, Hebron and Debir

paragraphs.text: Sheshai, Ahiman and Talmai: chiefs of the tribes of the Anakim, who were among the original inhabitants of the land and were distinguished by strength.
Kirjath-sepher: that is, the city of the book, a city distinguished by learning and knowledge.

This portion was mentioned earlier in the Book of Joshua (ch. 14:13, 14; 15:16-19), and it is mentioned here to complete the account of the victories of the tribe of Judah and its leader Caleb, in order to show the power of God supporting them. So refer to the explanation of this portion in the Book of Joshua.

If you are obedient to God and rely on Him, be sure that He supports you in every circumstance of life, however much the wicked oppose you or seize your rights. God keeps them away from you because of their wickedness and upholds you as long as you hold fast to your purity and righteousness.

entries.section: (3) The rest of the wars of Judah

paragraphs.text: The Kenites: they are the descendants of Moses' father-in-law. The meaning of Kenite is smith, since some of them worked in smithing. Many tribes branched out from them, most of which were at peace with the Jews, such as the Rechabites, and lived beside them (Jer 35), but a few of them were wicked, and these are the ones God promised Abraham that He would drive out (Gen 15). The Kenites were dwelling in the city of palm trees when the tribe of Judah was carrying out its wars, and when the city was struck they fled from it and settled in the desert lands lying west of the Dead Sea and east of Jerusalem, where pasture is abundant, and they lived there with the peoples of those regions, who were Canaanites.

entries.section: (3) The rest of the wars of Judah

paragraphs.text: Judah and Simeon continued their wars and defeated the Canaanites who lived in Zephath and killed its people.

entries.section: (3) The rest of the wars of Judah

paragraphs.text: Then the tribe of Judah, with the tribe of Simeon, faced the Philistines in three of their five great cities, which are Gaza, Ashkelon and Ekron, together with the small towns surrounding each of them, and they captured them all.

entries.section: (3) The rest of the wars of Judah

paragraphs.text: The Lord was their helper, so they succeeded in possessing the mountain lands, but they were unable to possess the plain of the valley because the Canaanites there were armed with chariots of iron. The faith of Judah and Simeon weakened and they were afraid before these chariots, especially since the Philistines had monopolized the making of iron until the days of David the prophet (1 Sam 13:19-22), who defeated them and introduced the use and manufacture of iron in Israel.

entries.section: (3) The rest of the wars of Judah

paragraphs.text: The inspired writer returns here once more to mention the giving of the city of Hebron to Caleb, which happened in the days of Joshua, repeating the account of the driving out of the three sons of Anak, in honor of Caleb, who was among the spies whom Moses sent to spy out the land and who declared that God was able to give them the land despite the strength of its inhabitants (Josh 14:13, 14; 15:13-14).

As long as God is with you, do not be troubled by the strength of those who oppose you or by their threats, but trust in His power and seek Him earnestly, and you will walk in assurance all your days.

entries.section: (3) The rest of the wars of Judah

paragraphs.text: Unto this day: that is, until the time the book was written, and this confirms that the book was written by Samuel the prophet before David became king.

Jerusalem lay on the border of Judah, so it was shared between the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, the southern part belonging to Judah and the northern to Benjamin. Both Judah and Benjamin were slack in driving out the Jebusites who were in Jerusalem, and this was a failure on their part to keep the commandment of the Lord. They thought that by leaving these peoples they would obtain tribute from them and make them work for them. David later drove them out (2 Sam 5).

entries.section: (4) Accounts of the wars of the tribe of Joseph

paragraphs.text: The two brothers, that is, the tribe of Ephraim and the half-tribe of Manasseh (the one living west of the Jordan), joined together in fighting Bethel, and the Lord was with them, so they captured it.

entries.section: (4) Accounts of the wars of the tribe of Joseph

paragraphs.text: The two tribes assigned a group of spies to learn the information needed about the city, to make it easier to fight it and capture it, which is what was done, and still is done, in many wars. The name of the city was formerly Luz.

entries.section: (4) Accounts of the wars of the tribe of Joseph

paragraphs.text: While watching the city, the spies saw a man coming out of it, and they asked him to show them the entrance to the city so that they could enter it, and they promised him a reward for guiding them.

entries.section: (4) Accounts of the wars of the tribe of Joseph

paragraphs.text: The man responded to their request and showed them the way into the city, which enabled the sons of Joseph to capture it and kill its inhabitants. They rewarded the man who showed them the entrance by leaving him alive, he and his family, and not harming him, as they did to the rest of the people of the city.

entries.section: (4) Accounts of the wars of the tribe of Joseph

paragraphs.text: As soon as he was given his freedom, the man went to the land of the Hittites, who lived in some regions of the land of Palestine (as they also lived in scattered places in Syria and Turkey). There he built a city and called it Luz, after the city of Luz which he had left, whose name was changed to Bethel. It should be noted that the pagan man who guided the Jews into the city went off afterward to live with the pagans and did not believe in God, who helped the Jews to possess the city. He saw God's victory and did not believe, as many do today: they guide others to the upright life, but they themselves do not repent.

As the tribes of Ephraim and the half-tribe of Manasseh cooperated in their war against Bethel, may you also cooperate with your spiritual brothers, encouraging them and supporting them in their battles with the devil, for God rejoices in this love of yours and rewards you with many blessings.

entries.section: (5) The failure of the tribes to drive out the pagan peoples

paragraphs.text: Beth-shean: a city about 6.5 km west of the Jordan River.
Taanach: a city in the middle of Palestine, about 21 km from Nazareth.
Dor: a city lying about 9 km southeast of Nazareth.
Ibleam: a city lying south of Jenin.

Megiddo: a city southeast of Haifa (Maps 10, 12). Just as the children of Israel of the other tribes failed to drive out the pagan inhabitants, so also the sons of the tribe of Manasseh did the same: they did not drive out the pagan peoples from the cities and villages they had taken, which were Beth-shean, Taanach, Dor, Ibleam and Megiddo. So the Canaanites resolved to remain in those places with the sons of Manasseh. The reason for this failure is what is mentioned in (v. 21).

entries.section: (5) The failure of the tribes to drive out the pagan peoples

paragraphs.text: In the periods when the children of Israel grew strong, they put the Canaanites under tribute and made them work for them. But in all cases they did not drive them out from among them. The main reason is the weakness of the faith of the children of Israel in the power of God that supported them in driving out the pagans, in addition to their slackness and negligence in carrying out God's commandment. The result of this was that these peoples rose up against them afterward, humiliated them and seized their good things, as appears in the later events of this book.

entries.section: (5) The failure of the tribes to drive out the pagan peoples

paragraphs.text: Gezer: a city northwest of Jerusalem at a distance of 29 km (Map 12). The sons of Ephraim fell into the same error into which their brothers had fallen, for they left the Canaanites to dwell in their midst in the city of Gezer, which later became one of the most important cities of Ephraim.

entries.section: (5) The failure of the tribes to drive out the pagan peoples

paragraphs.text: Kitron: it lies about 11 km south of Haifa.
Nahalol: it lies south of Acre (Map 10). The tribe of Zebulun also failed to drive out the Canaanites, and the matter was limited to imposing tribute on them.

entries.section: (5) The failure of the tribes to drive out the pagan peoples

paragraphs.text: Accho: Acre.
Zidon: that is, Sidon.
Ahlab: it lies northwest of Tyre.
Achzib: it lies north of Acre.
Helbah: it lies near Ahlab.
Aphik: southeast of Acre.

Rehob: to the east of Aphik (Map 10). The tribe of Asher also did not drive out the Canaanite inhabitants from the cities that fell within its portion of the land, and those cities are Zidon, Ahlab, Achzib, Helbah, Aphik and Rehob. And so the tribe of Asher dwelt with the Canaanites, the original inhabitants of the land.

entries.section: (5) The failure of the tribes to drive out the pagan peoples

paragraphs.text: Beth-shemesh: a city in the land of Naphtali, northeast of Nablus.

Beth-anath: a town in the land of Naphtali, east of Acre (Maps 10, 11). The same thing happened with the tribe of Naphtali, as if the contagion of slackness in driving out the pagan peoples had spread among them and they began to imitate one another. So Naphtali did not drive out the inhabitants of Beth-shemesh or the inhabitants of Beth-anath, but left them in their midst and was content to impose tribute on them.

The children of Israel left the pagan peoples to dwell in their midst, and this proved to be a calamity for them. So also we, if we leave a sin lurking inside our hearts, it will become a point of weakness, like a small hole through which the enemy of good slips in to gain strength against us afterward. May we be alert to these holes in our hearts and put an end to them, so that we do not give the devil a place.
The Amorites: a Semitic people who ruled parts of Palestine, and they were among the strongest of the Canaanite peoples.

When the tribe of Dan attacked the Amorite tribes, they gathered in the plains, so the tribe of Dan was confined to the mountainous places and was afraid to attack the Amorites gathered in the plains. So it grew slack and did not trust in God, and dwelt beside them.
Mount Heres: east of Jerusalem on the road to Jericho.
Aijalon: it lies near Jerusalem.

Shaalbim: east of the Jordan River, in the middle of its extent (Map 11). When the tribe of Dan was slack in driving out the Amorites, the Amorites dwelt in Mount Heres, in Aijalon and in Shaalbim. But it seems that the two tribes of the sons of Joseph were jealous for their brothers the Danites and grieved at their dwelling in the narrow mountain regions because of the siege imposed by the Amorites, so they helped their brothers the Danites and imposed their might upon the Amorites and forced them to pay tribute to the tribe of Dan. And because of the narrowness of the places the tribe of Dan had taken, it later fought Laish, which lies north of the land of the Jews, and they captured it as is clear in (Judg 18), and they called the city by the name of their father, Dan.
The ascent of Akrabbim: south of the Dead Sea.

Sela: to the south of the ascent of Akrabbim (Map 11). Before Joshua fought them, the Amorites occupied wide lands east of the Jordan, and the borders of their lands extended from the ascent of Akrabbim and Sela in the south to the far north.

When Satan sees slackness in the believer, he covets overcoming him. Therefore the believer must strive continually, resisting the forces of evil, armed with the whole armor of God according to the saying of Paul the Apostle, by practicing the sacraments of the Church, which give a person grace and strength in facing the forces of evil. The consequences of not driving out the inhabitants of the land are a summary of what happened repeatedly in the era of the Judges.

entries.section: (1) God's rebuke for their not driving out the pagans

paragraphs.text: An angel: either God appeared in the form of an angel, or a real angel speaking a message from God.

Bochim: it lies near Bethel and is higher than the land surrounding it, and the meaning of its name is the weepers, because the people of God wept there (v. 5). I will never break: I will not go back on My covenant.

God had appeared in the form of an angel at Gilgal to Joshua (Josh 5:13; 6:2), and now He goes up from Gilgal to appear to the people at a place called Bochim, and reminds them that He had brought them up out of the land of Egypt, where Pharaoh had enslaved them, and had fulfilled His promise to their fathers by giving them the land of Canaan. He had promised them that He would never break His covenant with them, and of course this is on condition that they obey His commandments. God fulfilled this with the new Israel, that is, the Christians, transferring them to Paradise and giving them the Kingdom of Heaven, that they may reign with Him forever.

entries.section: (1) God's rebuke for their not driving out the pagans

paragraphs.text: God commanded them not to make a covenant with the inhabitants of the land from among the pagan peoples and not to mingle with them, but to throw down their altars so that every trace of paganism would vanish. But despite the Lord's repeated warnings they did not heed His counsel; rather they allowed them to dwell in their midst and mingled with them, as we saw in the previous chapter. The question here is one of rebuke, showing the Lord's astonishment and displeasure at their deeds.

entries.section: (1) God's rebuke for their not driving out the pagans

paragraphs.text: A snare: a trap and a stumbling block.

The Lord's response to their disobedience was only to let them reap the reward of this disobedience, so that the recompense would be of the same kind as their deed: those peoples whom they left in their midst would become a source of disturbance and trouble to them in the future, fighting them and plundering their possessions. Indeed, the gods those peoples worship would be a snare and a stumbling block to the children of Israel, as those peoples would draw them to become like them and to share in their worship, forsaking the worship of the true God.

entries.section: (1) God's rebuke for their not driving out the pagans

paragraphs.text: When they heard this message from the Lord, they were deeply moved and repented of their deeds and of their disobedience to His guidance. In remembrance of their grief and weeping they called the name of the place "Bochim", a Hebrew word meaning weepers. And they offered sacrifices there to atone for their sin.
The sacrifices used to be offered on the altar of God in Shiloh, but because God appeared in this place, they made a temporary altar and offered the sacrifices on it, and this was an exception.

It should be noted that despite the weeping and the remorse, the people did not move to drive out the pagans from among them according to the Lord's message to them. For to be content with weeping, without hope and without the work of repentance, changes nothing in God's sight; it is a false repentance.

May your repentance be joined with works that confirm it, so that you put right your wrongs, that is, you apologize to the one you wronged or return what you stole... in addition to drawing near to God through holy acts of worship in which your love for Him appears, so that your repentance is a true repentance.

entries.section: (1) God's rebuke for their not driving out the pagans

paragraphs.text: A generation that did not know the Lord: it seems that the fathers failed to teach their children faith in God and His works with His people, so that when the generation that was contemporary with Joshua died, and the elders who were contemporary with him, the devout ones who had taught the people, this new generation neglected the teaching of its children, and they drifted away from the knowledge of God and the keeping of His commandments. Timnath-heres: it means the portion of the sun, and it was mentioned in (Josh 34:3) as Timnath-serah, meaning a double portion; perhaps they changed the name of the city to the portion of the sun after Joshua stopped the sun in his war with the five kings (Map 12). This is a repetition of what is in (Josh 24:28-31...); refer to the Book of Joshua.

The repetition by the inspired writer here is for a spiritual wisdom, which is to remind the people of their spiritual state in the days of Joshua and the glory they achieved in their wars against the pagan peoples, so that they might compare what was then with what is happening now, in that they have allowed the pagan peoples to remain in the land in their midst, contrary to the divine command.

entries.section: (2) The pagans' attacks on the people of God

paragraphs.text: Baalim: the plural of Baal, a famous pagan god.

From this verse to the end of the chapter, the picture of the life the people lived in the period called the era of the Judges is brought together. This verse tells us that the children of Israel committed the great sin which the Lord had forbidden repeatedly, and which was the first commandment of the Ten Commandments, which calls for the worship of the true God alone, without the false pagan gods. So the people betrayed God and worshiped those false gods.

entries.section: (2) The pagans' attacks on the people of God

paragraphs.text: They forsook the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, who loved them and freed them from slavery in the land of Egypt, for He brought them out from there with signs and wonders and brought them to a land flowing with milk and honey to possess it. They imitated the other peoples whom they had left in their midst in worshiping false gods and bowed down to them, forgetting the first commandment the Lord had given them at Sinai, and by this they disobeyed God and defied Him.

entries.section: (2) The pagans' attacks on the people of God

paragraphs.text: Ashtaroth: she is the chief goddess in Babylon and Assyria, the mother of the goddesses, and her worship involves very licentious practices, and her priestesses were harlots, because she is always worshiped together with a male god, Baal, the husband of Ashtaroth and lord of fertility, and human sacrifices were offered to him.
Gathered unto his fathers: he died and was buried with his fathers.
They abandoned the worship of the living God and worshiped false gods that the pagan peoples worshiped, such as Baal and Ashtaroth.

entries.section: (2) The pagans' attacks on the people of God

paragraphs.text: The Lord was greatly angered against them, so He left their enemies to plunder their wealth and the produce of their land and to take their wives and children as male and female slaves. God did not defend them as He used to before; rather divine providence forsook them, so they became unable to repel their enemies and protect themselves.

entries.section: (2) The pagans' attacks on the people of God

paragraphs.text: He delivered them into the hands of spoilers: He handed them over to the might of their enemies who plundered them.
The hand of the Lord was against them for evil: the hand of the Lord is a figure for the power and work of the Lord, so the Lord was working against them for harm and to bring evil and woe upon them.

Wherever they went, whether to carry on their daily work, or to trade with the surrounding peoples, or to face their enemies and fight them, in every case the Lord allowed them to be hurt by everything harmful and injurious. In this the Lord did not take them by surprise, for He had warned them again and again against breaking their covenant with Him, and had cautioned them that He would punish them most severely if they broke the covenant, so they were greatly distressed by the pagans' humiliation of them.

Do not persist in your sins and your disobedience to God, defying Him and provoking Him, for who are you that you should resist God? But if you sin because of your weakness, repent quickly, for His mercies are many, and He cares for His weak children and forgives them all their sins.

entries.section: (3) The raising up of judges to deliver them

paragraphs.text: When the people of God were distressed they cried out to Him, so He raised up judges for them from among them, who judged by His law, led their armies and delivered them from their enemies.

entries.section: (3) The raising up of judges to deliver them

paragraphs.text: After God freed them by means of the judge and they kept His commandments, they would turn back and forsake God's teachings which they had heard from the mouth of the judge, and worship idols, resembling a woman who commits adultery and leaves her husband, and by this they had forsaken the way of their devout fathers who worshiped God.

entries.section: (3) The raising up of judges to deliver them

paragraphs.text: The Lord repented because of their groaning: this is a figurative expression in our human language, for the Lord is not moved by passions as human beings are. The intended meaning is that the Lord hears His people when they cry out to Him repenting of their deeds, and He prepares for them someone to rescue them.

entries.section: (3) The raising up of judges to deliver them

paragraphs.text: After the death of the judge they would turn away from the Lord and return to their sins, and even go further in them than those before them had done. They worshiped the pagan gods and did not cease from their evil deeds and the hardness of their hearts.

Do not waver between good and evil, worshiping God while at the same time allowing yourself some sins, or offering repentance and then returning to sin through negligence. Ask God's help that you may remain firm in the life with Him and enjoy His fellowship.

entries.section: (4) The pagans left with the people of God

paragraphs.text: Because the people of God allowed themselves the worship of idols, did not remain firm in repentance and broke their covenant with Him, God decided, as a punishment for them, to leave the pagans dwelling among them and troubling them, that perhaps they might repent with a true repentance.

entries.section: (4) The pagans left with the people of God

paragraphs.text: God's purpose in not helping them to drive out the pagans was to test His people, whether they would worship Him faithfully and keep His commandments, so that He would help them to drive out the enemies, or would be negligent in worshiping Him, so that He would allow the enemies to humiliate them.

entries.section: (4) The pagans left with the people of God

paragraphs.text: God left the pagan peoples in the days of Joshua, since his old age did not allow him to complete the driving out of all the pagans, and this was a test for the people, whether they would obey God's word through the mouth of Joshua and complete the liberation of their land, or be negligent. Sadly they were negligent, so the enemies troubled them greatly in the era of the Judges, but for the sake of David's righteousness, God helped him to drive out these peoples.

Our repeated transgressions of God's commandments provoke divine anger against us, and then we return and complain, asking why the Lord is angry... Earnestness in repentance is what draws God's help, and by it victory is achieved.

The judges Othniel, Ehud, Shamgar. From this chapter to (ch. 16) the judges are recounted: when their people grew negligent, the pagan peoples rose against them and humiliated them, so they cried out to God and He sent them the judge who delivered them, but they returned and grew negligent, so the pagan peoples humiliated them, and so on.

entries.section: (1) The peoples who remained in the midst of Israel

paragraphs.text: The people of God were negligent in completing the driving out of the wicked inhabitants of the land, so they dwelt beside them. These peoples had not known the wars that took place at the hand of Joshua, either because they did not believe them or because they had not witnessed them, so they made light of them and did not fear God, who leads His people and protects them. God allowed them to remain in order to test His people, that is, to make them know the consequences of their negligence in carrying out His commandments. For these peoples enticed them to worship their idols and they intermarried with them, so God forsook them and these peoples humiliated them.

entries.section: (1) The peoples who remained in the midst of Israel

paragraphs.text: Only: the men who had not taken part in the previous wars.

Here he makes clear a principal reason for God's allowing these peoples to remain with His people: that the men of His people who had not taken part in the previous wars, because of their youth, might learn how to fight these peoples and drive them out, so as to possess their land and fulfill God's promise, through their reliance on God, their seeking help from His power in war, and their upright conduct. By this they would always be ready and not become slack. This shows how God turns their sin, which was the negligence in leaving the pagans, into a blessing by teaching them vigilance and constant readiness.

entries.section: (1) The peoples who remained in the midst of Israel

paragraphs.text: Lords: chiefs or rulers.

The five: this means the rulers of the five famous Philistine cities, which are Ashdod, Gaza, Ashkelon, Gath and Ekron. They lie between the Brook of Egypt in the north of Egypt and Ekron in the north (Josh 13:3). The Canaanites: they represent the original inhabitants of the Promised Land, who were spread throughout its regions.
The Hivites: one of the Canaanite tribes, who lived in the villages that are in Mount Lebanon.
The Sidonians: the inhabitants of Sidon, which lies on the Mediterranean Sea in Lebanon.
Mount Baal-hermon: which is now called Mount Hermon (Jebel el-Sheikh), where there was a temple of Baal (Map 12). The entering in of Hamath: a city on the Orontes River in Syria.

He mentions here the peoples whom the children of Israel did not drive out, who dwelt with them and troubled them afterward when they mingled with them. Joshua had captured three of the great Philistine cities, which are Gaza, Ashkelon and Ekron, and Judah followed him (ch. 1:18), and Shamgar followed him when he fought the Philistines and killed six hundred men of them (ch. 3:31), but the Philistines were afterward able to recover their cities, and enmity and wars continued between the children of Israel and the Philistines.

entries.section: (1) The peoples who remained in the midst of Israel

paragraphs.text: Those are the ones God allowed to be left, in order to show in the following generations how far Israel would obey the Lord, and whether they would be influenced by the immoral ways of pagan worship or keep their faithfulness to the Lord their God.

God allows the presence of evil around you, not for you to fall into it, but for you to hold fast to God and seek His help, so that evil has no authority over you, but He removes it from you and lets you enjoy His fellowship.
The Hittites: the sons of Heth, son of Canaan.
The Amorites: the inhabitants of the mountainous regions.
The Perizzites: the inhabitants of the villages.
The Hivites: the inhabitants of the northeastern part of Palestine.
The Jebusites: the inhabitants of Jerusalem.

He mentions here six of the original peoples of the land, groups of whom remained because the children of Israel were negligent in driving them out, so they mingled with them and intermarried with them, against God's repeated commands (Deut 7:23), and they worshiped their idols under the influence of their pagan wives.
Baalim: the plural of Baal, who is the sun god.
Groves: wooden pillars carved with images of pagan gods.
By this the children of Israel forsook God and worshiped the pagan gods, the most important of which were Baal and Ashtaroth, for whom they set up the pillars.
Mesopotamia (Aram-naharaim): the land between the Tigris and the Euphrates.
Chushan-rishathaim: a name meaning Chushan of the double wickedness.
The Lord was greatly angered against His people because of what they did in the previous verses, so He allowed the king of Aram to prevail over them and enslave them for eight years.
Othniel: a name meaning the power of God.

Because of the humiliation of slavery the people cried out to God and repented, so He had compassion on them and sent them a judge, Othniel, the younger brother of Caleb, who fought the city of Kirjath-sepher and possessed it and married Achsah, the daughter of Caleb (Josh 15:17). Othniel led them and defeated the Arameans and delivered his people. It should be noted that the strength and wisdom that were in Othniel were the result of the Holy Spirit coming upon him, so his hand prevailed, that is, grew strong, against Chushan and he defeated him.

After their victory over the Arameans and their deliverance from their slavery, the people of God lived in rest for 40 years, that is, they lived without slavery and without mingling with idols and evil desires. And after 40 years Othniel died.

The Spirit of God dwelling in you is able to give you strength and wisdom in every circumstance of life, so that you dwell in peace and overcome the evils you meet, if you submit to the Holy Spirit by keeping God's commandments and by repentance.
Eglon: a name meaning a fat calf.
Moab: a son of Lot; they are peoples who live east of the Dead Sea.

After the death of Othniel, the people turned away from the worship of God and worshiped idols when they mingled with the pagan peoples. Because of their negligence and their departure from God, He allowed the king of Moab to rise against them and enslave them. This shows the importance of the servant and his leading of others, and on the other hand the importance of steadfastness in the spiritual life and holding fast to the worship of God.
The Ammonites: the sons of Ammon, son of Lot, who lived east of the Jordan, to the north of Moab.

The Amalekites: tribes that lived in Sinai and whom Moses defeated under the leadership of Joshua (Ex 17). Eglon allied himself with two other peoples, the sons of Ammon and Amalek, and attacked the children of Israel and defeated them and killed many of them, then took the city of palm trees, that is, Jericho. Most likely Eglon attacked them by crossing the Jordan River at a time when its waters were low, and he fought them and took possession of their land and enslaved them for eighteen years. We note here that the period of slavery increased, because Chushan-rishathaim, king of Aram, had enslaved them for eight years (v. 8), and God allowed the affliction upon them to increase until they should repent, because they were negligent the first time after God had given them rest, and returned to the worship of idols and various desires.

The people suffered the humiliation of slavery and were pricked in their hearts, so they cried out to the Lord, and the Lord in His wide mercy never overlooks the cry of the distressed and accepts their return to Him. So He appointed a deliverer for them, Ehud the son of Gera, of the tribe of Benjamin, who was left-handed, that is, he used his left hand (ambidextrous). The people sent with him a valuable present for Eglon, king of Moab; it was large in size, so a number of men carried it with him, and its apparent purpose was to appease Eglon so that he would lighten his enslavement of the children of Israel, while the hidden purpose will appear in the following verses.

Ehud made for himself a sword sharp on both sides, about half a meter long, that is, relatively short, so that he could hide it under his clothes when he went in to King Eglon, and he girded it on his right thigh, for he was left-handed, since the sword is usually placed on the left thigh by one who uses his right hand. This also helped him to hide it from the eyes of those watching at the king's door.

Ehud presented the present to King Eglon, who was very pleased with it, which made him feel safe with Ehud who presented it and not expect any evil from him, as we shall see in what follows. Eglon was a very fat man.

With Ehud were several men who had accompanied him to carry the present. After presenting it to the king, Ehud sent them away so that he would be alone when he returned to the king, as will come in the rest of the story, so that no one would be suspicious of the number of men accompanying him.
The carved images that were at Gilgal: these are carved statues of the gods and idols, and pillars for the gods.
Keep silence: an imperative verb meaning be quiet, that is, he silenced his guards and sent them away from him.

Ehud sent away his companions who carried the present, and he returned alone from the statues of the gods and the carved idols in the region of the city of Gilgal to where the king and his attendants were, and he spoke to the king saying that he had a very secret matter that he wished to tell him. So the king commanded everyone to keep silence, and this command of his was a sign meaning that the men should leave from around him to make room for the bearer of the message to speak to the king in secret. This shows the grace God gave Ehud in the eyes of Eglon, so that he trusted him and sent his guards away from him.

A summer parlor: a room on an upper floor with a pleasant atmosphere in summer. The king sat in it away from the heat of the weather, since the air enters it from more than one side. It was for the king alone.

Ehud went in to the king while he was sitting in the summer parlor, and to give importance to his words, Ehud claimed that the message was directed from God to the king. So the king rose out of respect and reverence for God, for the pagan kings and peoples had a religious sense despite their ignorance of the true God. This confirms Ehud's courage and faith in God in his speech, and then Eglon's submission and his trust in Ehud's words because this was from God.
Quickly and skillfully Ehud drew the sword from under his clothes with his left hand and struck the king with it in the belly.
The haft: the handle of the sword.
The blade: the weapon part of the sword.
The porch: prayer.

The haft went in after the blade, the whole blade, into the king's belly, for he struck him hard, and since the king was very fat the blade disappeared in the king's belly, for the fat of his fleshy body covered it, and Ehud did not draw the sword out but left it in his belly. The sword went through in its full length in his belly and its pointed end came out below the king's body, that is, from between the thighs at the anus, and this is an interpretation of the word "dirt". There is another opinion, which may be the more likely, that the pronoun in the verb "came out" refers to Ehud and not the sword, and that the word translated "dirt" means the window, which looked out on a porch or corridor leading to the porch, so Ehud went out through it after shutting the doors of the parlor from the inside firmly, that is, with the key, and passed through the porch and met the guards and greeted them and then departed. This shows the extent of Ehud's faith and steadfastness.
Covereth his feet: a polite expression meaning that the king is relieving himself in the toilet.

When Ehud left, the king's men came and saw the doors locked, and they thought that the king was in the bathroom relieving himself, and for that reason had locked the doors of the parlor, and that they must wait outside. The meaning of "covereth his feet" may be that he was asleep with his feet covered with a sheet or some other cover, so they were ashamed to open the doors lest they wake him from his sleep.

They stayed a long time without the king opening the doors for them as they were expecting him to do after he relieved himself or got up from his sleep. They fell into perplexity and embarrassment, but finally decided to open the door of the parlor, and as soon as they entered they were horrified to find the king lying on the ground dead.

The king's men remained amazed and overwhelmed by the horror of the situation, almost lost in their thoughts, not knowing how to act. This confusion of theirs helped Ehud to make use of the time to flee and save himself, so he passed the carved stones at Gilgal and continued his way until he reached Seirath, a place full of trees in the mountains of Ephraim, and hid there, and so he was safe.

When Ehud came to Seirath he blew the trumpet so that the people would gather to him. The people heard the sound of the trumpet and answered the call, and he went down from the mountain, that is, from Seirath which lies in the mountain of Ephraim, and the people followed him to fight the Moabites.
The fords of Jordan: the Jordan River at the time of its low water, for people could wade through it on foot at certain places, whose number was about fifty.

Ehud asked the people to follow him to face the Moabites because he realized that the death of the king would be followed by the collapse of the whole people. The Jordan River had many fords at the time of its low water, so that they could be crossed on foot, so Ehud and his men took control of the fords, and by this they separated the Moabite forces stationed west of the Jordan from the rest of their armies that were east of the Jordan, so that the one could not help the other.

The Moabite forces west of the Jordan became almost besieged, so the children of Israel overpowered them and killed about ten thousand warriors of them, every one who was able to fight and every mighty man, that is, they were all killed and not one escaped.
Moab was subdued under the hand of Israel: the Moabites were defeated before Israel and submitted to them, and the Israelites gained dominion over them.

With the destruction of the king of the Moabites and his army, they submitted to the rule of the children of Israel, and humiliation and disgrace came upon them. By this deliverance that Ehud achieved, peace, quiet and security returned to the land of Israel, and the land had rest from the harshness of subjection to the pagan peoples for eighty years.
Ehud risked his life to rescue his people, and God saved him. Let us labor in the service of our brethren and not be afraid, for God will keep us and uphold us and bless our service.
An ox goad: a long stick that was used to prick any animal if it lagged in its walking.

The Philistines were among the fiercest enemies of Israel, and they were always hostile to them, contending with them over the possession of lands in the regions near the coast of the Mediterranean Sea. A war arose between them during which Israel was led by one of the judges whom the Lord raised up, "Shamgar the son of Anath", who was a contemporary of Ehud, and Shamgar used a pointed piece of iron suitable as a goad for pricking oxen, and with it he killed six hundred men of the Philistine army. That was enough to discipline the Philistines, so they ceased troubling the children of Israel. Here appears Shamgar's faith in the power of God that supported him against the enemies, for although he had no weapons available, he used the ox goad, a weak instrument, to fight with it the armies of the enemies that numbered in the thousands, and killed six hundred men of them, and the rest were afraid and fled. He did not rely on human strength, but God gave him courage, since he believed in Him, to attack the enemies alone so that they feared him, and he gave peace to his people.

God uses the weakest of persons and the simplest of tools to carry out His plan and fulfill His good will. Here He delivers His people by an ox goad, just as He helped Samson, who killed a thousand men with the jawbone of an ass, and David faced Goliath with a sling and a stone, and He even used simple apostles to spread the Gospel in the whole world. God works through all for the glory of His name and the salvation of those who love Him. So do not fear your weakness, but come forward with confidence to serve God and live with Him.
Deborah and Barak

entries.section: (1) The agreement of Deborah and Barak

paragraphs.text: The end of the previous chapter told us about another judge, Shamgar the son of Anath, but at the beginning of this chapter it returns to tell us about Ehud the son of Gera, mentioned before Shamgar. The explanation of this is that both judges were contemporaries, each judging a certain region other than the region of the other, and that Shamgar died before Ehud. So after the death of Ehud the children of Israel returned to their evils, as was their habit after the death of the judge.

entries.section: (1) The agreement of Deborah and Barak

paragraphs.text: The Lord sold them: the Lord delivered them into the hand of their enemies.

Harosheth of the Gentiles: a mixture of nations, and the town was so called because many nations lived in it (Map 11). The Lord delivered them into the hand of another pagan king, Jabin king of the Canaanites, who dwelt in the capital of his kingdom, Hazor, in the north of Palestine (Joshua had captured it, but the Canaanites returned and recovered it). This Jabin is not the King Jabin who lived in the days of Joshua (Josh 11). The commander of his army, "Sisera", was encamped with his soldiers in the city of "Harosheth of the Gentiles."

entries.section: (1) The agreement of Deborah and Barak

paragraphs.text: This king was cruel and merciless, and he treated the children of Israel with violence and harshness for twenty years, and his army was equipped with nine hundred chariots of iron, which frightened the children of Israel from making any attempt to stand against him. Perhaps Sisera was taking revenge for the first defeat of the Canaanites at the hand of Joshua (Josh 11).

entries.section: (1) The agreement of Deborah and Barak

paragraphs.text: Deborah: the meaning of her name is bee, and indeed she was active like a bee.

The judge of the people at that time was a prophetess, and she was the wife of a man named Lapidoth. Her being a prophetess means that she received spiritual messages from God with which she taught the people, in addition to her knowledge of the Law and her judging the people by it.

entries.section: (1) The agreement of Deborah and Barak

paragraphs.text: Ramah: the intended city is Ramah, belonging to the tribe of Benjamin, which is 8 km from Jerusalem. Bethel: it lies halfway between Jerusalem and Nablus (Map 11). Came up: Deborah used to sit in a high place, so they would go up to her.

Deborah the judge lived in a house under a palm tree named after her, and she used to sit outside it to receive those of the people who came to her so that she might judge between them. The location of her dwelling was in the mountainous land that was the portion of the tribe of Ephraim in the middle of Palestine. The palm tree and the house were in this land which lies between Ramah and Bethel.

The palm tree under which the prophetess Deborah sat to judge was called the palm tree of Deborah, in perpetuation of her memory. So also we name churches after the saints in remembrance of their lives, their faith and their service to the Lord.

entries.section: (1) The agreement of Deborah and Barak

paragraphs.text: Kedesh-naphtali: there are many cities named Kedesh, and this Kedesh lies in the tribe of Naphtali (Map 12). Hath not the Lord God of Israel commanded: that is, the Lord commanded...
Go toward: advance quietly and slowly, then attack the Canaanites.
Mount Tabor: it is now Jebel et-Tur and lies about 9 km southeast of Nazareth.
Of the children of Naphtali and of the children of Zebulun: the two tribes were neighbors and near the city of Hazor in which the king of Canaan lived, so it was easy for them to gather for war.

God sent a message to the prophetess Deborah to summon a man named "Barak the son of Abinoam" from the city of Kedesh, and she informed him that the Lord had commanded him to go toward Mount Tabor and to take with him ten thousand men (because the Lord knows that the war requires this number). And He specified the two tribes from which he was to draw this number, the tribes of Naphtali and Zebulun, because the portions of the two tribes lie near the center of residence of their enemies.

entries.section: (1) The agreement of Deborah and Barak

paragraphs.text: The river Kishon: a river that springs from Mount Tabor, passes through the plain of Acre and empties near Haifa, and on its bank Elijah the prophet killed the priests of Baal (1 Kgs 18:40). I will draw unto thee: God allows Sisera to rush forward to attack the children of Israel, so Barak defeats him and many of them are drowned in the river Kishon.

The Lord prompts Sisera to move with his armies toward the army of Barak to face him and fight him, so he heads to the broad place where the river Kishon flows, and the Lord breaks Sisera and many of his soldiers are drowned in the river, and Barak defeats him.

entries.section: (1) The agreement of Deborah and Barak

paragraphs.text: Barak insisted that the prophetess Deborah accompany him in his battle, for he esteems her spiritual standing and with her accompanying him he trusts that God will help him, and also that she may advise him of the things he should do as he fights Sisera, and also so that his men may be encouraged by her presence among them.

entries.section: (1) The agreement of Deborah and Barak

paragraphs.text: Deborah informed him of her readiness to go with him to encourage him, but she told him that her accompanying him deprives him of the full glory of the victory, which may be ascribed to her. At the same time she prophesied that the one who would decide the battle (by killing Sisera) would be a woman, Jael, as will come in (v. 21). Barak did not mind to whom the glory would go, and Deborah did not mind the hardship of the journey, so she went out to accompany him in the battle.

God rejoiced in the cooperation of Deborah and Barak. How beautiful it is to cooperate with those around you to achieve the needed success, and not to mind if the glory is ascribed to you, but rather to wish that it be ascribed to others, so that you keep your humility and the devil does not fight you with praise.

Barak called both tribes, Zebulun and Naphtali, for he himself was of the tribe of Naphtali, while Zebulun was the tribe neighboring it in the land. So the men of war came to him from the two tribes, and their number was ten thousand as the Lord had commanded him, and they all went up to Mount Tabor, next to the city of Kedesh in Galilee, and the prophetess Deborah accompanied them, whose going up with them was a strong factor in raising their morale and encouraging them.

Deborah went up with them. How great is the lesson we take from the conduct of this woman of great heart, for she did not carry within her a spirit of pride and domination but a spirit of love and gentleness; she did not issue commands with grandeur and arrogance but took part with support and encouragement; she did not plead her womanhood, and perhaps her advanced age, but went before the men, filling them with enthusiasm, strength and blessing.
Heber the Kenite: he was of the children of Hobab, the father-in-law of Moses.
The children of Hobab: a part of the Kenites.
Kedesh: a city in Galilee.

We learned earlier in (ch. 1:16) that the Kenites pitched their tents in the wilderness of Judah. And here the inspired writer mentions that Heber the Kenite separated from them, perhaps because of the scarcity of pasture and the fewness of springs of water, and went with his tents until he reached the oak trees in one of the outskirts of Zaanaim in the middle of Naphtali by the city of Kedesh. The place where Heber settled was near the battlefield where the fight between Barak and Sisera would take place.
Mount Tabor: a mountain in the land of Galilee.

The reconnaissance carried out by Sisera's men, whom he had spread throughout the land to report to him what was happening, brought word that Barak had gone up with his army to Mount Tabor in preparation for war.

Harosheth of the Gentiles: a town in the north of Palestine inhabited by a mixture of nations (Map 11). Sisera gathered his chariots and mustered an army from the region in which he was encamped, which lies between Harosheth of the Gentiles and the river Kishon, and prepared with them to fight the children of Israel under the leadership of Deborah and Barak.
Is not the Lord gone out before thee: it means that the Lord is going before you, leading your armies and achieving victory for you.

Deborah said to Barak, Up, and go down to meet Sisera, giving him the good news that God would deliver the Canaanites into his hand and he would defeat them on this day, assuring him that the Lord was going before him, leading his armies. Barak believed God's promise, so he did what Deborah called him to do and went down from Mount Tabor with his ten thousand men.

The Lord fulfilled His promise to Barak, spoken by the prophetess Deborah, that he would defeat Sisera. May we cling to the Lord's true promises and believe with complete faith everything He promised His beloved ones, He who said "I will not leave you comfortless", "Lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world", "I will never leave you nor forsake you", "In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world", Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest."

Let us take these promises as provision for the road, walking in it with assurance of the Lord's presence with us at all times, upholding our steps and raising us from our stumblings and leading us to a happy eternal life.

Here divine providence intervened, and Sisera was thrown into confusion and was troubled by the strength and courage of Barak and his men, who plied their swords among Sisera's soldiers and killed many of them. Sisera's fear increased, so he got down from his chariot to avoid being recognized by Barak and his soldiers and in order to be able to flee faster than he could if he stayed in his chariot, and to be able to hide behind the mountains or in the forests among the trees.

Sisera's army drew back and fled before Barak and his army, and Barak followed them and pursued them to Harosheth of the Gentiles, where their main camp and the headquarters of their commander Sisera were, and they were all killed by the sword of Barak and his men, and not one of them was left alive.

Sisera, in the state of terror and confusion that had seized him, decided to flee to the tents of Heber the Kenite that were near the battlefield, and took refuge in the tent of Jael, the wife of Heber, thinking that he would be safe, for it would not occur to his pursuers that he had taken refuge with a woman.
Jael was in the tent alone, perhaps because her husband was busy with his work, and it was the right of a woman to receive as a guest one who was in distress so as to rescue him and help him.

Jael heard someone running toward her tent, so she went out and saw that it was Sisera, the commander of the Canaanite army, between whom and the clan of her husband there was peace. She welcomed him to receive him in her tent, and he went in to her, very tired from running in addition to his severe psychological exhaustion because of his defeat, so she arranged a place for him to sleep and covered him with a mantle so that he could rest and sleep.
A bottle of milk: the bottle is a skin bag in which milk is placed and ferments, which helped Sisera to fall into a deep sleep when he drank it.
He asked her to give him water to drink, so she opened the skin of milk and he drank from it, and when he had finished she covered him again with the mantle.

After Sisera felt secure with Jael, and this was by God's arrangement, he asked her to stand at the door of the tent, so that if she saw one of his pursuers and he asked her whether there was a man with her, she would answer no, and he would be ashamed to go in to search the tent because she was alone in it. This shows that he was still anxious and afraid that his enemies would overtake him.
A nail: a wooden stake pointed at its end, fixed in the ground and used to tie the ropes of the tent when it is pitched.
A hammer: a hand tool resembling a mallet, used to drive the nail into the ground.
Went softly unto him: walked toward him quietly.
Temples: the cheek.

While Sisera was deep in his sleep, Jael took the pointed tent nail in one hand and the hammer in the other and walked quietly toward Sisera, and she placed the nail on Sisera's temple and struck it with the hammer, and it pierced Sisera's head until it reached the ground and fastened his head to the ground, and because he was deep in sleep he did not wake to resist her, and he died.

Although the clan of the Kenites was at peace with Jabin king of Canaan, Jael and her husband were at the same time on strong terms with the children of Israel, for they lived next to the tribe of Judah. And Jethro, the father-in-law of Moses, was of the Kenites, so there was a strong tie and love between the people of God and the Kenites. When the Kenites saw the injustice and enslavement of the children of Israel by Jabin for many years, they were troubled by him and sympathized with their Jewish brethren, and this sympathy increased in the heart of Jael by the grace of God, so she became opposed to the injustice of the Canaanites, whom Sisera, the commander of their armies, represented, and her faith in the goodness of the children of Israel increased when God strengthened His people and they defeated Sisera, so she moved to help them and to kill the commander of the unjust enemy armies.

Do not exalt yourself or boast of your strength, however great, because it is God who gave it to you, and do not wrong others lest God take away your strength and humble you before others until you repent and return to Him. For God gave you your gifts and abilities so that you might thank Him and glorify Him and use them to bring happiness to those around you.
The song of Deborah and Barak

The Lord had delivered His people from the tyranny of the Chaldeans and their king Jabin by the hands of Deborah and Barak. So the two set out praising the Lord and singing the song of victory. This reminds us of the singing of Miriam, the sister of Aaron, after the deliverance from the slavery of the Egyptians. Thanking God is a necessary thing for the spiritual person, but sadly many ask, and after they obtain what they ask for, neglect thanksgiving.

For that the leaders took the lead: glorify the Lord for raising up leaders who achieved deliverance for the people. For that the people offered themselves willingly: glorify the Lord who called thousands to fight for His people, and they answered His call. Deborah calls her people to glorify God for two things:
1- The commanders of the army by whom the victory was won under the leadership of Barak.
2- The soldiers of the children of Israel who fought and conquered.
And we learn here to encourage everyone, for Deborah encourages the commanders and the soldiers and does not ascribe the glory to herself.
A call to the kings and great men of the pagan peoples, who often showed hostility and stirred up wars against the people of God, to look and know how God gives victory to His people.

I am Deborah, and the Lord brought about that great victory by my hand, therefore I sing to Him, rejoicing in the victory and in His great work with me and with my people. I do not sing with the tongue only, but with the pipe and instruments of music, as an expression of my great joy at the victory.
Seir: the land of Edom, the descendants of Esau, which lies in the northeast of the wilderness of Sinai.
The earth trembled: it quaked.
The heavens dropped: rain came down from heaven.

Deborah reminds the people of God's former dealings with them when they crossed the wilderness at their exodus from Egypt, and how the Lord went out with His people to go around Edom (which is sometimes called the land of Seir) by a hard and wearisome road after the Edomites refused to let the people pass through their land (Num 20:22, 21:4). The matter of the earth trembling when the people passed was not mentioned before, but tradition preserved it until Deborah mentioned it in her song. The trembling of the earth was accompanied by the coming down of rain, and these phenomena took place by the Lord's arrangement as a declaration of His glory and a condemnation of the Edomites' defiance of His people.

Deborah also reminds them of what happened on the day the Law was given on Mount Sinai, when the mountains quaked at the awe and majesty of the glory of the Lord who was manifested on the mountain. This was mentioned in (Ex 19:18).

Thanking God and glorifying Him for His gifts to you gladdens your heart, confirms your faith in Him and drives you with enthusiasm to bear the various difficulties and responsibilities, so that you enjoy a surpassing divine work in you.

entries.section: (2) The judges rescue the people from humiliation

paragraphs.text: Shamgar the son of Anath: one of the judges of the children of Israel, a contemporary of Deborah and Barak, who struck six hundred men of the Philistines with a long staff like that used to prick an animal if it lagged in its walking.
The highways were unoccupied: the roads became empty.
By-ways: side roads that were not paved.

Because the enemies occupied the lands of the children of Israel in the days of Shamgar and Jael, chaos and thieves spread, and the main paved roads were full of highwaymen, and instead of traveling on them, travelers were forced to walk on unpaved roads to avoid falling into the hands of highwaymen, which lengthened the time of travel, besides the hardship and weariness the travelers suffered.

entries.section: (2) The judges rescue the people from humiliation

paragraphs.text: The rulers of Israel were unable to deliver their people from the oppression of the enemies and their humiliation of the children of Israel until the Lord raised me up and urged me to work to rescue my people. And Deborah's leadership of the people was not domination but care and motherhood toward her people, so she was like a spiritual mother to them.

entries.section: (2) The judges rescue the people from humiliation

paragraphs.text: They chose new gods: the people forsook their true God and chose to worship new gods, newly invented and strange, which their fathers had not known before.
Then was war in the gates: the enemies attacked the gates of the children of Israel.
A shield: a piece of wood covered with leather which the warrior carries to protect himself from arrows.

All the disgrace and humiliation that came upon the people was caused by their forsaking the worship of the living God and choosing new, strange gods which their fathers had not known. And the result of their betrayal of the Lord was that He forsook them and allowed their enemies to lie in wait for them at the gates of their cities and besiege them, so as not to let them pass through them.

And among the signs of the humiliation of the people of God by their enemies was that they forbade them to bear arms, by taking their weapons from them, so none of the men able to fight had military equipment such as shields and spears, and his saying forty thousand is an estimated number for the people in this region.

entries.section: (2) The judges rescue the people from humiliation

paragraphs.text: My heart's love and my thanks I direct to the judges of Israel whom God chose from the people, who accepted the task they were assigned and rose to work in the midst of difficult circumstances. And we, the people of the Lord, must thank Him and glorify Him because it is He who prepared these leaders for us and strengthened them with His help and support.

entries.section: (2) The judges rescue the people from humiliation

paragraphs.text: She asses: the plural of she-ass, the female donkey.
Ashen (al-sahr): the plural of "ashar", a dusty color or a red tinged with white.
Rugs (al-tanafis): the plural of "tinfisa", a precious rug.

Deborah calls the rich, whom she symbolized as those who ride on red asses (a rare kind of donkey that none but the rich can afford to own), and whom she also symbolized as those who sit on precious carpets; she called them and the poor alike, who walk on their feet to move from place to place because they do not own she-asses to ride, she called everyone to praise the Lord and glorify Him.
The leader has importance in achieving success and joining people to God. So be faithful in bearing your responsibilities toward those around you and guiding them in the way of God.

entries.section: (2) The judges rescue the people from humiliation

paragraphs.text: Those who divide the spoil between the watering troughs: those who divide the spoils into portions and bring them to the water troughs to drink.
The people of the Lord went down to the gates: after the victory was achieved, the people were able to return to sit at the gates of the city for judgment, recreation or counsel.

She also calls those who divide the spoils of war into portions after their victory under the leadership of the judges, each one taking his portion and bringing it to the water troughs to drink. The animals were an important part of the spoils of war. These sing at the troughs, glorifying the Lord for His justice in vindicating His people and vindicating their rulers and restoring their rights seized from the hand of their enemies. For after the great victory the Lord granted to His people, the people were able to sit at the gates of the city as they used to before, for counsel and conversation, and to go out and come in through them with a freedom of which they had been deprived during the enemies' siege. And by this security prevailed and the chaos and injustice that were in the days of the occupation came to an end.

entries.section: (2) The judges rescue the people from humiliation

paragraphs.text: Deborah addresses herself saying: Rise up and awake to sing the song of victory, for the time of sorrow has passed and the time of joy has come. Then she addresses Barak saying: Arise to take the captives and the spoils from the enemy over whom the Lord gave you victory.

entries.section: (2) The judges rescue the people from humiliation

paragraphs.text: The one that remaineth (the fugitive): the one of the children of Israel who fled in the days of the occupation.
The fugitive had dominion over the nobles of the people: the children of Israel who were formerly fleeing before their enemies today have dominion over them and over their great men.
The children of Israel who were formerly fleeing before their enemies have today become their masters and have dominion over them and over the great men of the Canaanite people.
Then Deborah recalls the great work of the Lord with her and with Barak, who sings with her the same song, in that the Lord gave them authority over the mighty enemies.

entries.section: (3) Praise of the tribes that took part in the war

paragraphs.text: Out of Ephraim: from the tribe of Ephraim, which includes large numbers of soldiers.
Whose root was against Amalek (their dwelling among Amalek): their dwelling among the Amalekites, who are among the oldest peoples of the region.
Benjamin: the intended tribe is Benjamin, one of the tribes of Israel. Although their number was small, they were strong.

Machir: the son of Manasseh (that is, the grandson of Joseph), from whom came army commanders, and they dwelt west of the Jordan. They that handle the pen of the writer (holding the commander's staff): bearers of the commander's scepter, which indicates their leadership of the army, and they used to count the soldiers.

From this verse to (v. 18) Deborah praises some of the tribes of the children of Israel who answered the call and took part in the war against the Canaanites, and she blames some other tribes that were slack about the war and the tribes dwelling far from the field of war for their negligence.

She begins with the tribe of Ephraim, who hastened to go out to the war despite the danger of leaving their land, which was surrounded by the Amalekites. And the tribe of Benjamin followed it to join the ranks of the fighters. Then she praises the descendants of Machir the son of Manasseh, who also went out to the war with their chiefs. And it is mentioned that the tribe of Zebulun had the leading position in making the plans and moving the army, and Barak had called the tribes of Zebulun and Naphtali to take part with him in the war and gave it the leadership (ch. 4:10).

entries.section: (3) Praise of the tribes that took part in the war

paragraphs.text: The divisions: branches of the Jordan River that run in the land of Reuben.
Great thoughts of heart (great searchings of heart): many discussions and consultations.

The princes of Issachar answered Deborah's call to war, and they did not content themselves with sending soldiers but took part in the war themselves. And as they supported her, they also supported Barak, her partner in declaring and leading the war, and showed him all loyalty, so they followed him in his going down to the plain, where they fought the battle under his leadership. As for Reuben, he let down his brothers, for he wasted time in discussions and deliberations, sitting by the streams of the rivers, over whether to go out to the war or not to go out, and it ended with a decision not to take part with his brothers in the war. And this deserves God's condemnation, spoken by Deborah.

entries.section: (3) Praise of the tribes that took part in the war

paragraphs.text: Why abodest thou among the sheepfolds, to hear the bleatings of the flocks: why did you prefer to stay among the folds of your sheep and hear the whistling of the shepherds to their sheep to lead them to drink, instead of going out to the war. For the divisions of Reuben there were great searchings (inquiries) of heart: by the tributaries of the Jordan River in the land of Reuben the Reubenites sat deliberating whether they should go out to the war to help their brothers or not.

The tribe of Reuben preferred to stay beside the folds of its sheep, hearing the whistling of the shepherds to the sheep, rather than listening to the sound of the trumpet of battle. Therefore Deborah mocks them, describing their decisions, which sprang from their own thinking, as great decisions, in mockery and derision, for they were of course very wrong decisions, since they preferred laziness and slackness to sharing the war with their brothers.

entries.section: (3) Praise of the tribes that took part in the war

paragraphs.text: Abode in his breaches (in his ports): the land of Asher was next to the sea, and he continued to dwell in its harbors without moving to take part in the war. Breaches = the plural of "farda", that is, harbor. (Farda: harbor.)

Gilead, that is, the sons of Manasseh who lived east of the Jordan, failed in their duty and chose to remain dwelling in their land and not take part in the war as their brothers, the sons of Machir the son of Manasseh, who lived west of the Jordan, took part. So also did the tribe of Dan, which was content to sit in its land next to the Mediterranean beside the ships and did not hasten to help its brothers who were fighting. And the position of Asher was like that of Dan, for it remained at rest in its portion of the land on the seacoast and in its harbors.

entries.section: (3) Praise of the tribes that took part in the war

paragraphs.text: High places (heights): the plural of "rabiya", a raised place, and there were heights in the field of battle.

Deborah had already praised the tribe of Zebulun in her song, and here she adds to the praise of it as evidence of its sacrifices and its disregard of any hardships and its giving of itself as a ransom for its people and its devotion to them. And the tribe of Naphtali took part with it with the same zeal and work, and did not mind any hardships in climbing the high places of Mount Tabor in the field of battle and being exposed thereby to the arrows of the enemy encamped there, but they stormed all the places, giving themselves as a ransom for their brothers.

We see here Deborah's concern to praise those who took part in the war, for the leader must praise those who labored with him and encourage them, and reproach the slack to encourage them to take part the next times.

Take care to share your brothers' afflictions, and labor and give as for yourself, because you are a member with them in one body, which is the Church, and God sees your labor and rewards you for it, in addition to your brothers' love for you.

Taanach: a city five miles southeast of Megiddo, in the portion of Manasseh west of the Jordan River (Map 10). The waters of Megiddo: a branch of the river Kishon mentioned in (ch. 4:7). Some other pagan kings joined the king of Canaan and allied with him in his war against the children of Israel, so they came to the city of Taanach, where their armies attacked the Israelites, thinking that they would defeat the people of the Lord and obtain spoils and release the Israelite captives for a ransom of silver, but they were defeated and obtained neither captives nor silver.
Their courses: their paths.

God supported His people, for He made the stars of heaven support the children of Israel in their victory over their enemies, and they sent lightnings that troubled them and then thick clouds that covered the sky with a near-darkness, which increased the enemies' confusion. And the moon too may have had an effect on the river Kishon in increasing the tide and ebb, which helped the enemies to drown.
That ancient river (the river of events): the river Kishon, in which important events took place over the course of history.

A severe tide and ebb occurred in the river Kishon, and the flooding of the tide waters helped the enemies to drown. Then Deborah calls the fighters to trample their enemies with strength because God is with them.
Hoofs (heels): heels.
Driving: the leading of horses.

Sisera's soldiers, in their flight before the armies of the children of Israel, were driving their horses hard, so the horses ran swiftly and their feet struck the ground hard. These represent the one who relies on his military strength and not on God: he is defeated and withdraws fleeing from the war, and the vanity of his strength appears.
Meroz: a city near the valley of Jezreel in Galilee, that is, the north of the land of the Jews, and it has now vanished from existence.

The people of the city of Meroz did not come to the help of the people of the Lord; they took a passive position when they saw Sisera fleeing, and did not seize him and hand him over to the people of the children of Israel as Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, did. It is a city that deserves a curse because they did not hasten to support the people of the Lord when they were fighting the mighty ones of Canaan, so the angel of the Lord curses them, that is, the one commissioned by God to help them in the war.

God loves you and is ready to support you in all your battles against the devil, and He moves the events of life, and even nature, to support you. So do not fear the harshness of the enemies, because your God is stronger than they, and persevere in your striving so that you may be victorious in the end.
In contrast to the curse that the city of Meroz deserves, Jael deserves every blessing above all women as a reward for the heroic courage she showed.

Deborah tells the details of what Jael did when she killed Sisera, and she added here a new detail not mentioned in the previous chapter, which is that she gave him butter to eat, not milk only, and presented it in an excellent bowl set aside for serving food to guests and the great men of the people.
Smote through: broke.
The workmen's hammer: it is the mallet, that is, the hammer of the workmen, and it is so called because the workmen or laborers drive the nails with it when they pitch the tent.
Jael took hold of the nail in one hand and the hammer in her right hand and struck Sisera's head, so she crushed it and pierced his temple.

Sisera fell down from exhaustion, lying before Jael, who was standing before him in his service, and he had hardly taken the milk when he slept from the extremity of exhaustion, and in the place where he lay down to rest he fell dead.
When anxiety seized the mother of Sisera about her son, she began to look out of the window, crying out and asking why the return of his chariots was delayed.

The women attached to her heard her, and one of them answered her, one of her relatives or friends and the wisest and most experienced of them, and indeed the mother of Sisera herself answered her own questions, and her answer agreed with what her friend had said to her.

Their answers were an expression of what they hoped for of the victory of Sisera's army, which was only dreams that were not fulfilled, for they were expecting the following to be happening as an explanation of the delay:
Sisera's soldiers were dividing the spoils among themselves.
The portion of each soldier would be a girl or two whom he would take as maidservants.
Sisera's portion would be the finest garments made in the most beautiful colors.

And the portion of Sisera's mother would be garments embroidered with beautiful threads and cloths dyed in wonderful colors on both sides, some of which she would wrap around her neck to adorn it and increase her beauty; that is, she believed that the reason for his delay was the abundance of spoils he had taken and was dividing among the soldiers.

As Sisera and all his men perished, so the enemies of the Lord and the enemies of His people perish, while His beloved ones are exalted and their light shines, and all the darkness of the powers of darkness is dispelled before them, as the sun appears and all the clouds are dispelled before it.

As happens in every cycle, as we said earlier at the beginning of the third chapter, which begins with the people's disobedience, then discipline from the Lord, then deliverance, so it is here also: when the deliverance from the enemy was accomplished by the hand of Deborah and Barak, the people lived a period of stability and quiet lasting forty years.
Do not be occupied with daydreams like the mother of Sisera, but be a striver in the way of God and seek spiritual things and not material things, and you will be satisfied with the blessings of God.
The choosing of Gideon

entries.section: (1) The Midianites humiliate the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: In this chapter and the two following chapters the story is repeated of the people of God turning away from Him, then the Midianites humiliating them and their crying out to God, so He sent them Gideon as judge and deliverer.
