So it is with a person: when God gives him rest, it is natural for him to thank Him, but if he grows slack in his life with God, he is exposed to falling into the sin that humbles him.

Midian: they are the descendants of Keturah, the wife of Abraham, and they lived east of the Gulf of Aqaba and north of it as far as the Dead Sea and east of the Jordan River, and the father-in-law of Moses was of them. They cooperated with the Moabites against the children of Israel in the days of Balaam the son of Beor, but Moses defeated them and destroyed them.

The children of Israel did evil by turning away from the law of the Lord and from His worship to the worship of idols, so the Lord allowed them to be delivered into the hand of Midian for discipline for a period of seven years.

entries.section: (1) The Midianites humiliate the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: The Midianites oppressed Israel and tightened their grip upon them harshly. Because of the Midianites' attacks upon them, they dug caves for themselves in the mountains to take refuge in during the Midianite raids, and they also dug dens in the mountains in which to hide their crops and livestock lest the Midianites seize them, and they built strongholds to shelter in.

entries.section: (1) The Midianites humiliate the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: The Amalekites: those living in the wilderness of Sinai, whom Moses fought (Ex 17). The children of the east: those living east of the Jordan and east of the Red Sea, among them the Moabites and the sons of Ammon. The Amalekites and the children of the east joined in plundering the children of Israel, attacking them and going up to the mountains where the children of Israel hid their crops and made their caves and dens, in order to seize those crops, and even coming down to them in the plains and valleys, uprooting and destroying the crops, ruining everything in their path from the Jordan River in the east to Gaza in the far west of the land, and plundering even the cattle, sheep and donkeys, leaving nothing good for the subdued people to live on.

entries.section: (1) The Midianites humiliate the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: They did not attack the land of Israel with men only, but brought their cattle with them to graze in the fields of the children of Israel, and also brought their tents to settle in their lands. They came in very great numbers, they and their camels, which devoured the plants as they pleased, so ruin came upon the land after they had exhausted all its good things.

entries.section: (1) The Midianites humiliate the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: Thus disgrace and humiliation came upon the people of Israel because of the oppression of those pagan peoples, and when the matter became very hard for them, they cried out to the Lord, repenting of having left Him and expressing the depth of their need for His mercy and help.

Examine yourself, lest your afflictions be because of your distance from God and His forsaking you, so that the devil gains dominion over you and troubles you. And if you discover that, return quickly to Him in repentance, for He is a tender Father who will not leave you.

entries.section: (2) A prophet rebukes the people of God

paragraphs.text: The Lord, who always awaits the return of His children to Him in repentance and the seeking of deliverance, answers them and does not leave them in their perplexity, but sent a prophet to reveal to them the cause of their humiliation, reminding them of His merciful works toward them, which they had met with ingratitude and disobedience. Therefore He delivers them to affliction and discipline so that they may come to themselves and know the measure of their rebellion, their disobedience and their offense against the Lord, and so resolve to repent and return to Him.

The prophet begins his speech by stressing that the words he is about to say to them are a message from God. He reminds them that He is the Lord who delivered them from slavery in Egypt and brought them out from there, and rescued them from the Egyptians and from all their oppressions, and led them to the new land He gave them, together with the accompanying miracles of the parting of the Red Sea by the hand of Moses and the victories they achieved with the Lord's help over the original inhabitants of the land and their driving out before them. Perhaps this prophet was Phinehas the son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron the priest.

entries.section: (2) A prophet rebukes the people of God

paragraphs.text: The prophet reminded them that God had reassured them so that they would not fear the pagans and their gods, however strong they appeared, after they had seen God's victories by their hands, and sadly they mingled with the pagans and worshiped their gods, and the pagans humiliated them.

Remember God's former works with you so that you may be reassured and trust in God and keep away from everything. Thank Him every day, and your confidence in yourself and your steadfastness in Him will increase.
Ophrah: it lies next to Bethel in the western portion of the tribe of Manasseh.

Gideon was sitting under a tree in his town of Ophrah, where his clan lived, the clan of the Abiezrites, one of the clans of the tribe of Manasseh. The Lord sent an angel to him to commission him to work at delivering the children of Israel from the slavery of the Midianites. This Gideon was the son of Joash, who was called the Abiezrite because he was of the clan of Abiezer. Gideon was beating wheat with a staff to get the grain out of the ears, and he was doing that inside the winepress so as not to attract the attention of the Midianites, who were watching the Jews to rob them of their good things.

The angel appeared to Gideon and began with a greeting, praying that the Lord would help him in the great work with which He would commission him, praising him as the strong man of resolve, to encourage him to undertake the task that would be entrusted to him.

Gideon replies and asks the angel with the freedom of love, inquiring that if God is with the children of Israel, why does His people not enjoy the Lord's protection, and why does the Lord not surround them with His care as He did with the previous generations and brought them out of the land of Egypt and rescued them from slavery. But now the Lord is angry with them and has delivered them to their enemies the Midianites, who have gained dominion over them.

Here it appears from the inspired text, and from the original word that is translated here as the Lord, which in the Hebrew text is "Yahweh", that the appearance of the Lord in the form of a man was one of the manifestations of the hypostasis of the Son. And the Lord said to him that by this holy zeal of his He would work with him and deliver Israel by his hand. So let him not hesitate, for God sent him and consequently it is He who will give him the victory.

Gideon mentions that he is a simple person belonging to a humble clan among the clans of Manasseh, and that he is the youngest among his brothers, so how, being an ordinary man, neither a chief nor a leader among his people, would he be able to gather fighters from the people around him and lead them in a war of liberation. Although he was distinguished by courage, he was humble, and humility is an essential condition for God to work with power in a person.

The Lord gives him the decisive answer to his question, which is that it is enough for him that He will be with him, for if the Lord is with a person no power can stand before him. And He assured him that he would defeat the Midianites and should not fear their great number, for he would destroy them as if he were destroying one man only.

Do not be troubled by your weakness and do not compare yourself with those who are stronger than you in any capabilities, because God is with you, and as long as God is with you, you will be able to overcome the wars of Satan and achieve every success.

The situation was perplexing for Gideon, for he knew perfectly well that he had none of the elements of strength in war, such as military equipment, organization of fighters and the wisdom of military leaders, while the Lord urged him to do the work. Therefore he asked a sign of the Lord to remove his doubts and perplexity. This shows that, besides his courage and humility, he had faith in the power of God able to work in him, but he needed signs to increase and confirm his faith.

Gideon asked the Lord not to depart from his place until he came to Him with an offering of food. Gideon's thought was that if He ate of it he would know that He was an ordinary man, and if some divine miracle happened he would realize that He was the Lord. Here God is longsuffering with human weakness, and promised him that He would remain until he returned with his offering. Here appears Gideon's simplicity, which gave him freedom before God, so he spoke with Him as a man speaks with his friend, just as Moses the prophet used to speak with God, and God's humility and fatherhood made Him accept Gideon's words and request and wait for him until he came with an offering to confirm his faith by seeing God.

God loves you and rejoices in your friendship with Him, so speak with Him as a son with his father and as a bride with her bridegroom... Express your feelings to Him, for He rejoices in your longings and upholds you and grants you an inexpressible joy.
Ephah: 23 liters.

Gideon went into his house and killed a kid of the goats and cooked it, and made unleavened cakes of flour in a large quantity sufficient for ten persons. He prepared this abundant amount to honor the guest. And he put the meat in a basket and the broth in a pot and went out to present it to the wondrous guest.

The Lord asked him to lay the meat and the unleavened cakes upon the rock and to pour out the broth over them, to confirm the miracle that was about to take place. Gideon obeyed and did as the Lord commanded him, and by this the rock becomes like an altar on which this offering is presented to God.

The Lord put forth the staff, which travelers usually carry, and touched the offering with its end, and fire came out of the rock and consumed the offering, despite the liquids that had been poured over the offering and had drenched it, which would normally extinguish the fire. Then the Lord suddenly vanished from his sight.

When Gideon saw the fire come out of the rock and the disappearance of the person who had spoken to him, he realized that he was the angel of the Lord or God Himself, so he was afraid and began to pray, asking mercy from the Lord, because he believed that a man dies if he sees the Lord, as the Lord had declared before to Moses, that man shall not see Him and live (Ex 33:20).

God spoke to Gideon a second time, either by a voice or by the appearance of an angel to him or in some other way, and reassured him, giving him the peace that carries the meaning of security and rest, removing all fear from him, because it is He who qualifies him to see Him without dying.
Jehovah (Yahweh): the name of God, and its meaning is God is, or He who is.
Shalom: peace.

Gideon was reassured and expressed his thanks to God, so he built an altar in the very place where the conversation between him and the Lord took place, that is, beside the terebinth, and called the altar "The Lord is peace" in remembrance of the peace the Lord gave him. And the altar still stands to this day, that is, to the day this book was written, in the city of the Abiezrites, which is Ophrah.

It should be noted that Gideon was not of the tribe of Levi, so he had no right to offer sacrifices according to the Law, and he did not offer them in the tabernacle of meeting in Shiloh. But the offering of the sacrifice here is an exceptional matter, the purpose of which is to declare allegiance to God and His worship, and not to Baal, but to despise the worship of idols by using the wood of the grove to kindle the fire for offering the sacrifice (vv. 25, 26).

entries.section: (5) The throwing down of the altar of Baal

paragraphs.text: Baal: a famous pagan god among the Moabites.
Grove (pillar): a wooden pillar set up for the pagan gods.

God commanded Gideon to take the bullock that his father owned and another bullock seven years old and to throw down with them the altar of Baal and its grove that stood beside it, that is, to remove the worship of idols into which his father and his clan had fallen, and so they provoked God, and He allowed the Midianites to humiliate them. And the second bullock was seven years old as a reminder to them that God feels their suffering during these seven years in which the Midianites humiliated them.

entries.section: (5) The throwing down of the altar of Baal

paragraphs.text: Likewise the Lord asked him to build an altar to the Lord, the true God, in a high and visible place as a declaration of the glory of the Lord, and that the building be orderly, to befit the dignity of the Lord. Then He commanded him to offer the second bullock as a burnt offering to the Lord, taking the wood of the grove which he had previously cut down (v. 25) as fuel on the altar of the Lord.

entries.section: (5) The throwing down of the altar of Baal

paragraphs.text: Since he was afraid of his brothers and relatives and the people of the city, he decided to carry out secretly at night what the Lord had asked of him, so that no one would obstruct his way. And he took ten men of his servants to help in throwing down the altar of Baal, cutting down the grove, building the new altar for the Lord and offering the burnt offering.

Gideon's completing the work by night is a kind of wisdom, so that the work would not be hindered, but it was not out of fear for his life, because they would know it in the morning and could then kill him if God allowed them to. It appears from this that Gideon lived among his family who worshiped idols, but he was not zealous for the worship of idols, as is shown by his immediate obedience to God and his clan's conclusion, when they saw the demolished altar, that it must have been by the hand of Gideon, because they knew his neglect of their pagan worship (v. 29). It should be noted that the offering of the burnt offering here was not on the altar that was in the tabernacle of meeting, and that exception was because of the appearing of God in this place, as happened with David in the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite (2 Sam 24:16, 25).

entries.section: (5) The throwing down of the altar of Baal

paragraphs.text: When the people of the city rose early, as was their custom, they were surprised to find the altar of Baal thrown down and the grove beside it cut down, and they were astonished at the building of a new altar in its place on which the sacrifice of the second bullock had been offered.

entries.section: (5) The throwing down of the altar of Baal

paragraphs.text: The people of the city began to ask, with astonishment and anger, who had committed this deed, wicked in their eyes, so they searched and inquired and finally learned that Gideon was the one who had done it.

entries.section: (5) The throwing down of the altar of Baal

paragraphs.text: Immediately they pronounced a swift sentence of death on Gideon, and asked Joash his father to hand him over to them at once so that they might carry out the death sentence on him, as a recompense for the offense he had committed in their eyes by throwing down the altar of Baal and cutting down the grove, which they considered an insult to their god and a defiance of their beliefs.

entries.section: (5) The throwing down of the altar of Baal

paragraphs.text: Joash rose to defend what his son had done, since he realized the inability of those false gods to defend themselves, and said to all who were gathered around him: Will you, human beings, contend for Baal, whom you consider a god, or will you save him from the hand of my son, who threw down his altar? If Baal is truly a god, let him defend himself. Then he threatened them that whoever tried to kill his son in defense of Baal, he and the people of his house would fight him at once.

entries.section: (5) The throwing down of the altar of Baal

paragraphs.text: Jerubbaal: that is, let Baal fight.

From that day Joash gave his son the title "he who fights Baal", saying that if Gideon had assaulted the dignity of Baal by throwing down his altar, let Baal avenge himself. He said that in mockery and contempt of him, because he was certain of Baal's inability to avenge himself on his son Gideon.

Be obedient to God however difficult His commandments appear and however contrary to the thoughts of those around you, and be sure that God will give you courage and support you in the face of other people's anger against you.

entries.section: (6) The gathering of soldiers and the two signs of the fleece

paragraphs.text: The valley of Jezreel: a valley in the middle of the land of Palestine extending from the Jordan River to the Mediterranean Sea at Mount Carmel, and because it lies in the middle of the land of Canaan many battles took place in it. The Amalekites and the children of the east joined the Midianites and gathered in the valley of Jezreel to attack the Jews.

entries.section: (6) The gathering of soldiers and the two signs of the fleece

paragraphs.text: The Spirit of the Lord came upon him (clothed him): the Spirit of God descended upon him.

Gideon was filled with strength and zeal to fight the Midianites when the Spirit of God came upon him, so he blew the trumpet to gather soldiers, and first his clan, the Abiezrites, gathered around him.

entries.section: (6) The gathering of soldiers and the two signs of the fleece

paragraphs.text: Gideon was encouraged by the swift change in his clan, which, after demanding his blood, had become the first to answer his call to gather for battle, so he sent messengers to other tribes, Asher, Zebulun and Naphtali, in addition to his own tribe, the tribe of Manasseh. He called these tribes because their dwelling was near him. It should be noted that the tribe of Asher had failed to take part in the war in the days of Deborah and Barak (ch. 5:17), but now it is zealous and joins Gideon in the war. So a person can learn from his failure and put right his state with God by repentance and take part in the spiritual striving, and so have victory over Satan.

entries.section: (6) The gathering of soldiers and the two signs of the fleece

paragraphs.text: The floor: the threshing floor, the place where the grain is gathered after its harvest.
Gideon asked a sign of the Lord to be sure that He would be with him in his war against the Midianites.

The sign Gideon asked for was that he would put a piece of wool on the floor, and if the dew fell in the morning on the piece of wool alone and wet it while the ground of the whole floor was dry, he would be sure by this that the deliverance of Israel would be by his hand. This was a second sign Gideon asked for, because he had first asked of the angel the acceptance of his offering as a sign (vv. 17-21).

entries.section: (6) The gathering of soldiers and the two signs of the fleece

paragraphs.text: A bowl: a vessel of clay.
Early the next day he went to the floor to see the result, and found the piece of wool wet with water, so he wrung it out and filled a medium-sized vessel with the water.

entries.section: (6) The gathering of soldiers and the two signs of the fleece

paragraphs.text: Gideon was not content with the first sign, so he asked the Lord for a second sign, the opposite of the first, so that he would find the piece of wool completely dry while the dew covered all the ground around it; and he besought the Lord not to be angry with him for repeating his requests.

entries.section: (6) The gathering of soldiers and the two signs of the fleece

paragraphs.text: The Lord answered Gideon and gave him what he wanted by a great miracle, for on the morning of the next day he found the piece of wool completely dry while the ground around it was covered with water.

Here appears God's longsuffering with His children who are weak in faith, for Gideon asked two signs with the fleece, in addition to the angel's acceptance of his offering. God does not hate the weak, but encourages them and upholds them, and even gives additional signs and encouragements, as we shall see in the next chapter.

Do not doubt because of your weakness, for God is ready to support you... Ask Him for all your needs and be earnest with Him because He is a tender Father. But be obedient to His commandments and you will find your rest.
The fight against the Midianites

entries.section: (1) The reducing of the number of soldiers

paragraphs.text: The well of Harod: a spring of water about 1.5 km southeast of Jezreel and northwest of Mount Gilead.

The hill of Moreh: the valley lying between Mount Gilboa (Gilead) on the south and Mount Tabor on the north, about 4 miles from the well of Harod (Map 12). Gideon made sure that the Lord stood by him in his war against the Midianites, so he gathered the men of his army and they made their camp at the well of Harod in readiness to face the enemies, while the camp of the Midianites was to the north of them at the hill of Moreh.

entries.section: (1) The reducing of the number of soldiers

paragraphs.text: God knew that His people might become proud if He gave them victory over the Midianites, and ascribe the victory to the greatness of their number, so He spoke to Gideon to reduce the number of soldiers with him, although they were far fewer than the number of the Midianites. This is a proof that strength is from God and that the fewness of His people's soldiers does not matter to Him.

entries.section: (1) The reducing of the number of soldiers

paragraphs.text: Mount Gilead: it lies in the valley of Jezreel west of the Jordan River, near the well of Harod. It is not the Mount Gilead which lies east of the Jordan River.

The Lord reminded Gideon of the law of war which He gave to Moses in the Book of Deuteronomy, which is that the leaders of the people proclaim among the soldiers that everyone who is fearful of the war should return to his house (Deut 20:5-8). So at Gideon's proclamation twenty-two thousand returned, and only ten thousand remained with him.

entries.section: (1) The reducing of the number of soldiers

paragraphs.text: I will try them: I will test them and prove them by what will happen to them.

Despite the smallness of the number that remained after Gideon's proclamation, as the previous verse relates, the Lord found that the number of ten thousand was still large and that they must be reduced. For this reason the Lord commanded Gideon to bring them down to the water, that is, the water of the well of Harod beside which they were encamped, to drink, and He would designate for him those whom he should take with him to the war and those whom he should not.

entries.section: (1) The reducing of the number of soldiers

paragraphs.text: Every one that lappeth of the water with his tongue, as a dog lappeth: that is, he drinks the water as a dog drinks, by sucking the water from the spring directly with his mouth or quickly with the palm of his hand.

The men went down to the water to drink, and the Lord commanded Gideon to watch how they drank: everyone who takes the water in his hand to his mouth to drink quickly he was to put on one side, and everyone who drinks the water from the spring with his mouth while kneeling, that is, who drinks quietly and gives himself a chance to wash and rest, he was to put on another side.

entries.section: (1) The reducing of the number of soldiers

paragraphs.text: The number of those who took the water in the palm to the mouth was only three hundred men, while the rest were of those who bowed down upon their knees to drink.

entries.section: (1) The reducing of the number of soldiers

paragraphs.text: After this sifting the Lord carried out among the men of war, He declared to Gideon that by the three hundred men who took the water in the palm to the mouth He would defeat the Midianites and deliver his people from them, and even deliver them into their hands so that they might carry out just judgment upon them, and that the others should return to their houses.

Kneeling on the knees to drink water directly with the mouth shows a lack of watchfulness and attention to what may happen before them, and takes longer than taking water by hand to the mouth, which gives the enemies a chance to attack with no readiness on the part of the one drinking in this way. But the one who takes the water by hand to the mouth does so in a shorter time, besides keeping his eyes directed forward, that is, toward the enemy, so he remains on his guard against him while he drinks.

entries.section: (1) The reducing of the number of soldiers

paragraphs.text: Victuals: food.

The three hundred men whom the Lord designated prepared themselves, taking their trumpets and the food they needed on their way, while Gideon sent the rest to their homes. Gideon and his men were in a place a little higher than the spot where the Midianites were encamped.

The standing of the three hundred men on the high place made it easy for them to see the very great numbers of the Midianites in the valley, so they felt their weakness and sought God, and by this the power of God that would give them victory appears.

God wants you to be always ready and watchful in your spiritual warfare with Satan, so that he does not seize the chance of your heedlessness and make you fall into sin. So be on guard and keep away from the sources of your sin, and fill your emptiness with constructive spiritual thoughts, and seek God's help, and you will secure your victory over your enemies.

God wanted to give Gideon a new sign to reassure him that He was with him and would help him achieve the victory, so He asked him on that night to go down to where the camp of the Midianites was in order to show him the new sign, and informed him that He would deliver the Midianites into his hand. The Lord said it in the past tense, "I have delivered it", to confirm that the matter must be accomplished.

To increase Gideon's assurance, God sent him with one of his faithful servants named "Phurah" to spy out the camp of the Midianites himself. Spying is a well-known thing in wars in order to learn the strength of the enemies, but God intended to show Gideon His power and His superiority over the enemies.

The armed men that were in the host: the soldiers prepared for war who were in the camp. The Lord had a purpose in Gideon's going down to the camp of the Midianites, which was that Gideon should hear a conversation going on among some of them, and the content of this conversation would encourage him more and reassure him of the achievement of the victory. The Lord knew what they would say and Gideon would hear, so that he would be more and more encouraged and not fear to face them. Gideon obeyed the Lord's command and went down, he and his servant, to the rear of the Midianite camp, without penetrating into their ranks so that they would not notice him.

God repeated what was mentioned in (ch. 6:5), likening the enemy army in its multitude to grasshoppers, and their camels, which were among the essentials of war in that time, to the sand of the sea in their multitude.

The new sign the Lord wanted to give Gideon to encourage him more was the content of a dream that one of the enemy soldiers had seen and related to one of his companions while Gideon was there listening to their conversation. The content of the dream was that he saw a loaf of barley bread rolling on the ground in the camp of the Midianites, and it struck their tents and threw them down and turned them upside down.

No sooner had the soldier finished telling his dream than his companion, by God's intervention, interpreted the dream to him: that the loaf of barley bread signifies the sword of Gideon, to whom the Lord gives strength and victory over the Midianites, so that he crushes their army. And the barley loaf is the weakest kind of bread and is the food of the poor; it resembles weak Gideon, but because God is with him he is able to defeat the many enemies.
Thank God for every encouragement He sends you and every grace you receive, and your enjoyment of it will increase, and God will pour out on you more mercies, so that you live assured and joyful.

When Gideon heard the dream and its interpretation, he was encouraged and became certain that God was with him, so he worshiped God in thanksgiving and returned to the camp of the children of Israel and roused them, saying: Arise, for the Lord has delivered the host of Midian into your hand. Here Gideon's humility appears, for he ascribes the victory to his soldiers, saying that the Midianites were delivered into your hand, in order to encourage them also.

God intervened at the last moment to remove the anxiety from Gideon's heart, that is, on the last night before he began the war. So be assured that God is near to you and will intervene at the right time to encourage you and give you victory over your enemies.

Gideon divided his army into three companies, spread over a wider area so as to make the enemies imagine that their numbers were greater than they really were, and commanded them that each soldier should carry a trumpet in his right hand to blow it at the time he would indicate to them, and in his other hand carry an empty pitcher with a lamp placed inside it.

Our reliance on the Lord in the steps we take does not mean not planning and organizing them. We must strive and arrange our affairs in the best possible way, and God completes and crowns this effort with blessing and success.
Gideon told them that he would be at the head of one of the three companies, and would advance to the edge of the camp occupied by the Midianites, and commanded them to do as they saw him do.

The plan was that when he blew the trumpets with his company, all the men of the other two companies should blow their trumpets while surrounding the camp and shout "For the Lord and for Gideon", that is, that the Lord would draw His sword, and the sword of Gideon His servant, against the enemies. As for the rest of the military plan which Gideon told his soldiers, it is mentioned in the following verses.

v. 19 The watch: the middle one: it is the second part of the night, which was divided into three parts, each of four hours, from six o'clock in the evening to six o'clock in the morning by our present reckoning. At midnight Gideon moved with his company, made up of a hundred soldiers, to the edge of the Midianite camp, and the Midianites were asleep and had assigned some soldiers to guard their camp. Gideon's company began to carry out the plan by blowing the trumpets and breaking the pitchers, throwing them hard on the ground, and at the same time showing the torches that they had been hiding inside them.
The sword of the Lord and of Gideon: that is, the Lord will unleash His sword and the sword of Gideon upon the enemies.

The other two companies imitated them, carrying out Gideon's orders when he told them that as they saw him do, so they should do, all crying out "The sword of the Lord and of Gideon." And they blew the trumpets and broke the pitchers and attacked the enemies, blowing the trumpets in their right hands with the lamps in their left hands, which greatly alarmed the enemies.

After they carried out the plan according to Gideon's instructions, they stood firm around the camp of the enemies, while these were terrified by the sounds of the trumpets and the sound made by the breaking of the pitchers in a single moment, and they were afraid of the fire of the torches, imagining that they were new weapons that would destroy them, so they fled before Gideon's soldiers, for the Lord cast terror into their hearts.

As the enemies were terrified by the sound of the trumpets and the breaking of the pitchers, so the soldiers of the enemy of good are terrified by the sign of the Cross and by our regular practice of the sacrament of Communion of the Body and Blood of the Lord, by which we abide in the Lord Jesus, so that serpents and scorpions and all the power of the enemy cannot prevail over us.

The three hundred soldiers continued to blow the trumpets so as to make the enemy imagine that they were a multitude of fighting men and not merely a small number of soldiers, so panic seized the enemy soldiers and in their confusion they began to kill one another, thinking that they were killing Gideon's men, and then they discovered that their comrades had been killed, from their cries, and thought that Gideon's men had killed them, so their fear increased and they hastened to flee. Chaos prevailed among them, each of them trying to save himself and flee from the field of battle, so they were scattered and withdrew to several towns, "Beth-shittah", "Zererath", the border of "Abel-meholah" and "Tabbath", and these places lie in the east of the valley of Jezreel as far as the Jordan River.

The tribes that lived in the regions near the field of battle saw the defeat of the Midianites and the flight of their men, so the men of war of the tribes of Naphtali, Asher and Manasseh were roused and went out to pursue those who fled from the army of the Midianites.

Take before them the waters: seize the gatherings of water of the Jordan River in order to block the way of those fleeing from the Midianite army, lest they escape by swimming in the waters of the Jordan.

Beth-barah: a city on the eastern bank of the Jordan River (Map 11). The tribe of Ephraim lived in the mountainous lands in the middle of the land of Canaan. So Gideon asked them to come down to the plains and take control of the gatherings of water connected with the Jordan River, to prevent the Midianites from crossing the river to its eastern bank to return to their country. The tribe of Ephraim carried out Gideon's request and by this prevented the Midianites from escaping, which would perhaps have helped them to reorganize their ranks in their own lands and return to fight the children of Israel anew.
The rock of Oreb: a place on the western bank of the Jordan River.

The Ephraimites succeeded in capturing the enemy soldiers during their retreat in flight from the field of battle, and seized two of their princes, "Oreb" and "Zeeb", and killed the prince Oreb on a rock which they named "the rock of Oreb", and killed the prince Zeeb at an olive press in which he was perhaps hiding and called it by his name, "the winepress of Zeeb", and they sent the heads of the two slain princes to Gideon to bring him good news.

The continuing of the victories over the Midianites (1) Ephraim's anger at Gideon (vv. 1-3) 1 And the men of Ephraim said unto him, Why hast thou served us thus, that thou calledst us not, when thou wentest to fight with the Midianites? And they did chide with him sharply. 2 And he said unto them, What have I done now in comparison of you? Is not the gleaning of the grapes of Ephraim better than the vintage of Abi-ezer? 3 God hath delivered into your hands the princes of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb: and what was I able to do in comparison of you? Then their anger was abated toward him, when he had said that.

Gideon's request to the tribe of Ephraim was to take control of the gatherings of the waters of the Jordan to prevent the fleeing Midianites from crossing to their country, as came at the end of the previous chapter; this request came almost at the end of the war. Although Ephraim answered Gideon's call, they held it against him that he had not summoned them from the beginning to the war against the Midianites, and they were angry with him, for they considered themselves among the greatest and most important of the tribes, and after the killing of the princes Oreb and Zeeb and the killing of many of the Midianite army, they became proud, especially as they have a readiness for pride because of their great number, although they are not as brave as the rest of the tribes, but they object a great deal because of their pride.

Is not the gleaning of the grapes of Ephraim better than the vintage of Abi-ezer: the gleaning is the fruit that remains on the tree after the fruit is gathered, and the vintage is the fruit that has been gathered. So the gleaning is the leavings compared with the vintage.

Here Gideon's wisdom in leadership appeared, and he met the matter with gentleness and humility, so he gave them back the greater credit for achieving the victory, telling them that what he had done in the war cannot be compared with the great work they had done. And he went further in his speech by saying that the least individual among them is greater than the greatest individual in the clan of Abi-ezer, of which he is one, so that the least work they did against the Midianites is greater in worth than the greatest work accomplished by him and his clan. By this his longsuffering appears, for he did not rebuke them for having yielded for seven years to the humiliation of the Midianites, but encouraged them and thanked them, to heal their pride or their smallness of soul and win their love by his humility.
Their anger was abated (their spirit was relaxed): their souls grew calm.

The Lord has given you to defeat the two princes of the Midianites, "Oreb and Zeeb", and to capture them and kill them, and this was among the most important causes of achieving the final victory over the Midianite army. Then he asked: What have I done like you? Your contribution to achieving the victory cannot be compared with my work of little value.

For Gideon regarded the blowing of the trumpets and the breaking of the pitchers as a small work, while Ephraim's pursuit of the fugitives and the killing of the two princes was a very great work, and by this he calmed the souls of the tribe of Ephraim and removed their anger against him.

By this gentle speech and great humility Gideon was able to calm the intensity of the anger of the tribe of Ephraim against him, so their souls grew calm and the fires of anger were quenched. So be longsuffering when others are angry with you, and by your humility and love you can calm them and win them, turning them by your praise of them from enemies into friends.

(2) The disobedience of the men of Succoth and Penuel and their punishment (vv. 4-17) 4 And Gideon came to Jordan, and passed over, he, and the three hundred men that were with him, faint, yet pursuing them. 5 And he said unto the men of Succoth, Give, I pray you, loaves of bread unto the people that are with me; for they be faint, and I am pursuing after Zebah and Zalmunna, kings of Midian. 6 And the princes of Succoth said, Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna now in thine hand, that we should give bread unto thine army? 7 And Gideon said, Therefore when the Lord hath delivered Zebah and Zalmunna into mine hand, then I will thresh your flesh with the thorns of the wilderness and with threshing instruments. 8 And he went up thence to Penuel, and spake unto them likewise: and the men of Penuel answered him as the men of Succoth had answered him. 9 And he spake also unto the men of Penuel, saying, When I come again in peace, I will break down this tower. 10 Now Zebah and Zalmunna were in Karkor, and their hosts with them, about fifteen thousand men, all that were left of all the hosts of the children of the east: for there fell an hundred and twenty thousand men that drew sword. 11 And Gideon went up by the way of them that dwelt in tents on the east of Nobah and Jogbehah, and smote the host: for the host was secure. 12 And when Zebah and Zalmunna fled, he pursued after them, and took the two kings of Midian, Zebah and Zalmunna, and discomfited all the host. 13 And Gideon the son of Joash returned from battle from the ascent of Heres.

14 And caught a young man of the men of Succoth, and enquired of him: and he wrote for him the princes of Succoth, and the elders thereof, even threescore and seventeen men. 15 And he came unto the men of Succoth, and said, Behold Zebah and Zalmunna, with whom ye did upbraid me, saying, Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna now in thine hand, that we should give bread unto thy men that are weary? 16 And he took the elders of the city, and thorns of the wilderness and threshing instruments, and with them he taught the men of Succoth. 17 And he beat down the tower of Penuel, and slew the men of the city.

Gideon and his men crossed the Jordan to the eastern bank to pursue the fugitives among the enemies who had succeeded in crossing the river. His men, as they pursued the fleeing enemies, had become very weary from the effort they had put forth in the war against the Midianites.

Succoth: a city about 6 km east of the Jordan River in the portion of the tribe of Gad, lying north of the river Jabbok. The meaning of its name is booths, because Jacob made booths for himself when he settled in it (Gen 33:17) (Map 12). Gideon and his men reached a town called Succoth, and they were weary and hungry. So Gideon asked the men of Succoth to give food to the men with him so that they might satisfy their hunger and be able to continue their march in pursuit of the two kings of the Midianites, "Zebah and Zalmunna", in order to seize them and kill them as a recompense for the evils they had committed against the people of Israel.

The men of Succoth replied to him coldly, saying to him: Have you actually seized Zebah and Zalmunna so that they are under your control? This was mockery of him on their part, for they saw the smallness of his army and made light of him and the men with him, believing that he and his few men could not do anything. Perhaps the refusal of the men of Succoth to help Gideon and his men was due to:
1- Extreme stinginess and selfishness.
2- The existence of interests between them and their neighbors the Midianites, or their fear of the Midianites, and their not fearing God and their distance from His worship.

Threshing instruments: the plural of "norag", a cart that runs on wheels, consisting of knives that cut the stalks of wheat after it is harvested in preparation for separating the grain from the straw, and this is called the process of threshing. Just as the grain is mixed with the straw, Gideon would mix the flesh of the men of Succoth with the thorns of the desert when he threshed them with the threshing instrument, that is, he would kill them and cut up their flesh.

Gideon was confident that the Lord would deliver his enemies Zebah and Zalmunna into his hand, and he warned the men of Succoth of the punishment with which he threatened them when that happened, that he would thresh their flesh with the thorns of the wilderness with threshing instruments, because he considered their words not merely an insult to his person but to the Lord, because they doubted the Lord's giving him victory.

Penuel: the meaning of its name is the face of God, and it lies east of the city of Succoth which is east of the Jordan, and in it Jacob saw God and wrestled with Him (Gen 32:30). Gideon and his small army continued to march until they reached the next city after Succoth, at a short distance, which is "Penuel", and he asked its people the same request that he had previously made of the men of Succoth, which was that they give food to his men, and they also refused.

Gideon's reply to the answer of the men of Penuel carried the meaning of complete confidence in the Lord's victory and in his returning in peace after accomplishing his mission. Then he threatened them with the throwing down of the tower in which the men of Penuel took refuge in time of danger.
Karkor: a city of the Midianites lying east of the Jordan.

The two kings of the Midianites, "Zebah and Zalmunna", were in "Karkor" and with them what remained of the army, 15 thousand, the army which was made up of the Midianites and the Amalekites and their allies from the peoples living east of the Jordan and east of the Red Sea.
The number of men of this army at the outbreak of the fighting was 135 thousand, of whom 120 thousand were killed by Gideon and his men, and there remained only 15 thousand bearers of arms.
Nobah: one of the cities of the tribe of Gad east of Gilead.
Jogbehah: it lies northwest of Amman at about 9.5 km.

Gideon did not take the usual road to reach Karkor, but chose another road on both sides of which nomadic groups lived. So his arrival at Karkor was a surprise to the two kings "Zebah and Zalmunna", for they were at ease and never expected him to arrive by this road. The surprise caused confusion in the ranks of the army of the two kings, so it was scattered after most of it was killed, and the two kings found no recourse but to flee.

Our confession that God is the One who works and orders our lives must not deter us from putting forth our effort in planning our lives and arranging our affairs. Here is Gideon, who, having become certain of the Lord's will to give him victory, did not lean on dependence and laziness but began to make plans that would guarantee him the achievement of this victory: there was the idea of the empty pitchers, the torches and the blowing of the trumpets, as came in the previous chapter, as was also his plan to reach Karkor by way of the dwellers in tents. We must share in the work with the Lord, even with our little effort, and the Lord completes.
The two kings fled, but Gideon overtook them and captured them after causing great confusion in the ranks of their army and destroying most of its fighters.

The ascent of Heres: a high city beside a mountain called Heres lying east of the Jordan. Gideon and his men returned victorious with "Zebah and Zalmunna" as captives in his grasp, and reached Succoth, passing through a region called the ascent of Heres.
Gideon seized a young man of the men of Succoth and asked him to write a list of the names of the princes of the city and its elders, and their number was seventy-seven men.

Gideon entered the city of Succoth and spoke to its people and showed them Zebah and Zalmunna, whom the Lord had delivered into his hand so that they had become captives with him, and reminded them of their failure to respond to his request when he asked them for bread for his men while he was on his way to fight the two kings, and reminded them of their insulting reply, full of mockery and doubt of his ability to face the enemy, and even doubt of the ability of God.
And with them he taught the men of Succoth: he gave them a lesson by this so that they would not repeat their mistake again.

Gideon carried out what he had threatened the people of the city with: he took the great men of the city and made them lie down on the thorns that he spread under them, and then had the threshing instruments tread them, and killed them in the worst way, making them an example to those who let down their brothers, and he disciplined the people of that city by what he did to their elders, who were the cause of the refusal to help Gideon and of stirring up the people of the city against him.
Gideon also carried out what he had threatened the people of the city of Penuel with: he threw down the tower in which they had fortified themselves and killed the men of the city.

The men of Succoth and Penuel tried to weaken the resolve of Gideon and his men, and their punishment was death. So do not cast doubt on the work of others, but encourage everyone to bear afflictions and overcome failure by the power of God, and He will bless you and give you victory in all your steps.

(3) Gideon kills the kings of Midian (vv. 18-21) 18 Then said he unto Zebah and Zalmunna, What manner of men were they whom ye slew at Tabor? And they answered, As thou art, so were they; each one resembled the children of a king. 19 And he said, They were my brethren, even the sons of my mother: as the Lord liveth, if ye had saved them alive, I would not slay you. 20 And he said unto Jether his firstborn, Up, and slay them. But the youth drew not his sword: for he feared, because he was yet a youth. 21 Then Zebah and Zalmunna said, Rise thou, and fall upon us: for as the man is, so is his strength. And Gideon arose, and slew Zebah and Zalmunna, and took away the ornaments that were on their camels' necks.

The Midianites' oppression of the children of Israel was not limited to seizing their crops, their cattle and their money, but went beyond that to the killing of the elite of their men and youths, out of a desire to wipe out the young men of the people of God and deprive their people of them. And here Gideon reminds them of their killing of his brothers at "Tabor" in the days of their domination over the children of Israel. And the two kings confessed to killing the excellent young men, describing them as having been in the beauty and strength of the sons of kings.
He told them who those young men were, that they were his brothers by his father and mother, and showed them that had they spared the lives of his brothers, he would pardon them now.
He drew not his sword: he unsheathes or draws his sword from its scabbard to kill.
Gideon commanded his firstborn son "Jether" to kill them, but the boy did not dare because of his youth. Gideon wanted a youth to kill them in order to humiliate them.
Fall upon us: stand yourself and kill us with your own hand.
As the man is, so is his strength: you are a strong man and can kill us with one strong stroke of the sword.
Ornaments (crescents): the plural of crescent, and they were made of gold or silver.

The two kings of the Midianites asked Gideon to kill them himself, because if the youth killed them he would not have the strength to cut off their heads with the first stroke of the sword, which would prolong and increase the pain of the two kings, while for Gideon one stroke of his sword was sufficient, and thus their pains would be less. In addition to that, it was an honor for them to be killed by the commander rather than by any soldier or youth. And after he killed them he took the golden and silver crescents which they hung on the necks of their camels for ornament.

The two kings were cruel in their killing of the young men of the great ones at Tabor, and that was the reason for their being killed. So do not be hasty in cruel or unjust acts lest they come upon you and God punish you with the same deeds, but be merciful and you will obtain mercy from God.

(4) Gideon refuses to rule over the people but makes an ephod (vv. 22-28) 22 Then the men of Israel said unto Gideon, Rule thou over us, both thou, and thy son, and thy son's son also: for thou hast delivered us from the hand of Midian. 23 And Gideon said unto them, I will not rule over you, neither shall my son rule over you: the Lord shall rule over you. 24 And Gideon said unto them, I would desire a request of you, that ye would give me every man the earrings of his prey. (For they had golden earrings, because they were Ishmaelites.) 25 And they answered, We will willingly give them. And they spread a garment, and did cast therein every man the earrings of his prey. 26 And the weight of the golden earrings that he requested was a thousand and seven hundred shekels of gold; beside ornaments, and collars, and purple raiment that was on the kings of Midian, and beside the chains that were about their camels' necks. 27 And Gideon made an ephod thereof, and put it in his city, even in Ophrah: and all Israel went thither a whoring after it: which thing became a snare unto Gideon, and to his house. 28 Thus was Midian subdued before the children of Israel, so that they lifted up their heads no more. And the country was in quietness forty years in the days of Gideon.

In acknowledgment of Gideon's merit toward the children of Israel, and out of loyalty on their part to the one who delivered them from slavery to the Midianites, they offered him that he and his descendants after him should rule over them. This was in imitation of the nations surrounding them, because God was the One who ruled over the children of Israel, and they did not set up kings until later, in the days of Samuel, when he made Saul king (1 Sam 8:5, 10:24).

Gideon was humble in his request and was not deluded by the victory he had achieved, so he was content to have brought them deliverance and was not covetous of kingship or authority, but reminded the people that he was only a mediator in achieving this deliverance, which was from the Lord alone, and He is worthy to rule over them. This shows Gideon's piety and humility, for he believes that God is the leader and king over His people and he did not exploit the people's submission to him to steal God's glory.

Beware of stealing God's glory when others praise you, but ascribe the glory to Him, and do not exploit the need or weakness of others to domineer over them, and know that you and they are servants of God; that is, be humble however much Satan adorns for you an opportunity for boasting and pride.
Earrings: the plural of earring, that which is worn in the ear for adornment.
His prey: what the children of Israel took as spoil from the Midianites.
They had: that is, the Midianites had.

Gideon asked the people to give him the golden earrings they had taken as spoil from the Midianites. For it was the custom of the Midianites that their women, and sometimes their men also, wore golden earrings in imitation of the Ishmaelites, with whom they had mingled by intermarriage and trade, for the Midianites are the descendants of Keturah, the wife of Abraham, and not the descendants of Ishmael.

When the children of Israel saw Gideon's humility and his renunciation of kingship, they did not hesitate for a moment to meet his request to collect the earrings, so they spread a garment on the ground and each of them cast in the golden earrings they had taken as spoil from the Midianites.
Collars (necklaces): the plural of necklace, that which a person wears around his neck.
Shekel: 11-15 grams.

The weight of the golden earrings that were collected was about 25 kg, which shows the wealth of the Midianites; this is apart from the golden crescents that were hung on the camels and horses and the jewelry made in the form of rings (anklets and necklaces), and the splendid garments of colored purple cloth belonging to the Midianite kings and chiefs, and also the golden collars which they placed around the necks of the camels as a kind of adornment and boasting of wealth.
All Israel went a whoring after it: they left the worship of the Lord and worshiped the ephod that Gideon had made.
Which thing became a snare unto Gideon and to his house: the matter of the ephod was a cause that brought Gideon and the people of his house into troubles.

The ephod: a short garment covering the chest, which was part of the garments of the high priest, worn when he judged the people, to give him awe and dignity. Samuel and David used to do the same thing on certain occasions (1 Chr 15:27). Gideon made an ephod of splendid cloth and adorned it with the gold he had collected from the people.

And he put the ephod in his city of Ophrah, and his intention in making the ephod was good, but matters came out the opposite way, for it was a stumbling block to the people, since they left the worship of the Lord and the ephod dazzled them with its golden gleam, so they worshiped it as they had done before with the golden calf during their exodus from Egypt to Sinai.

The people's falling into the worship of the ephod grieved Gideon and the people of his house, and perhaps some of them turned aside to conceit and pride and the seeking of leadership and authority, which led Abimelech, one of the sons of Gideon, to start his movement, whose victims were seventy sons of Gideon (chs. 9, 10).

The victory of the children of Israel over the Midianites humbled them, while the children of Israel held up their heads throughout the period Gideon spent as judge of his people, a period of 40 years, so the people rested from the oppressions of the Midianites and from the acts of plunder, pillage and killing that they used to commit.

(5) The death of Gideon (vv. 29-35) 29 And Jerubbaal the son of Joash went and dwelt in his own house. 30 And Gideon had threescore and ten sons of his body begotten: for he had many wives. 31 And his concubine that was in Shechem, she also bare him a son, whose name he called Abimelech. 32 And Gideon the son of Joash died in a good old age, and was buried in the sepulchre of Joash his father, in Ophrah of the Abi-ezrites. 33 And it came to pass, as soon as Gideon was dead, that the children of Israel turned again, and went a whoring after Baalim, and made Baal-berith their god. 34 And the children of Israel remembered not the Lord their God, who had delivered them out of the hands of all their enemies on every side: 35 Neither shewed they kindness to the house of Jerubbaal (Gideon), according to all the goodness which he had shewed unto Israel.
After his struggle that was crowned with victory, Jerubbaal, which is the other name of Gideon, returned to dwell in Ophrah his city to carry out the task of judge for his people.
Of his body begotten: that is, from his own descendants and not by adoption.
Gideon had many wives, as was the case with many in those ages, and he begot seventy sons by them.

Gideon had a concubine whom he took as a wife in addition to his other original wives, and who was considered, according to the traditions of that age, to be of lower standing than the original wife; his concubine bore him a son whom he called "Abimelech."
After a long struggle and good service, Gideon died and was buried in the tomb of his father Joash in the city of Ophrah, in which lived the clan of Abiezer to which Gideon belonged.
Once again the people of God return and forget what the Lord had done for them and His rescuing them from the hand of the Midianites.

For as soon as Gideon died, they betrayed the Lord and worshiped false gods, imitating the pagan peoples by giving names to these gods, so they called the god whom the people of Shechem worshiped "Baal-berith", that is, "lord of the covenant" or "master of the covenant", as if they had made a covenant with him.
They forgot the Lord their God and did not remember His great works repeatedly done with them when He rescued them from their enemies such as the Midianites.

The people denied the Lord and also denied Gideon, who had done them a great kindness and delivered them from the Midianites, and they did not preserve gratitude toward him and his family, for they did not intervene afterward, as we shall see in the following chapters, to prevent the killing of his seventy sons, but even took part in this wicked and cruel deed to please his son Abimelech.

Hold fast to the teachings of your fathers and teachers even if they have died, for they are an example to you and taught you God's commandments. So do not be negligent of them, and know that they look at you from heaven and pray for you that you may live uprightly before God. The reign of Abimelech son of Gideon

In this chapter we are told how the people did not preserve their gratitude to Gideon and his family. After Gideon's death, Abimelech went to his mother's family to stir up a rebellion against his seventy brothers, relying on the fact that he was of their bone and flesh, because his mother, that is, Gideon's concubine, belonged to a family of a Canaanite tribe. What drove him to this was his feeling that he would not inherit together with his seventy brothers because he was the son of a concubine, since the sons of concubines do not inherit with the sons of the free wives.

Shechem: it is the present-day Nablus (map 11). He asked the sons of his mother's clan to speak to the people of the city of Shechem so that they would accept him as their ruler, claiming that it was better for them that he alone should reign over them than that seventy rulers, the seventy sons of Gideon, should have dominion over them. He added to this that he was related to the people of Shechem on his mother's side, and therefore he was closer to them than his other brothers.

His maternal uncles and his mother's relatives responded to his request and were convinced by his arguments, and they spoke to the rest of the people of Shechem what Abimelech had said, and welcomed his idea, feeling that he was related to them by kinship, since his mother was one of them.
The shekel: 11-15 grams.

To show the loyalty of the people of Shechem and their support for Abimelech, they gathered seventy shekels of silver from the treasury of the pagan temple which they worshiped, called Baal-berith, and gave it to him to help him in his pursuit of rulership. Abimelech used this sum to hire some wicked men to be soldiers who would help him achieve his evil goal.

As soon as he had obtained the support of the people of Shechem, he went to Ophrah, the town of his father's clan, and seized his seventy brothers and killed them all, by putting the head of each one on the same stone and striking off his neck with the sword. Only one of the brothers, the youngest, whose name was Jotham, was able to escape and save himself from that massacre.

Thus the unfaithfulness of the children of Israel to Gideon and to his sons was shown, because no one opposed Abimelech or stood in his way as he killed the seventy sons of Gideon. So they helped the murderer who loved rulership to gain dominion over them; they sinned against God and helped him in evil.
The fortress: a tower in Shechem.

The people of Shechem and the lands around it agreed together to accept Abimelech as their ruler, and they went to him to enthrone him as king over them. Their allegiance was made at a famous oak called "the oak of the pillar," the one under which Jacob buried the images of the pagan gods (Gen 35:1-4), and beside which Joshua set up a stone to confirm the covenant between the people and God (Josh 24:26, 27). This is the first time that the name of a king is mentioned in Israel, but he was not a king over all the people like David and Solomon; he was a king over a small part of the people who dwelt in Shechem and the region around it.

Abimelech's reigning does not mean that he was the judge who came after his father Gideon, since God had not called him to that; besides, his aim was the love of rulership, not teaching the people God's commandments and judging for them. This event is recorded to show the danger of the love of rulership. On the contrary, it shows how humble his father Gideon was and how far he kept from the love of rulership.

Do not let your heart be attached to positions, for they pass away; besides, your attachment may drive you to use means that are against God's commandments. Rather let your aim be the love of God, and He will bless your life and your works and secure for you your peace and happiness on earth and then in heaven.

entries.section: (2) Jotham rebukes the people of Shechem

paragraphs.text: Gerizim: the mountain at which the blessings were pronounced for those who obey God (Josh 8:30-33) (map 11). Jotham was very angry with the people of Shechem for killing his brothers, so he went up to Mount Gerizim, which overlooks the city of Shechem lying in the valley before it, between Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal, and called to its inhabitants to hear him, so that God might accept them and hear their requests. This was a wise beginning on his part, by which he drew them to listen to his words, because he spoke from the mountain of blessing; besides this, he began his speech with a parable to make them eager to hear his words. And from a mountain in the wilderness a voice can resound and be heard throughout the whole valley, and even on the opposite mountain as well.

entries.section: (2) Jotham rebukes the people of Shechem

paragraphs.text: "Anoint a king over us": set a king over them. It is said "anoint" because among the rites of setting up the kings of Israel was anointing them with the holy anointing (the holy oil). He gave them a parable from nature, saying that the trees decided to set a king over themselves, and they offered the kingship to the olive tree.

entries.section: (2) Jotham rebukes the people of Shechem

paragraphs.text: The olive tree refused the kingship, saying that it would not give up its good oil, with its many benefits, from lighting the lamps to making the holy anointing oil and adding it to delicious foods; it would not leave all this to exchange it for a passing greatness that no one benefits from. By this parable he declares that a man's work and his service to those around him are more important than his love of rulership, behind which stand pride and domination, as Abimelech did.

entries.section: (2) Jotham rebukes the people of Shechem

paragraphs.text: The trees turned to another useful tree, the fig tree, and offered it to reign over the rest of the trees, but it also refused, because it was not ready to leave its services to the people, giving them good, sweet-tasting fruit, in order to boast of the false greatness of kingship.

entries.section: (2) Jotham rebukes the people of Shechem

paragraphs.text: The wine: the juice of fresh grapes before it ferments.

The trees made the same offer to the vine, and it answered with the same reply as the other useful trees, namely that it would not leave the juice of the grape, which gladdens the hearts of men and is poured out upon the sacrifices, so that God is pleased with it and is well pleased with those who offer them.

entries.section: (2) Jotham rebukes the people of Shechem

paragraphs.text: When the trees found no response from the splendid, useful trees, they were compelled to offer the kingship to a tree that gives neither fruit nor shade, and is all thorns, the bramble, whose thorns they used as fuel because it catches fire quickly.

entries.section: (2) Jotham rebukes the people of Shechem

paragraphs.text: The bramble knew of the other trees' refusal of the kingship, and knew that resorting to it was not because of its worthiness. Therefore it challenged the other trees that if they truly wanted it as king over them, they should come and take refuge in its shadow. It said this knowing that it has no shadow for the trees to find shade in, and therefore it cannot protect them and is not fit to be a king over them. It added that if they were not able to take refuge in its shadow - and that is certainly the actual state of affairs - then strife would arise between them, because the trees would realize the bramble's uselessness to them and turn against it, and it would meet their turning with violence, for fire would come out from it and consume the trees, even the great ones among them, such as the cedar, known for the massiveness of its trunk and the height of its stem.

By this parable Jotham was pointing to the people of Shechem by the trees, and the useful trees and the cedars by the sons of Gideon whom Abimelech had murdered, and he points to the wicked Abimelech by the bramble, showing the foolishness of the people of Shechem in rallying around him and enthroning him as king over them. He also points to the slain sons of Gideon as being like the olive, the vine and the fig tree, who do not seek the love of rulership but serve those around them in quietness. As for Abimelech, he points to him as the bramble, unable to serve others because it has no shadow, but on the contrary harms those around it with its thorns and burns easily, so that it burns those around it, who are the people of Shechem who supported him. Here we see that a bad choice of leader harms both the people and the leader as well.

entries.section: (2) Jotham rebukes the people of Shechem

paragraphs.text: The people of Shechem committed two great errors: the first was making Abimelech king, and the second was their unfaithfulness and failure to preserve their gratitude to Gideon and his sons. So Jotham rebuked them in the form of a question, which he answered at the end of his speech (v. 20). He asks them whether making Abimelech king was just and was done on the basis of a worthiness they found in him, and he asks them whether by this conduct of theirs they had preserved the gratitude owed for what Gideon had done for them.

entries.section: (2) Jotham rebukes the people of Shechem

paragraphs.text: He reminds them of what Gideon did in his wars to rescue the children of Israel from the oppression of their enemies the Midianites, and of the dangers he bore to secure for them freedom and safety.

entries.section: (2) Jotham rebukes the people of Shechem

paragraphs.text: The people of Shechem did not object to Abimelech's deeds in killing the seventy brothers, the sons of Gideon, and did not rebuke him for his evil work; rather they flattered him and swore allegiance to him as king, though he is not the son of a free wife but the son of a maidservant, and thus has no right to inherit his father, neither in wealth nor in authority.

entries.section: (2) Jotham rebukes the people of Shechem

paragraphs.text: Jotham shows his intense contempt for what the people of Shechem did to Gideon and his household, in a manner that makes light of their conduct, for he says to them that if what they did toward the house of Gideon was a just deed, then happy they are with Abimelech as king.

entries.section: (2) Jotham rebukes the people of Shechem

paragraphs.text: But if it was not a just deed but an unjust one - as is in fact the case - then their deed will turn against them, and the fire of strife and wars will be kindled between them and Abimelech, so that many of them will die, and Abimelech will die in it also.
What Jotham said was indeed fulfilled, as will come in the following verses.

entries.section: (2) Jotham rebukes the people of Shechem

paragraphs.text: After Jotham delivered his speech, which radiated bitterness and boldness at the same time, he fled so that Abimelech would not find him and strike him down as he had done before to his seventy brothers. He fled to a place called "Beer," which lies between Shechem and Jerusalem.

Be brave and proclaim the truth so that the wicked may take heed and turn back from their sins, taking care not to go beyond the proprieties of speech, and let your intention be the salvation of others and not merely anger on your part or any personal purpose or interest; and precede your speech with prayer, so that the words may be from God and by His power.

entries.section: (3) The treachery of the people of Shechem toward Abimelech

paragraphs.text: With all the evil that Abimelech did, and his plotting against his brothers and killing them out of greed to be alone in rulership over Israel, he enjoyed the kingship for only three years, after which events and rebellions occurred that overthrew his kingdom and even his life, as the recompense for his wicked, unlawful ways and his shedding of innocent blood. And when it is mentioned that he ruled over Israel, the meaning is not all the tribes but a part of them, namely the tribe of Manasseh and some of the tribes surrounding it.

entries.section: (3) The treachery of the people of Shechem toward Abimelech

paragraphs.text: God allowed Satan to spread a spirit of hatred and division between Abimelech and the people of Shechem, so his recompense was of the same kind as his deed: as he betrayed his brothers, the people of Shechem betrayed him.

He who founds his life on injustice is destined to fall; a friendship built on self-interest and corrupt aims is destined to turn into enmity and hatred; and every gain or position that its owner obtains by unlawful means is destined to vanish, and its owner's end is destruction.

entries.section: (3) The treachery of the people of Shechem toward Abimelech

paragraphs.text: God used Satan to punish through him Abimelech and the people of Shechem for their injustice toward the sons of Gideon whom Abimelech had killed, for God's justice must be accomplished, and He repays each one according to his work.

entries.section: (3) The treachery of the people of Shechem toward Abimelech

paragraphs.text: The result of the spirit of hatred that crept into the hearts of the people of Shechem toward Abimelech was that they thought of a way to rid themselves of him, so they set some of their own men as lookouts on the roads in the mountains around the city of Shechem to play the part of highwaymen and rob the travelers, so that security would be disturbed and the people would rise against Abimelech for his inability to keep security, and news of those ambushes reached Abimelech. Perhaps they aimed to provoke him so that he would go out to investigate the matter and restore security, and they would kill him.

entries.section: (3) The treachery of the people of Shechem toward Abimelech

paragraphs.text: During those events a new adversary of Abimelech appeared, "Gaal the son of Ebed," who coveted seizing the kingship, and saw that the disturbances taking place might cause the people to gather around him because of their aversion to Abimelech's rule, and that the time was suitable to revolt against him. So "Gaal" came to Shechem, and what he had expected came to pass, for the people of Shechem rallied around him, trusted him, and supported him in his endeavor.

entries.section: (3) The treachery of the people of Shechem toward Abimelech

paragraphs.text: The time coincided with the gathering of the fruit, so the people of Shechem performed a pagan religious rite as a beginning for carrying out their plan against Abimelech. They went out into the field and gathered their vineyards and trod the grapes in the winepresses, and then made a glorification for their gods and praised them inside the temple of "Baal-berith," their god, and they ate and drank in the temple (the temple of Baal), and prayed to their gods that Abimelech might be cursed by those gods, so that it would be made easy for them to gain the victory in their war against him.

The rite of the glorification of the saints still remains among the rites of the Church to this day. But how great is the difference between those who glorify the saints in order to follow their life, their striving and their holding fast to their faith in the hardest situations, and to ask for their blessings and their intercessory prayers, and how vast is the difference between their holy glorifications and the glorifications of the pagans, whose aim was worldly merriment, during which they practiced drunkenness and debauchery as worship of their gods.

entries.section: (3) The treachery of the people of Shechem toward Abimelech

paragraphs.text: "Who is Abimelech, and who is Shechem, that we should serve him?": what is meant here is to exalt the standing of the people of Shechem and to remind them of their lofty position when compared with the lowly Abimelech, who does not deserve to be served by an ancient people such as the people of Shechem.

"Gaal" began to incite hatred of Abimelech and revolt against him, describing him as a lowly person unworthy of ruling over them, for the people of Shechem are too lofty to submit to Abimelech; he is the son of Gideon, who tore down the altar of Baal which they worship, so how can they make king a man who fought their worship? Likewise he described Zebul" l," Abimelech's officer, as incompetent and unworthy of the position of deputy of a king. He added to that that the ones more entitled to the kingship were the descendants of Hamor, the founder of the city, and not this stranger, the son of a concubine. "How, then, is it right for us to obey Abimelech and submit to his rule, when he is a man without integrity and an evil murderer?"

entries.section: (3) The treachery of the people of Shechem toward Abimelech

paragraphs.text: "If the people respond to me and obey me, I shall be able to overthrow the rule of Abimelech." Then "Gaal" sent a message to Abimelech, mocking him and challenging him, and inviting him to increase the number of his soldiers as much as he wished and come out to face him.

entries.section: (3) The treachery of the people of Shechem toward Abimelech

paragraphs.text: Abimelech had appointed "Zebul" as ruler of the city of Shechem and his officer there, while he himself dwelt in the town of "Arumah" (v. 41). What "Gaal" had said reached "Zebul's" ears, and he pretended to agree with his conduct while hiding something else inside himself, for he was angry at what "Gaal" had said and done, and was in truth working for the benefit of his master Abimelech.

entries.section: (3) The treachery of the people of Shechem toward Abimelech

paragraphs.text: Tormah: it is Arumah (v. 41), which lies 16.5 km northeast of Shechem (Nablus) (map 10). "Zebul" secretly sent messengers to Abimelech at "Tormah" to tell him what had happened, of the arrival of "Gaal" in the city of Shechem and his stirring up its people against Abimelech.

entries.section: (3) The treachery of the people of Shechem toward Abimelech

paragraphs.text: "Zebul" was a loyal officer to Abimelech, so he drew up for him a successful plan to confront "Gaal," asking him not to enter the city but to lie in wait by night in the fields, where he would hide until morning, when "Gaal" and his men would come out at the gates of the city and would be exposed, with no fortifications to shelter in; then he could surprise "Gaal" and his helpers and defeat them utterly and do to them whatever he pleased.

Abimelech lay in wait in the fields by night as "Zebul," his officer, had advised him, after dividing his army into four companies in preparation for fighting "Gaal" and those of the people of Shechem who followed him.

"Gaal" went out - as Zebul had expected - in the morning to take up his position at the entrance of the city, to defend it and to prevent Abimelech's army from entering it. Then Abimelech came out of his ambush to begin the battle according to a plan he had drawn up beforehand, as will come in the following verses.

Abimelech's men began to come down from the tops of the mountains surrounding the city, and Gaal saw them, and wanting to verify what he had seen, he asked "Zebul" whether he saw what he himself saw (and "Zebul," as we have already explained, was pretending to support Gaal while in truth he was obstructing his plan for the benefit of his master Abimelech). So "Zebul" deceived Gaal by saying that what he saw were not men but the shadows of the mountains as they appear in the early hours of the morning, so that the onlooker thinks they are persons.
The soothsayers: those who practice augury, which was originally scaring a bird so that it would fly, and people would see the direction in which it flew and take it as an evil or a good omen.

Gaal looked again and saw the men coming down from the mountains increasing more and more, and saw one of the companies coming from another direction, the way of the oak of the soothsayers, those occupied with knowledge of the unseen. This shows that Abimelech's dividing of his army into four companies was for the purpose of attacking his enemies from more than one side in order to confuse them. Gaal went back to assure Zebul that they were companies coming for war.
"Thy mouth": your mouth.

When the companies drew near to face Abimelech and his army, "Zebul" realized that "Gaal" had become entangled, so he ended his pretense of supporting "Gaal," and the truth of his alliance with Abimelech appeared. He said, "You are speaking empty words, and you have no power to face Abimelech. Are not the soldiers whom you see coming against you from every direction the soldiers of Abimelech, whom you despised and made light of, however many they are? So now show us your courage and your abilities, and go forward to fight him, if you can."
