Gaal found no escape from the confrontation, so he went out at the head of his supporters, who had followed him from among the people of Shechem, to fight Abimelech.
The battle took place and Gaal was defeated and fled, after many of his men had fallen and their corpses covered the battlefield, reaching as far as the gate of the city of Shechem.

"Abimelech" came out of the war victorious and returned to the city which he had chosen as his place of residence, Arumah, near Shechem. "Gaal" and the remnants of his army had fled from before Abimelech's army into the city of Shechem, but Zebul, Abimelech's officer, drove them out of it so as to be safe from their starting a new rebellion in the future.

Do not rush into threats that are not calculated and that you are not able to carry out, and be deliberate in your speech so that it may have value and others may respect you, and so that all your decisions may be practical, and then people will love you and trust you.

entries.section: (5) Abimelech destroys Shechem and burns the stronghold

paragraphs.text: After the revolt of "Gaal" against "Abimelech" was put down, the people of Shechem thought that matters had settled, so they went out to their fields to do their usual daily work. But Abimelech did not look at the matter in the same way. Although he had returned to his residence in Arumah, his heart had not become clear toward the people of Shechem, who had betrayed him and supported "Gaal" against him, so as soon as he learned that the people of Shechem had gone out to their usual work, he began to plan how to destroy them.

entries.section: (5) Abimelech destroys Shechem and burns the stronghold

paragraphs.text: Abimelech gathered his army again and divided it into three companies, and went to the region surrounding the city of Shechem and lay in wait outside it until the people of the city went out to their work, and then he fell upon them and struck them according to a plan he had drawn up, the details of which will come in the following two verses.

entries.section: (5) Abimelech destroys Shechem and burns the stronghold

paragraphs.text: The details of the plan he had drawn up were that he himself would lead one of the three companies into which he had divided his army, and its task would be to kill everyone who tried to go out to his work and everyone who returned from his work to the city. As for the other two companies, their task was to kill everyone they found outside the city in the fields.

entries.section: (5) Abimelech destroys Shechem and burns the stronghold

paragraphs.text: "Sowed it with salt": he sprinkled salt on its farmland so that it would remain barren and not be sown afterward. This expression may mean the ruin of the city and the lands around it.

The next stage in the plan he drew up and carried out was that, after he had finished off those outside and inside the city and those beyond it, he stormed the city and fought against it all day and took it and killed those in it and laid waste its land so that it would not be sown afterward.

entries.section: (5) Abimelech destroys Shechem and burns the stronghold

paragraphs.text: The stronghold of the house of El-berith: a high fortress attached to the temple of Baal-berith, which the people of Shechem worship, a fortress adjoining the tower of Shechem.

The reaction of the inhabitants of the tower of Shechem to what had happened in their city was to take refuge in the fortress of "the house of El-berith" attached to the citadel, which is more strongly fortified than the tower of Shechem, to fortify themselves in it and resist from it Abimelech's attack on their city.

entries.section: (5) Abimelech destroys Shechem and burns the stronghold

paragraphs.text: Mount Zalmon: a part of Mount Gerizim near Shechem, full of trees.

Abimelech learned that the people of Shechem had fortified themselves in the tower, so he began to draw up a plan to seize it. He took his army and went up to Mount Zalmon and cut with his axe a bough from the branches of the trees that cover the mountain, and commanded his men to do likewise, and they did so, and each soldier carried a bough on his shoulder, and they laid them around the stronghold and set fire to them, and everyone who was in the stronghold and its tower died, burned or suffocated by the smoke, and the number of the dead was a thousand persons.

Do not support the wicked, lest harm befall you and God punish you for your encouragement of evil. Be strong, and if you do not rebuke evil, at least do not encourage it, so that perhaps the wicked may repent and so that you may save yourself from God's punishment.

After Abimelech took Shechem and subdued its people, he continued his campaign against another city that had joined Shechem in its revolt against his rule, the city of "Thebez," which lies 10 miles northeast of Shechem; he and his soldiers entered it and took it.

As usual, to shelter from the enemy soldiers, all the people of the city, men, women and children, took refuge in the stronghold in a strongly built tower erected in the middle of the city, and went up to the safest place in the tower, which is its top, and from it they could also watch the movements of the enemy army.
Abimelech tried to attack the tower and take it in the same way he had done in his attack on the stronghold of Baal-berith, so he drew near to the door of the tower in order to burn it with fire.
"Brake": broke.
As he drew near to the door to burn it with fire, a woman cast a piece of a millstone, with which grain is ground, upon his head, and broke his skull.

Abimelech felt that he was close to death, so he commanded his young man, the bearer of his sword and his weapons of war, to draw the sword and kill him, lest the shame of dying at the hand of a woman attach to him; and the young man obeyed and carried out his master's command.
With the destruction of Abimelech, the members of the army that had rallied around him were scattered, as were all who had supported him in his wars, and each one went his own way.

This was the just judgment of heaven upon the great evil that Abimelech had done in killing without right his brothers, the seventy sons of Gideon; it was also a fulfillment of the saying of the Lord of glory in the Gospel, "All they that take the sword shall perish with the sword."

The Lord may be patient with the wicked and warn them once and twice, but if the wicked take advantage of His longsuffering to persist in their evil, God will not leave them to corrupt the earth but will bring upon them the fitting punishment. But if they respond to the call of wisdom and turn back from their injustice, God forgives them. And in the Holy Bible we have many events that confirm this meaning, such as the story of Jonah and the people of Nineveh.

Abimelech had partners in the evil that he did, for which the Lord punished him: the people of Shechem, who supported him at the beginning and agreed with him in what he did, so their punishment too was a repayment of their evils upon them. Thus the curse of which Jotham had warned them in his speech was fulfilled, and the fire of hatred and wars came out between Abimelech and the people of Shechem, and burned their fortresses with those in them, and in the end it burned Abimelech himself.
The judges Tola and Jair, then the enslavement of the people of God
Shamir: it lies between Hanin and Samaria.

Mount Ephraim: mountainous lands lying in the portion of the tribe of Ephraim (map 12). Abimelech died, and, as we mentioned, he is not counted among the judges because he seized the kingship out of love of rulership; and after that God raised up a judge to rule by His law, "Tola." He was of the tribe of Issachar but dwelt in Ephraim, and peace prevailed in his days, and the people lived by God's commandments, and the enemies did not attack the children of Israel.
After Tola had fulfilled his task as deliverer and judge of his people for twenty-three years, he died and was buried in his city.

If you are in a position of responsibility in your home, in the Church or in any place, follow God's commandments and teach by them, and you will strengthen the faith of those around you and give them the divine peace, so that they live in faith in God's hands.

After "Tola" another judge arose to judge, "Jair," who was called the Gileadite because he dwelt in the land of Gilead east of the Jordan. The length of his judging the people was 22 years, during which nothing happened to disturb the calm and security that prevailed throughout the period of his rule. He taught the people God's law and judged by it to settle the disputes and problems among them. It appears that peace prevailed in his time, for no wars are mentioned throughout the length of his judgeship.
Havoth-jair: that is, the farms of Jair, lying in the northwestern part of Bashan, east of the Jordan.
The land of Gilead: the region east of the Jordan inhabited by the clan of the Gileadites, named after their head, who was the son of Machir and the grandson of Manasseh.

Camon: a place in the land of Gilead (map 12). The ancients married at an early age and rejoiced in an abundance of offspring, and Jair had a number of wives, by whom he begat thirty sons, each of whom had an ass, as the notables of the people did in that age, and they had thirty farms in the land of Gilead, with buildings and installations, which were therefore considered cities; and they were called "the farms of Jair," and the names of those cities were preserved as they were until the time the book was written.
After Jair had judged his people, he died and was buried in one of the cities of Gilead, which was called "Camon."

Hold fast to God's commandments so as to apply them in your life, and then you will be able to teach them to others, and they will be what governs your works and with which you guide others, and you will live in tranquility and peace.

entries.section: (3) The Philistines and the children of Ammon humble Israel

paragraphs.text: Ashtaroth: plural of Ashtar, who is the goddess of the moon.
Aram: lies northeast of Canaan; it is the land of present-day Syria, and its capital is Damascus.
Zidon: it is Sidon, lying on the Mediterranean south of Tyre.
Moab: they dwell east of the Jordan and the Dead Sea.
The children of Ammon: they dwell east of the Jordan and north of Moab.
The Philistines: they dwelt in the south of the land of Canaan, from the Dead Sea to the Mediterranean.

As has often been repeated in the Book of Judges, the people had rested for a period of time from the harassment of the enemies, and then repeated the same transgression they had committed before, which had been the cause of the Lord's leaving them to fall into the hands of their enemies. Here they are, after the death of Jair the Gileadite, grieving the Lord anew, for they began to worship the gods of the pagan nations surrounding them.

entries.section: (3) The Philistines and the children of Ammon humble Israel

paragraphs.text: Since they forsook the Lord, He too forsook them, and in His anger against them He withdrew His protection and left them as spoil in the hand of their enemies who surrounded them, the Philistines from the west and the children of Ammon from the east, so they fell under their grip and became slaves to them.

entries.section: (3) The Philistines and the children of Ammon humble Israel

paragraphs.text: "They vexed and oppressed the children of Israel": that is, they struck them with blows that left clear marks on their bodies and crushed them; the meaning is that they humbled them greatly by beating and exploitation.

The people tasted the bitterness of slavery anew as the fruit of their evil; since they despised the Lord and forsook His worship, their enemies humbled them and they remained in humiliation for 18 years, and they were greatly distressed. Those who suffered the most harm by reason of their location were the tribes of Reuben and Gad and the eastern half-tribe of Manasseh, the tribes that dwelt east of the Jordan on the lands that had belonged to the Amorites before the children of Israel took them from them, among which are also the mountains of Gilead.

entries.section: (3) The Philistines and the children of Ammon humble Israel

paragraphs.text: The weariness and humiliation were not confined to the eastern tribes alone, but the Ammonites crossed the Jordan to fight the tribes dwelling in the west, among them the tribes of Judah, Benjamin and Ephraim, which are the largest tribes of Israel, to bring them under their control, which plunged Israel into severe distress.

If you neglect your relationship with God, you will lose His care and protection, and consequently the devil will gain dominion over you through many sins and will humble you, because he is fierce and wants your destruction. So return quickly, for God your Father is merciful, and He will forgive you and embrace you and save you from the humiliation of Satan.

From the distress of slavery the children of Israel cried out to God to save them, as this was repeated several times in the age of the judges, and they confessed their sin, that they had worshiped the pagan gods and forsaken God.

God reminded them, by the tongue of the high priest or one of the prophets, how He had saved them when they cried to Him to rescue them from the slavery of the surrounding nations who humbled them, such as His delivering them from the Egyptians: He brought them out of their slavery by the hand of Moses.

And from the Amorites: He gave them victory over their kings and gave them their land (Num 21:21-35, Josh 11:3). And from the children of Ammon: He prepared His servant Ehud, who killed Eglon their king (ch. 3:12-30). And from the Philistines there was Shamgar, who killed 600 men of them with an ox goad (ch. 3:3, 21). And from the Zidonians the Lord delivered His people by the hand of Barak and Deborah (ch. 5:19). And from the Amalekites the Lord delivered them, whether in the days of Moses by the hand of Joshua (Ex 17) or by the hand of Gideon (ch. 6:3). And from the Maonites the Lord delivered His people by the hand of Ehud and Gideon (chs. 3, 6). The Maonites are the inhabitants of Maon, which lies in the land of Edom east of the Jordan.

But the people, in return for these kindnesses of God, betrayed His covenants and forsook His worship and departed from Him and went after other, false gods; therefore He will not save them, since they have denied Him and become strangers to Him. Why then do they cry to Him now? So God says to them: Go to those whom you have chosen as your gods, that perhaps they may save you from your distress. This is a style of reproach, by which God mocks them, because the pagan gods are unable to save them.

The people confess their fault and place themselves in God's hands, to punish them or to pardon them as He wills, but they entreat Him repentantly to rescue them from the enemy and then to discipline them if He wishes.

"His soul was grieved for the misery of Israel": God condescends and expresses His feeling in emotions that human beings understand, namely His being distressed because of their humiliation, and this shows His tenderness and fatherhood; for if He threatens His people, it is that they may repent and He may have mercy on them.

The repentance of the people was a practical repentance, for they broke the idols and tore down their altars and returned to obedience to their heavenly Father and to His worship, and the Lord's heart was softened because of the hardship to which His people were exposed.

Confession of the fault alone is not enough to obtain forgiveness, but it must be accompanied by an act that shows regret and repentance, and the removal of every cause of the sin into which a person had fallen, the correction of bad conduct, and a sincere resolve not to repeat it; and what confirms the soundness of his resolve is that good works take the place of the corrupt works he had committed before. Let us then be earnest in our repentance by offering good works that please the Lord.

entries.section: (5) The children of Ammon prepare to fight Israel

paragraphs.text: Mizpah: it lies in the portion of the tribe of Gad and was called Mizpah of Gilead (ch. 11:29) and Ramath-mizpeh (Josh 13:26); it is the place of the heap which Jacob and the people of Laban set up as a witness to the covenant between them (Gen 31:49). The children of Ammon gathered their armies to fight the children of Israel, beginning with the tribes dwelling in Gilead. And the children of Israel prepared with their armies to defend themselves and encamped in one of the places of Gilead called "Mizpah."

entries.section: (5) The children of Ammon prepare to fight Israel

paragraphs.text: The children of Israel were taking counsel among themselves as to who should be the leader to lead them in this war of theirs, and this brave person would be worthy of their swearing allegiance to him as head and ruler over them in all their lands east of the Jordan.

Do not be disturbed by the snares of the devil and his wars, for your God is stronger than he and is able to give you victory over him; but be watchful and hold fast to your spiritual striving, and you will certainly win.
The victory over the children of Ammon

entries.section: (1) The choice of Jephthah as head over Gilead

paragraphs.text: In this chapter the inspired writer begins by narrating the Lord's intervening anew to rescue His people in response to their prayers, their repentance and their supplications. From this verse onward he makes known to us the person of the new judge whom the Lord chose to save His people by him, "Jephthah," surnamed the Gileadite, after his father Gilead and his homeland, the land of Gilead.

Gilead's wife bore no sons, so Gilead sinned with a harlot woman, and she bore him Jephthah. Here appears the mercy of God, who does not punish a man for the evil of his father so long as he walks with God and holds fast to His commandments, but rather chooses him as a leader of his people.

entries.section: (1) The choice of Jephthah as head over Gilead

paragraphs.text: But after the birth of Jephthah his lawful wife bore sons, and when they grew up they drove Jephthah out from among them, saying to him that he was the son of a harlot woman and had no right to inherit with them.

entries.section: (1) The choice of Jephthah as head over Gilead

paragraphs.text: After Jephthah was driven out from his brothers, he dwelt in the land of Tob on the border of Gilead, and idle men gathered around him who had no means of livelihood except plundering the money of travelers on the traveled roads and working as mercenaries for whoever paid the price, and Jephthah accompanied them and led them in their adventures.

entries.section: (1) The choice of Jephthah as head over Gilead

paragraphs.text: The children of Ammon began to fight the children of Israel in order to enslave and humble them.

entries.section: (1) The choice of Jephthah as head over Gilead

paragraphs.text: The elders of Gilead were exchanging views and counsel as to who could lead their armies to face the Ammonites. The opinion settled on Jephthah because of his bravery and strength, so they went to him and asked him to lead them in the war against the children of Ammon.

entries.section: (1) The choice of Jephthah as head over Gilead

paragraphs.text: Jephthah reminded them of their bad conduct toward him when they agreed with his brothers to drive him out from among them, and he marveled at their new behavior toward him, for how, after they had driven him out of his father's house, could they come and ask him to help them when they were exposed to the harassment of enemies?

And Jephthah, whom his brothers drove out and then returned asking for his leadership to save them, is a symbol of Christ, whom His people rejected and crucified, and then returned asking for salvation at His hands when they believed in Him.

entries.section: (1) The choice of Jephthah as head over Gilead

paragraphs.text: "Be our head": be a ruler over us and a leader to us.

The content of the elders' reply carried a tone of apology for what had gone before on their part, and that they were coming to him now to set right what had passed, and here they ask him to be head over all the inhabitants of Gilead.

entries.section: (1) The choice of Jephthah as head over Gilead

paragraphs.text: Jephthah made it a condition for the children of Israel that if they brought him back to his country to fight the children of Ammon, and if God gave him victory in his war against them and delivered them into his hand, he would become head over them. Jephthah set this condition to confirm the agreement, lest they return to their former way with him and deny him after the victory.

entries.section: (1) The choice of Jephthah as head over Gilead

paragraphs.text: The elders assured him of their readiness to set him up as head, and called the Lord to witness to their covenant with him.

entries.section: (1) The choice of Jephthah as head over Gilead

paragraphs.text: "Jephthah uttered all his words before the LORD": he prayed to the Lord and pledged before Him to act.
Mizpah: a city in Gilead east of the Jordan River, at which Jacob made a covenant with Laban. There are five other cities named Mizpah in other places.

Jephthah went with them, and the people appointed him head over them and commander of their armies. Then he set out for the war with a deep prayer in the place where they had gathered to set him up as head, "Mizpah," and in this prayer of his is a confession that God is the One able to give him victory, and he asks Him to be with him.

How beautiful it is to begin every new work with prayer to the Lord, asking His help and the accomplishment of His good will. If the work agrees with His good will, may He guide us to the right way to complete it with all sincerity and faithfulness, and if it is harmful to us, may He keep us away from it.

(2) Jephthah's correspondence with the kings of the Ammonites, Edom, Moab and the king of the Amorites (vv. 12-28:) 12 And Jephthah sent messengers unto the king of the children of Ammon, saying, What hast thou to do with me, that thou art come against me to fight in my land? 13 And the king of the children of Ammon answered unto the messengers of Jephthah, Because Israel took away my land, when they came up out of Egypt, from Arnon even unto Jabbok, and unto Jordan: now therefore restore those lands again peaceably. 14 And Jephthah sent messengers again unto the king of the children of Ammon: 15 And said unto him, Thus saith Jephthah, Israel took not away the land of Moab, nor the land of the children of Ammon: 16 But when Israel came up from Egypt, and walked through the wilderness unto the Red sea, and came to Kadesh; 17 Then Israel sent messengers unto the king of Edom, saying, Let me, I pray thee, pass through thy land: but the king of Edom would not hearken thereto. And in like manner they sent unto the king of Moab: but he would not consent: and Israel abode in Kadesh. 18 Then they went along through the wilderness, and compassed the land of Edom, and the land of Moab, and came by the east side of the land of Moab, and pitched on the other side of Arnon, but came not within the border of Moab: for Arnon was the border of Moab. 19 And Israel sent messengers unto Sihon king of the Amorites, the king of Heshbon; and Israel said unto him, Let us pass, we pray thee, through thy land into my place. 20 But Sihon trusted not Israel to pass through his coast: but Sihon gathered all his people together, and pitched in Jahaz, and fought against Israel. 21 And the LORD God of Israel delivered Sihon and all his people into the hand of Israel, and they smote them: so Israel possessed all the land of the Amorites, the inhabitants of that country. 22 And they possessed all the coasts of the Amorites, from Arnon even unto Jabbok, and from the wilderness even unto Jordan. 23 So now the LORD God of Israel hath dispossessed the Amorites from before his people Israel, and shouldest thou possess it? 24 Wilt not thou possess that which Chemosh thy god giveth thee to possess? So whomsoever the LORD our God shall drive out from before us, them will we possess. 25 And now art thou any thing better than Balak the son of Zippor, king of Moab? did he ever strive against Israel, or did he ever fight against them, 26 While Israel dwelt in Heshbon and her towns, and in Aroer and her towns, and in all the cities that be along by the coasts of Arnon, three hundred years? why therefore did ye not recover them within that time? 27 Wherefore I have not sinned against thee, but thou doest me wrong to war against me: the LORD the Judge be judge this day between the children of Israel and the children of Ammon. 28 Howbeit the king of the children of Ammon hearkened not unto the words of Jephthah which he sent him.

entries.section: (1) The choice of Jephthah as head over Gilead

paragraphs.text: This verse and the following verses relate the content of the two messages of Jephthah which he sent to the king of Ammon, asking for peace and explaining his right to the land over which the king of the children of Ammon was disputing with him. The king of the children of Ammon replied to his first message but did not reply to his second message. The content of his first message was his asking what had happened that the king of the children of Ammon had come intending war against the children of Israel.

entries.section: (1) The choice of Jephthah as head over Gilead

paragraphs.text: The reply of the king of the children of Ammon to Jephthah's messengers contained a historical fallacy, for he accused Israel of seizing what he claimed had been his own land, the region lying between the two tributaries of the Jordan east of the river, namely Arnon and Jabbok (Num 21:13, 21-30). These lands the children of Israel had taken from the king of the Amorites, not from the king of the children of Ammon as he claimed. The king of the Amorites had taken them earlier from the children of Ammon and Moab, so Israel took nothing of these lands from the hand of the children of Ammon.

entries.section: (1) The choice of Jephthah as head over Gilead

paragraphs.text: On the basis of the reply of the king of the children of Ammon, Jephthah sent him what refutes this claim of his, in a lengthy account of the true history of the possession of these lands.

entries.section: (1) The choice of Jephthah as head over Gilead

paragraphs.text: He showed him historical facts proving that the children of Israel had not taken any of the lands of the children of Ammon, nor even of the children of Moab, the cousins of the children of Ammon.

entries.section: (1) The choice of Jephthah as head over Gilead

paragraphs.text: "Came up": because the land of Palestine is higher than the land of Egypt.
Jephthah relates that the children of Israel, when they came out of Egypt, walked in the desert lying east of the barren Delta and crossed the Red Sea, and from it to Kadesh (Num 20:1).

entries.section: (1) The choice of Jephthah as head over Gilead

paragraphs.text: "The king of Edom would not hearken": he did not respond to their request.
"He would not consent": he did not agree.

From Kadesh Israel sent messengers to the king of Edom, asking permission merely to pass through his land, but the king of Edom refused and threatened to wage war on Israel if it dared to enter his land, and the same story happened with the king of Moab. So they were forced to remain for a short time in Kadesh to replan their journey toward the Promised Land, after the roads through the land of Edom and the land of Moab had been closed to them (Num 20:14-18).

entries.section: (1) The choice of Jephthah as head over Gilead

paragraphs.text: "Compassed the land of Edom and the land of Moab": the children of Israel went around the land of Edom and the land of Moab in a barren desert to avoid passing through the land of Edom and Moab when they refused that.
"Arnon was the border of Moab": the boundary of the land of Moab is one of the tributaries of the Jordan, called Arnon, which separates Moab from the Amorites.

In their journey the people avoided the land of Moab and the children of Ammon so as not to stir up a war against them, and made a hard journey going around the land of Edom and the land of Moab, then came from the east side to reach, from outside the borders of the land of Moab, the other bank of the river Arnon, being careful in this not to touch the lands of Moab.

entries.section: (1) The choice of Jephthah as head over Gilead

paragraphs.text: Heshbon: it lies between the rivers Jabbok and Arnon (map 11). From there the children of Israel sent messengers to the king of the Amorites, asking him to allow them to pass through his land so as to reach the land which the Lord had promised the children of Israel, but the king of the Amorites did not permit him either (Num 21:21-30).

entries.section: (1) The choice of Jephthah as head over Gilead

paragraphs.text: Jahaz: a Moabite city (map 11). The king of the Amorites was fearful of the request of the children of Israel and suspected deceit on their part, for perhaps their purpose was not only passing through but occupying his land, so he hastened and formed an army and rushed to fight the children of Israel at the town of "Jahaz" (Num 21:23).

Jephthah was patient in his dealing with the king of the children of Ammon, despite the latter's false claims and his evil intention toward the children of Israel. This is a good example for us to try to take every possible way of achieving peace between us and others, acting on the saying of the Gospel, "If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men."

entries.section: (1) The choice of Jephthah as head over Gilead

paragraphs.text: The Lord delivered the Amorites into the hand of the children of Israel, and they possessed the lands which the king of the Ammonites now claims without right.

entries.section: (1) The choice of Jephthah as head over Gilead

paragraphs.text: By their victory over the Amorites the children of Israel took all the lands of the Amorites lying between the river Arnon in the south and the river Jabbok in the north, and from the desert in the east to the river Jordan in the west.

entries.section: (1) The choice of Jephthah as head over Gilead

paragraphs.text: Jephthah says in this message of his to the king of the children of Ammon that the Lord had supported the children of Israel and given them victory over the Amorites, and thus it is God who granted them those lands to dwell in, so how do you think of taking them from them by your false claims?

entries.section: (1) The choice of Jephthah as head over Gilead

paragraphs.text: Jephthah continued his words to the king of the children of Ammon, saying to him that it is his right to take possession only of the lands that his god "Chemosh" enables him to have, while they have the right to take possession of the lands that God Jehovah enables them to have. By this Jephthah mocks the pagan god Chemosh, whom the children of Ammon worship, who is unable to support his worshipers.

entries.section: (1) The choice of Jephthah as head over Gilead

paragraphs.text: Jephthah goes on, saying to him: Are you stronger than Balak king of Moab, who was afraid of the victories that our people had won over the peoples of the region and did not dare to face the children of Israel, so he summoned Balaam the son of Beor to curse Israel so that they would not be able to invade his land (Num 22-24)? And he never thought of fighting them.

entries.section: (1) The choice of Jephthah as head over Gilead

paragraphs.text: Heshbon: the capital of the kingdom of Sihon.

Aroer: it lies north of the river Arnon (map 10). Three hundred years: the children of Israel took the lands of the Amorites in 1452 B.C., and Jephthah's victory over the children of Ammon was in 1143 B.C., so the period that had passed was about 300 years. "Three hundred years have now passed since our settling in these lands, namely Heshbon and Aroer and the cities of Arnon, since our victory over the Amorites who dwelt in them before us, so where was your people throughout all this time, and none of their kings thought of recovering them as you are trying to do now?"

entries.section: (1) The choice of Jephthah as head over Gilead

paragraphs.text: In this Jephthah showed his people's right to the land over which the king of the children of Ammon was disputing with him, and that he had not encroached on any of his lands and had never sinned against him. As for the king of the children of Ammon, by thinking of war against him he had committed a great error, and it is God, who is just and knows the intentions of men, who will judge for all.

entries.section: (1) The choice of Jephthah as head over Gilead

paragraphs.text: Despite all these proofs and evidences that Jephthah brought, the king of the children of Ammon did not wish to be persuaded by them, but clung to his mistaken thought and rejected Jephthah's peace overtures and decided to go on with the decision for war.

The stand of the king of the children of Ammon after the long defense that Jephthah presented shows the hateful clinging to one's opinion even if it is wrong, which is a vice that may bring its owner to utter destruction, just as happened to the king of the children of Ammon. The man in whom there is not the Spirit of the Lord does not accept the call to the truth, does not listen to the counsel of others, and does not like to heed one who warns him of the danger of his position. So the end of such a man is a ruin to him. May the Lord grant us spiritual senses so that we perceive the advice that others may offer us, and listen, and humble ourselves before our spiritual guides.

The Holy Spirit came upon Jephthah, granting him courage and confidence to do what he had been charged with, and guided him to pass through the cities to stir up the people and rouse them to defend their cities and to gather the soldiers who would be his army. The cities through which he passed were Gilead and Mizpah of Gilead.

Jephthah vowed a vow to offer to the Lord at his victory in his war against the children of Ammon, namely that the first one who would meet him from his house on his return victorious he would offer up as a burnt offering to the Lord. In this vow Jephthah was influenced by the customs of the pagan peoples, who offered human sacrifices, which God absolutely forbade. This is a great error on Jephthah's part. As for God's asking Abraham to offer Isaac as a sacrifice, it was to test him, and he did not in fact offer him (Gen 22).
Minnith: an Ammonite land (map 10).

Jephthah attacked the children of Ammon and the Lord gave him victory over them, and he defeated their armies with a crushing defeat in a wide region that included twenty cities, from Aroer even to Minnith, and extended to "the plain of the vineyards," so the children of Ammon surrendered and submitted to the control of the children of Israel and tasted the humiliation of the defeat which they had wanted to inflict on the people of the Lord.

When he returned from the war victorious, he came back to his house at "Mizpah," and then came the tragedy, for he was surprised that the first to come out to meet him was his only daughter. She came out to meet him with her companions with timbrels and dances, as was the custom anciently.
"He rent his clothes": as is the custom of the people of the East when something happens that greatly grieves them.
"I have opened my mouth unto the LORD": I have vowed a vow and cannot go back from it.

When her father saw her, he realized the tragedy into which he had fallen, so he rent his clothes in grief and cried, Alas, my daughter, and was distressed because of the vow he had vowed and could not go back on.
"According to that which hath proceeded out of thy mouth": as you pronounced your vow.
The girl said to her father that since the Lord had given you victory over your enemies and you have vowed a vow, fulfil your vow to which you pledged yourself.

The girl made her father understand that she was ready to carry out the vow, on condition that he give her a respite of two months before carrying it out, which she would spend on the mountains with her companions, bewailing her virginity with them.
Her father agreed to her request and permitted her to go with her companions as she asked, so she went to the mountains with her companions.
"He did with her according to his vow which he had vowed": he offered her as a sacrifice.

The daughter of Jephthah kept her promise and returned after the two months had passed and gave herself up to her father. Her father carried out his vow, and she died a virgin who had not married. And it became a custom for the women of the children of Israel to go to the mountains and remain there four days, during which they lament the daughter of Jephthah.
It is to be noted that Jephthah made three errors ...

The first is that he vowed his daughter, that is, a human being, and God never accepts this; and the second error is that he completed the wrong vow and carried it out, whereas he should rather have drawn back from it and not completed the first error with a second error .. As for his third error, it is that he did not consult any of the priests responsible for the law, who would have dissuaded him from completing his wrong vow. In the New Testament also, the priest, through the authority of the sacrament of the priesthood, can release a person from his wrong vow.
God allowed Gideon to kill his daughter to warn all his children to keep away from haste in decisions, lest they lose what is dearest to them, that is, their children.

Be careful when you vow, and vow what you are able to fulfil and what at the same time does not violate God's commandments, and it is better to consult your father of confession; for a vow is a great thing that strengthens your faith, but do not spoil it by your rashness and by vowing things beyond your ability.
Ephraim's fighting Jephthah, and the judges Ibzan, Elon and Abdon

The tribe of Ephraim was accustomed to protest against the leaders of the people, as they had protested against Gideon before, and he answered them humbly and calmed their anger (ch. 8:1-3). The tribe of Ephraim is always marked by pride, which drives them to anger and objection, and now they not only object to Jephthah but gathered the men of war and went north and crossed the Jordan to fight Jephthah, and threatened to burn him and his house and all who were in it, and made the false claim that he had not asked them to join him in fighting the children of Ammon. The truth is that he had called them, but they were slack in answering his call. It appears that they were marked by stubbornness and protest, relying on their large numbers and strength, yet at the same time slack, speaking but not doing any positive work, rather stirring up problems. Their violence appears here in that they did not merely reproach him but threatened him with death.

It is clear that they were proud, for when Jephthah achieved the victory it was hard on them not to share in the glories of the victory, so the cause of their revolt was pride and not defending the people against the occupiers. It would have been more fitting for them to thank Jephthah for his bravery and to comfort him over his only daughter, but their pride made them hard of heart.

Jephthah reproached them that when he and his people, the men of Gilead, cried out to them, asking their support against the children of Ammon, they did not respond to their calls and left him and the men of Gilead to face the children of Ammon alone.
"I put my life in my hands": I faced the danger without fear, making light of death.

Jephthah told them that when it became clear to him that they were not ready to join him in his war against the children of Ammon, he was compelled to fight the battle with his people alone, and the Lord gave him victory over them. Therefore they have no right today to come out to fight him.

Be positive and do not stir up problems, and search in every matter for what you may learn for the benefit of yourself and all those around you, and do not create a problem to assert your personality. Be humble so that you may offer love to those around you and work for your good and the good of others.
"Ye Gileadites are fugitives of Ephraim": you are a band of fugitives from the tribe of Ephraim, because you are thieves and rabble and have no worth in society.
"Among the Ephraimites, and among the Manassites": the land of Gilead is adjoined by the land of Ephraim on the west and by the land of Manasseh on the east and on the north.

The Ephraimites who said this phrase meant to despise the Gileadites, for they were saying to them: You fled and settled in this region between the two tribes because you did not dare to settle in either of them, since you are outcasts and despised by both.
Jephthah gathered the warriors from Gilead and fought Ephraim and overcame them. Ephraim had been taunting the Gileadites that they were thieves, fugitives from their tribe.
"Fugitives of Ephraim": the Ephraimites, because of their feeling of defeat.
"The passages of Jordan": the shallow gatherings of water adjoining the river Jordan.
Shibboleth: a word meaning an ear of grain.

The men of Gilead seized the fords of the river Jordan so that the Ephraimites could not escape by them, and so that Jephthah's men could recognize the fugitives from the soldiers of Ephraim, they would arrest anyone who passed through these fords and ask him to say the word "Shibboleth." The men of Ephraim used to pronounce the letter shin as "sin." Since the fugitives were in fear and not expecting the question, they would say "Sibboleth," and the Gileadites would know that they were men of Ephraim and kill them, and in this way they killed 42,000 Ephraimite men, which is considered most of the army of Ephraim. Here the lack of wisdom in Jephthah appears, for he resisted the pride of Ephraim with his own pride, and so the people of God lost a great number of its sons; whereas Gideon is distinguished here from Jephthah by humility and wisdom.
The length of Jephthah's judging his people was short, six years, but full of the work of salvation and striving for his people, and he was buried in one of the cities of the region of Gilead.

Bethlehem: it is either the Bethlehem which is in the tribe of Zebulun and lies west of Nazareth at a distance of 9 km, or the one in the tribe of Judah, which lies south of Jerusalem at a distance of 9 km, and which is where Christ was born.

After the death of Jephthah, the next judge was Ibzan of Bethlehem. We can infer from the fact that the inspired writer does not mention any military work of his that the time of his judging was a peaceful time in which the people enjoyed calm, and his work was limited to judging his people and guiding them to God's commandments and law.

He had a large number of sons and daughters (thirty sons and thirty daughters), for the custom in that time was marrying more than one wife. And he gave his daughters in marriage to men from outside his clan or outside his city, perhaps because the clan was small, or there were no young men in the city suitable for becoming his in-laws. The period of his judging was seven years.
He died in quietness after begetting many sons and daughters and marrying them all off.

Ibzan was followed in judging by another judge, Elon the Zebulonite, called the Zebulonite because he was of the tribe of Zebulun. The inspired writer does not mention any wars that took place in his days, so he judged Israel in quietness ten years.

Elon: a town, the meaning of whose name is an oak, and perhaps oak trees were plentiful in this city, which lies in the portion of the tribe of Zebulun; it is different from the Elon that lies in the portion of the tribe of Dan (Josh 19:43). Elon died and was buried in his city, "the town of Elon," in the land of Zebulun.
Pirathon: it lies southwest of Nablus (Shechem) at a distance of 11 km.
After "Elon," "Abdon the son of Hillel" of the town of Pirathon in the land of Ephraim judged Israel.

It appears from the inspired text that he lived long, for he begat forty sons, and lived to see thirty grandsons, who also grew up to ride with their fathers on seventy ass colts, as was the way of the notables of the people in those times. The length of his judging was eight years.
He died and was buried in his town Pirathon in the land of Ephraim, beside the mountain named after the Amalekites, where the Amalekite people dwelt at one period of ancient history.

If God gives you peace, make use of it to live by His commandments and teach them to those around you, so that you bind everyone's hearts to Him and they are not disturbed if troubles come upon them because of their holding fast to God.

The birth of Samson (1) The angel of the LORD appears to Samson's mother (vv. 1-5:) 1 And the children of Israel did evil again in the sight of the LORD; and the LORD delivered them into the hand of the Philistines forty years. 2 And there was a certain man of Zorah, of the family of the Danites, whose name was Manoah; and his wife was barren, and bare not. 3 And the angel of the LORD appeared unto the woman, and said unto her, Behold now, thou art barren, and bearest not: but thou shalt conceive, and bear a son. 4 Now therefore beware, I pray thee, and drink not wine nor strong drink, and eat not any unclean thing: 5 For, lo, thou shalt conceive, and bear a son; and no razor shall come on his head: for the child shall be a Nazarite unto God from the womb: and he shall begin to deliver Israel out of the hand of the Philistines.

The Philistines: a strong people who dwelt in the south of the land of Canaan; they are of the descendants of the Caphtorim, who dwelt on the island of Crete and then migrated to these lands and took possession of them.

Beginning with this chapter and through the following three chapters, the inspired writer acquaints us with one of the most prominent judges of Israel and gives us many details about his life and works. In the first verse of this chapter he gives us the condition of the people of God before the birth of Samson. The people had suffered from the Philistines' enslaving them for forty years, which ended with what is related in (1 Sam 7:13), that is, in the days of Eli the priest. This was a divine punishment for them for turning away - again - from the worship of the living God, as though they had not benefited from the lessons of their former falls.

Zorah: a city at the southern edge of the tribe of Judah, about 14 miles west of Jerusalem and 23 miles southeast of Joppa (map 10). Here the inspired writer begins by mentioning Samson's family and the story of the good tidings of his birth. His father, whose name was "Manoah," was from the town of Zorah, of the tribe of the Danites. And Manoah's wife was barren.

The angel of the LORD: either an ordinary angel or one of the appearances of God, as proved by what is said in (vv. 17, 22) that his name is wonderful, and also by Manoah's saying "We have seen God" (v. 22). The angel of the LORD appeared to Manoah's wife, announcing to her that God would remove her barrenness and she would conceive and bear a son.

"Drink not wine nor strong drink": wine is fermented grape juice, with a small proportion of alcohol, while strong drink is aged wine with a large proportion of alcohol. This applies to any kind of wine, whether taken from grapes or from something else.

The angel commanded her not to drink wine or strong drink, and also warned her against eating what the law had forbidden of animals and birds (Lev 11). By this he meant her purity and her keeping away from forbidden strong drink, and also not being occupied with material pleasures, that is, drinking naturally fermented wine, which has a small proportion of alcohol.

This shows the importance of the preparation of expectant mothers to receive the newborn. Since they are a grace from God, they ought to prepare by strengthening their relationship with the Church and the Holy Sacraments, prayers and readings, and keeping away from sins in a repentance that purifies their souls, so that they may be worthy to be mothers of these children, and not affect their unborn children with any foreign substances that they drink.
"He shall begin to deliver": Samson began delivering his people from the Philistines, and Samuel, Saul and David completed the deliverance.
"No razor shall come on his head": hair was shaved with the razor, and the law of the Nazarite required that the Nazarite not shave his head throughout the period of his vow.

The purity which the angel required her to keep was necessary for her sanctification, because the son who would be born of her would be a Nazarite to the Lord from his birth and all his life, and had to apply the law of the Nazarite, as it is said in (Num 6:
3-21), among which is that he not shave the hair of his head. The angel also announced to her that this son of hers would deliver Israel from the hand of the Philistines.

(2) The angel instructs Manoah (vv. 6-14:) 6 Then the woman came and told her husband, saying, A man of God came unto me, and his countenance was like the countenance of an angel of God, very terrible: but I asked him not whence he was, neither told he me his name: 7 But he said unto me, Behold, thou shalt conceive, and bear a son; and now drink no wine nor strong drink, neither eat any unclean thing: for the child shall be a Nazarite to God from the womb to the day of his death. 8 Then Manoah intreated the LORD, and said, O my Lord, let the man of God which thou didst send come again unto us, and teach us what we shall do unto the child that shall be born. 9 And God hearkened to the voice of Manoah; and the angel of God came again unto the woman as she sat in the field: but Manoah her husband was not with her. 10 And the woman made haste, and ran, and shewed her husband, and said unto him, Behold, the man hath appeared unto me, that came unto me the other day. 11 And Manoah arose, and went after his wife, and came to the man, and said unto him, Art thou the man that spakest unto the woman? And he said, I am. 12 And Manoah said, Now let thy words come to pass. How shall we order the child, and how shall we do unto him? 13 And the angel of the LORD said unto Manoah, Of all that I said unto the woman let her beware. 14 She may not eat of any thing that cometh of the vine, neither let her drink wine or strong drink, nor eat any unclean thing: all that I commanded her let her observe.

Manoah's wife was outside her house when the angel came to her, and when he spoke to her what is said in (vv. 4, 5) she hastened to the house to tell her husband what had happened, that a messenger from God had come to her whose appearance was awesome, and because of the awe of the situation she was not able to ask him where he had come from, and he too did not tell her his name.

She also told him the good tidings he had brought, that she would conceive and bear a son, and that she must not drink wine or anything intoxicating and must not eat any of the unclean foods that the law had forbidden, because her coming son would be a Nazarite to the Lord from his formation as an embryo in his mother's womb and throughout all the days of his life.

Manoah believed what his wife said, and since he was a devout man he prayed to God, asking that the angel whom He had sent to them return and make known to him how to deal with his son and guide him to the kind of upbringing in which he should raise him.
"God hearkened": God answered.

God answered Manoah's request, and the angel came again to his wife while she was in the field alone and her husband was not with her. It appears that Manoah's wife was devout, so he appeared to her first, and then a second time, while she was alone, before she called her husband.
The woman ran to where her husband was and told him that the messenger who had come to her some days before had appeared to her again in the field.

They hastened together to the field where his wife had seen the messenger, and he found him and asked him whether he was the very person who had spoken with his wife, and he answered him that he was the same.

Manoah said to him, when what he had announced to them was fulfilled, that God would give them a son, how they should act toward him in terms of upbringing and dealing with him, and what their duties toward him were.

It is good for parents to ask guidance and wisdom from the Lord in raising their children and dealing with them, so that they grow up in the fear of the Lord and grow in the bosom of the teachings of their mother Church, and thereby guard them from any deviations or evil company that might lead them into crooked ways; rather the word of the Lord embraces them and is their guide and educator, and the Lord blesses them and they grow spiritually, mentally and physically, and His blessing works in them and supports their steps.
"Anything that cometh of the vine": everything that comes from the grapevine, that is, moist grapes or raisins whose fermentation has begun.

The angel assured him that what was required of them was the same as he had said before to his wife at his first appearing to her, and repeated to him what he had commanded her, namely that she not eat of the grapes, which is the same as what is said in (Num 6:4) of details forbidding the Nazarite to eat anything fermented that comes from the grapevine; and that she not drink wine or any strong drink, and not eat of the birds and animals that the law had specified as unclean. He also repeated to him his warning to his wife that she keep entirely from all that he had mentioned to her. And Manoah and his wife carry out these warnings, and also the child who will be born to them and be a Nazarite to God.

(3) Manoah's feast for the angel (vv. 15-20:) 15 And Manoah said unto the angel of the LORD, I pray thee, let us detain thee, until we shall have made ready a kid for thee. 16 And the angel of the LORD said unto Manoah, Though thou detain me, I will not eat of thy bread: and if thou wilt offer a burnt offering, thou must offer it unto the LORD. For Manoah knew not that he was an angel of the LORD. 17 And Manoah said unto the angel of the LORD, What is thy name, that when thy sayings come to pass we may do thee honour? 18 And the angel of the LORD said unto him, Why askest thou thus after my name, seeing it is secret? 19 So Manoah took a kid with a meat offering, and offered it upon a rock unto the LORD: and the angel did wondrously; and Manoah and his wife looked on. 20 For it came to pass, when the flame went up toward heaven from off the altar, that the angel of the LORD ascended in the flame of the altar. And Manoah and his wife looked on it, and fell on their faces to the ground.
"Let us detain thee": allow us to delay you for some time.

Manoah and his wife rejoiced at the good tidings, and desiring to honor the guest, and having thought the angel to be a man, a messenger or a prophet, they asked him to stay a little with them so that they might prepare something for him to eat, that is, slaughter a kid and cook it to perform the duty of hospitality toward him.

The angel answered him that even if he stayed with him a longer time and he offered him food, he would not eat of his food, and by this he drew Manoah's attention that he was not a man who eats and drinks. And the angel guided him that what he wished to offer, he should offer as a burnt offering to the Lord.

Up to this moment Manoah had not realized the identity of the man who was speaking to him, for he still believed that he was a man, that is, a prophet or a man of God, but in the end a man. Therefore he asked him his name, so that when what he had announced to them was fulfilled he might do for him what would express in a fitting way his thanks and gratitude to him.

The angel rejects Manoah's asking him his name, showing him that his name is wonderful, higher than his understanding. And God told Isaiah that His name shall be called Wonderful, referring to it (... Isa 9:6). He means that he is not a man but an angel from God, who has no ordinary name like the rest of mankind, or he is God Himself, whose name is above the names of all men.

Manoah obeyed the angel in what he guided him to, offering up the offering as a burnt offering to the Lord, so he took the kid and put it on a rock, which was like an altar, and kindled the fire in it, or put it there, and fire came out of the rock to consume the sacrifice, as happened with Gideon (ch. 6); and a wonderful thing accompanied that offering, at which Manoah and his wife were astonished, and the surprise stunned them, for they found the person who had been speaking to them ascending in the flame of the fire toward heaven, so they were greatly afraid and trembled at this wonderful sight, and bowed to the ground in awe and worship and thanksgiving to the God who had accepted their offering, because they were sure that this person was the angel of God or God Himself, for he is spirit and not a man with a body.

It is good to honor everyone who brings you glad tidings, and especially one who speaks to you about God and the salvation of your soul, for you honor God by honoring His servants, and He also, seeing your love, will bless you and reveal Himself to you more clearly.

(4) The birth of Samson (vv. 21-25:) 21 But the angel of the LORD did no more appear to Manoah and to his wife. Then Manoah knew that he was an angel of the LORD. 22 And Manoah said unto his wife, We shall surely die, because we have seen God. 23 But his wife said unto him, If the LORD were pleased to kill us, he would not have received a burnt offering and a meat offering at our hands, neither would he have shewed us all these things, nor would as at this time have told us such things as these. 24 And the woman bare a son, and called his name Samson: and the child grew, and the LORD blessed him. 25 And the Spirit of the LORD began to move him at times in the camp of Dan between Zorah and Eshtaol.

The coming out of the fire from the rock and the ascent of the angel in the flame of the fire confirmed to Manoah and his wife that the person who had spoken to them was the angel of the Lord, who had appeared to them in the form of a man. And with God's message having reached them, the angel ended his mission, and there was no need for him to appear to them again.

The children of Israel kept what Moses had said to them on the basis of the Lord's declaration to him that man shall not see God and live. And Manoah believed that the One who had appeared to him was God, who had appeared to him in some form, so he said to his wife that they would die immediately because they had seen God.

His wife was devout, so she reassured him, saying that if God had wanted them to die He would not have shown them those wonderful, joyful things: His glad tidings to them by means of the angel whom He sent to them, of their soon begetting a son who would be a Nazarite to the Lord, and also His acceptance of the offering from their hands by the coming out of the fire from the rock, which consumed the offering.

Samson: a word meaning exalted or great, or meaning the sun for its strength and greatness. The Lord's promise was fulfilled and Manoah's wife bore a son, after she had been barren, and called him Samson. And the boy grew spiritually and physically, and the Lord blessed him to qualify him for the great work that He would entrust to him.
Zorah: a city lying about 22 km west of Jerusalem on the border between the tribes of Dan and Judah.

Eshtaol: it lies about 2.5 km east of Zorah (map 10). The Spirit of the Lord began to work in him, and the features of a distinguished personality worthy of the esteem of his people appeared in him, and he was active among them in the region where the tribe of Dan dwelt, between the towns of Zorah and Eshtaol.

The Spirit of God who worked in Samson dwells in you permanently and is able to bring you nearer to the worship of God and the love of all, if you submit to Him by repentance, holding fast to the commandments and accepting God's arrangements in your life. Samson's marriage to a Philistine woman

entries.section: (1) Samson asks his parents to get him a Philistine girl as wife

paragraphs.text: Timnath: a city in the tribe of Judah, given to the tribe of Dan (Josh 15:10, 19:43), but the Philistines recovered it. It lies near the city of Zorah but at a level about 250 meters lower, because Zorah, the city of Samson and his parents, stands about 50 meters above sea level (map 12). Samson went down from Zorah to Timnath, inhabited by the Philistines, and took a liking to a Philistine girl there.

entries.section: (1) Samson asks his parents to get him a Philistine girl as wife

paragraphs.text: When he returned to Zorah he told his parents that he had seen in Timnath a Philistine woman who pleased him and that he wanted to marry her, and he asked them to betroth her to him as a wife. It is a tradition still followed in most societies that parents betroth wives for their sons.

entries.section: (1) Samson asks his parents to get him a Philistine girl as wife

paragraphs.text: "The uncircumcised Philistines": that is, those not circumcised. Circumcision was a symbol or sign of the covenant between God and His people (Gen 17:10, 11 - Deut 21:10); what is meant is the uncircumcised Philistine men, of whose people this girl was.

These steps were contrary to the law and to the Lord's warnings to His people not to mix with strangers and intermarry with them, lest they draw His people into pagan worship (Deut 7:3, 4). His devout parents knew what the law imposed, so they questioned him about his choice and proposed to him marriage to the daughters of his own kin, but he insisted on his request. Here the mastery of the desire for women over Samson appears, for when he took a liking to a pagan girl he broke the law and wanted to marry her, forgetting that he was a Nazarite of God, and the Nazarite today is equivalent to the consecrated servant, that is, one who holds fast to God's commandments with exactness.

Do not submit to your desires and so break God's commandments, especially at marriage, and neglect the guidance of your parents, for you will meet troubles you will be forced to bear all your life; rather let God be your guide through many prayers, in addition to the guidance of all who are loyal to you.

entries.section: (1) Samson asks his parents to get him a Philistine girl as wife

paragraphs.text: "But his father and his mother knew not that it was of the LORD": it was by the guidance of the Lord, to be the cause of fighting the Philistines.

His parents did not know that God, in His arrangement for the deliverance of the children of Israel by the hand of Samson, had allowed this situation in order to take vengeance on the Philistines who had humbled His people. This does not mean that God pushed him into the error, but He used his error to be the cause of disciplining the Philistines and requiting them, because the Philistines were dominating the children of Israel and harassing them. As the Scripture says, "All things work together for good to them that love God" (Rom 8:28). And this expression which the inspired writer used, "that it was of the LORD," means by God's permission to discipline the Philistines; so what Samson did was an error which God turned to the good of His people.

entries.section: (2) The story of Samson's killing the lion

paragraphs.text: "The Spirit of the LORD came mightily upon him": the Holy Spirit came upon him to give him courage and strength.

Samson's parents yielded to his request, on which he insisted, and went with him to Timnath, and passed through a place full of grapevines. Samson's steps were faster than his parents' steps, and behold a young lion met him on his way, and as soon as it saw Samson before it, it began to roar, ready to attack. Here divine providence intervened to give Samson strength and courage to seize the lion and rend it in two as though it were a small kid, and what Samson did was without a weapon in his hand. Samson did this without telling his parents what he had done, out of humility on his part and giving the credit to the One who deserves it, God, who grants strength.

entries.section: (2) The story of Samson's killing the lion

paragraphs.text: They all reached Timnath and went forward to betroth the Philistine woman whom Samson had liked earlier from her appearance, and now his liking for her increased after he had talked with her. And after he betrothed her he returned with his parents to the city of Zorah.

entries.section: (2) The story of Samson's killing the lion

paragraphs.text: "The carcase": the body of the lion and its skeleton.
"A swarm of bees": a group of bees making a hive.

They all returned to Zorah, and after several days they travelled again to Timnath - after the period of betrothal had ended - to complete the marriage. On their way toward Timnath Samson turned toward the place where he had wrestled with the lion to see what had become of the carcass of the lion, and its body had turned into a skeleton and had become a suitable place for bees to form a hive to make honey.

entries.section: (2) The story of Samson's killing the lion

paragraphs.text: "He took thereof": he took from it.

Samson took some of the honey in his hands and ate of it, and carried some of it to his parents, and did not tell them that he had taken it from the mouth of the lion, perhaps so that they would not refrain from eating it because it was from the inside of a dead animal, which the law forbids.
The law forbade touching dead bodies, but the body may have decomposed and nothing remained but the skeleton, or it may have been a weakness in Samson that he was not exact in carrying out the law.

God is able to give you strength to face dangers however hard they are, and is able also to turn tribulation into a blessing, as Samson overcame the lion and even turned its bones into a beehive from whose honey Samson ate. So do not be disturbed by tribulations, but ask God's help and trust in His support.
They all reached Timnath to complete the marriage and stayed as guests with the woman's family, and Samson held a wedding feast, as is customary in all ages and even now.

According to the customs in force in those times, when the bride's family saw that Samson was preparing a wedding feast, they invited thirty Philistine young men to sit with him at his feast and rejoice with him.
"Sheets": the garment worn underneath, which may be short.
"Change of garments": a robe reaching to the feet and worn outside, which may be embroidered.

The time of the feast came, and it was customary for it to be seven days, and Samson proposed to the Philistine young men who sat with him that he would tell them a riddle; if they could solve it he would give them thirty shirts and thirty robes, and if they could not, they had to give him thirty shirts and thirty robes. The young men accepted the conditions Samson set both in case they arrived at the solution of the riddle and in case they did not. And they showed readiness to hear the riddle, thinking that it was one of the common riddles that would not be hard for them to solve.

Samson told them the riddle in a beautiful poetic form: that out of the eater (he means the lion) came forth meat (that is, food), and out of the strong (he means the carcass of the lion, which had become bones) came forth sweetness (he means honey). The Philistine young men thought for three days and could not solve the riddle.
"Have ye called us to take that we have? is it not so?": was your inviting us to the feast intended to rob us, by our presenting robes and shirts to you.
"Entice thy husband": use guile on him.

The Philistine young men resorted to trickery to reach the solution of the riddle, so they went to the bride, Samson's wife, and urged her to use guile on Samson so as to learn from him the solution of the riddle, and they threatened her that they would burn her and her father's house with fire if she did not learn from him the solution of the riddle and bring it to them. They were extremely angry, denouncing the idea that the purpose of their invitation to the wedding was to rob them and force them to present shirts and robes.

Samson's wife pressed him and began to beg him in every way and flatter him, and wept to move his heart, and accused him of not loving her, for how could he tell a riddle to the young men of her people without making her know the solution of the riddle? And Samson would tell her that he had not told anyone, not even his parents, the solution of the riddle, so how could she be angry that he did not tell her the solution?
"She told the riddle to the children of her people": she told the children of her people the solution of the riddle as Samson had told it to her.

Samson's wife was most insistent on knowing the solution of the riddle, for the alternative was the Philistine young men's carrying out their threat to burn her and her family. So she persisted in her begging and weeping until she spoiled for him the joy of the wedding, and the feast turned for him into a lamentation instead of joy, and she troubled him so much that in the end he was compelled to tell her the solution of the riddle, and all she did was pass the solution on to the sons of her people. This shows Samson's weakness before the tears of women, for the desire for women had gained mastery over his heart and abolished his reason.

"If ye had not plowed with my heifer, ye had not found out my riddle": the heifer is the female of the cow or the buffalo, which was used in pulling the plow, and what is meant by it here is his wife; this is a deliberate comparison, meaning that if they had not resorted to his wife and pressed her, they could not have solved the riddle.

When the Philistines learned the solution of the riddle before the seventh day ended, they went to Samson and told him the solution, meaning that there is nothing sweeter than honey and nothing stronger than a lion. Samson was enraged, telling them that had they not laughed at his wife and resorted to her to learn the riddle, and pressed her as with a plow until they drew out what was inside her, as the plow brings out of the earth what is in its depths, they could not have solved it.
"He slew thirty men of them, and took their spoil": he took their clothes as booty after killing them.

Here a new coming of the Holy Spirit upon Samson took place to give him courage and strength, and he went to Ashkelon, one of the coastal cities of the Philistines, lying north of Gaza, and there he killed thirty men and brought their garments to the thirty young men who had revealed the solution of the riddle, according to the agreed wager. And Samson was very angry because the Philistines had used guile on his wife and because his wife had told them the solution of the riddle, so he did not complete the days of rejoicing at the wedding and did not enjoy it, but left his wife and went back to his father's house in Zorah.

We notice that the strength that was with Samson came from the coming of the Spirit of the Lord upon him and not from his hair; rather his hair is a sign of his love, his vow and the consecration of his life to God, and therefore, because of his submission to God, the Spirit of the Lord works in him.
"His companion, whom he had used as his friend": one of Samson's acquaintances, who perhaps helped him in the arrangements for the wedding.

The bride's father thought that Samson's leaving his wife without completing the days of rejoicing and returning to his country meant that he hated her and no longer wanted her as a wife, so he gave her to his companion, and this was a rashness on the part of the bride's father that led to bad results that we shall learn of afterward. Samson's leaving his wife was because of his anger at her for exposing his riddle, and afterward he would return to her.

Do not be hasty in your judgments, but seek God in prayer and also the counsel of your father of confession and of those who are loyal to you, so that you do not err, especially in great decisions, for what comes out of your mouth may be hard to correct. Samson takes vengeance on the Philistines for giving his wife in marriage to another

entries.section: (1) Samson's anger at his wife's marriage to another

paragraphs.text: "Visited his wife": he wanted to visit his wife.

After some time since leaving his wife and returning to his father's house, when the fierceness of his anger over the matter of the riddle had calmed, he decided to visit his wife, perhaps to be reconciled with her, and he took with him a kid as a gift, as was common in those days. This was in the days of the wheat harvest, that is, the days of spring.

entries.section: (1) Samson's anger at his wife's marriage to another

paragraphs.text: Samson wanted to be alone with his wife in the room set apart for her, but her father prevented him and told him that she was no longer his wife, for when he left her in his anger and went away they thought that he no longer wanted her as a wife, and one of his companions had come forward asking for her hand and they had in fact given her to him in marriage. And wishing to appease Samson, her father proposed to him that he marry her younger sister, praising her as better than the first.

entries.section: (1) Samson's anger at his wife's marriage to another

paragraphs.text: This matter again aroused Samson's anger greatly, and he told them that now there was no blame on him if he punished the Philistines for the wrong they had done him, for the error was not the father's alone but was shared by his people, who could have prevented the girl's father from this conduct.

entries.section: (1) Samson's anger at his wife's marriage to another

paragraphs.text: "Firebrands": materials that can be kindled, such as cloth.
Jackal: an animal living in Palestine, in size between the wolf and the fox.
"Burnt up the shocks": the shocks are the heaps of grain found on the threshing floors, which are wide areas beside the fields.

Samson took three hundred animals called jackals, and tied every two tails together and tied firebrands to the tails and then kindled them and let them loose among the fields of the Philistines. The animals, their tails on fire, began to run in madness at speed and burned the heaps of grain, the grapevines, the olive orchards and all the crops.

entries.section: (1) Samson's anger at his wife's marriage to another

paragraphs.text: "The Timnite": Samson's father-in-law, who was from the city of Timnath.

The Philistines asked one another who could have done this, and learned that it was Samson, and that he had done it because his father-in-law had given his wife to his companion. The Philistines were very enraged at Samson because he had caused them heavy losses, so they seized Samson's father-in-law and burned him and his daughter and all his house, in vengeance on their part and as a satisfaction to Samson so that he would cease harming them.

entries.section: (1) Samson's anger at his wife's marriage to another

paragraphs.text: Samson's anger did not abate after the burning of the woman and her father, and he was not appeased, as the Philistines had intended by burning her, but threatened the Philistines with more acts of vengeance on them in keeping with the wrong they had done him, and after that he would cease from them.

entries.section: (1) Samson's anger at his wife's marriage to another

paragraphs.text: "He smote them hip and thigh": that is, he achieved a great victory over them.
"Top" (cleft): a cave.

Etam: a Hebrew word meaning the lair of wild beasts; it lies east of Zorah at a distance of 4 km. Samson won a great victory over them and killed a great number of them, and it was a great slaughter, and then he went to hide in a cave.
Know that God is just and will punish you for your sins if you do not repent of them, and the punishment of sin is death, so hasten to repentance to obtain God's forgiveness and mercies.

entries.section: (2) The Philistines try to seize Samson

paragraphs.text: "Went up": the Philistines dwell south of the tribe of Judah, so their going up means their moving northward. Lehi: a high place, so called after Samson's victory over the Philistines with the lehi of an ass, that is, the jawbone of an ass.
Large numbers of the Philistines entered the land of Judah and spread out in a place near Zorah - Samson's homeland - in order to seize him and take vengeance on him.

entries.section: (2) The Philistines try to seize Samson

paragraphs.text: "Why are ye come up against us?": why have you entered our lands?

The men of Judah asked the Philistines the reason for their coming into their lands, since there was at present no reason to fight them, for they were subject to slavery and had not declared disobedience or risen against them or fought them. The Philistines answered that they had come to look for Samson in order to take vengeance on him because he had burned their farms and crops and killed great numbers of them.

entries.section: (2) The Philistines try to seize Samson

paragraphs.text: The men of Judah knew the place where Samson was hiding, so three thousand men of them went to him at the rock of Etam and reproached him for provoking the Philistines, who dominated them and whom they were unable to face. His answer to them was that he had not begun evil toward them, but it was they who began to wrong him, so what he did to them was a repayment of the wrong they had done him.

entries.section: (2) The Philistines try to seize Samson

paragraphs.text: The men of Judah wanted to guard against the evil of the Philistines, who were poised against them, by handing Samson over to them, and they told him what they intended to do, which was to seize him and deliver him bound to the Philistines. Samson agreed with them on condition that they themselves would not harm him or kill him, and he asked them to swear to that.

Perhaps the children of Israel felt that one, Samson, should die for the whole people exposed to the Philistines' attacks. By this they signify the Jewish nation, which delivered Christ to the Romans to die, not for the nation only but for the whole world, as Caiaphas the high priest prophesied (Jn 11:50).

entries.section: (2) The Philistines try to seize Samson

paragraphs.text: "Two new cords": that is, in perfect firmness and strength.

They promised him that they would not kill him but would bind him with ropes and deliver him to the Philistines, and then they bound him with two new cords and brought him out of the cave to deliver him into the enemies' hand.

Do not let fear move you to betray God and wrong His servants, as the tribe of Judah did by handing Samson over, but when fear fights you, ask God's help, and He will protect you and the servants of God.

entries.section: (3) Samson kills a thousand Philistine men with the jawbone of an ass

paragraphs.text: They brought him, bound with the ropes, to the town of Lehi, where the Philistines were waiting, and as soon as they saw him they raised their voices in exultation as they advanced toward him to get at him. And once again God gave him mighty strength, and he broke the strong ropes with which he was bound, which before his strength became a frail, weak thing like burnt flax.

entries.section: (3) Samson kills a thousand Philistine men with the jawbone of an ass
