paragraphs.text: "The jawbone of an ass": the jaw of an ass.

Samson had no weapon of any kind in his hand, but he looked around him and found the jaw of an ass that had recently died, a fresh, supple jaw that does not break easily as a dry one does, so he seized it and struck the Philistines with it and killed a thousand men of them, and the rest fled.

entries.section: (3) Samson kills a thousand Philistine men with the jawbone of an ass

paragraphs.text: "With the jawbone of an ass, heaps upon heaps": he heaped their bodies in heaps with the jawbone of an ass.
Samson looked at the corpses piled on one another and began to say that with the jaw of an ass he had turned the enemy into heaps of slain: he had killed a thousand men and heaped them in two heaps.

entries.section: (3) Samson kills a thousand Philistine men with the jawbone of an ass

paragraphs.text: The words that Samson said were like a song of victory, and as soon as he finished chanting them he cast the jaw of the ass from his hand and called the place where he threw it "Ramath-lehi," which in the Hebrew language means the place where the jaw was cast, as expressed in Arabic.

entries.section: (3) Samson kills a thousand Philistine men with the jawbone of an ass

paragraphs.text: Samson was tired from striking the Philistines and exhausted from wrestling with them, and he became extremely thirsty, until he felt he was nearly dying of his thirst. So he turned to the Lord and prayed to Him, saying: You have wrought by my hand this great victory, and this is a confession from Samson that the strength is from God and not from himself, so will You be content that I die now of thirst and fall into the hand of the uncircumcised, that is, the uncircumcised Philistines?

entries.section: (3) Samson kills a thousand Philistine men with the jawbone of an ass

paragraphs.text: "God clave an hollow place that was in the jaw": the hollow is a concave spot in the ground, that is, a pit, from which God brought out much water by a divine miracle.

En-hakkore: a Hebrew word meaning "the spring of the one who called," since Samson called upon the Lord in this place when he was thirsty (map 12). Since Samson had confessed that the victory achieved was from God, God answered his prayer and brought forth water for him from a dry spring, which is a spring of water that dries up in the summer season; God made water in it at a time when there was none. Samson drank and his spirit revived after he had almost died of thirst. And as a memorial of God's answering his prayer, the place was called En-hakkore, and the spring became a permanently flowing spring until the time the book was written.

entries.section: (3) Samson kills a thousand Philistine men with the jawbone of an ass

paragraphs.text: Samson judged Israel in the days when the Philistines were dominating the children of Israel, and the length of his judging was twenty years; and although he did not deliver his people with a decisive deliverance, he was a source of fear and anxiety to their enemies and so broke the sharpness of their tyranny over his people.

As long as God is with you, do not be disturbed by the power of demons or of your enemies however many they are, and do not fear them however weak your means, for God is your strength and your victory.
The death of Samson

After the great victory that Samson achieved over the Philistines who wanted to seize him, he became feared in all the five great Philistine cities, so he would enter and leave them without anyone daring to molest him. On one of his visits to the city of Gaza, the greatest of the Philistine cities, desire was stirred in his heart when he saw, or heard of, a harlot, and he went into her house to sin with her. This shows two things:
1- The importance of being on guard after victory against the devil, because he devises snares for us, and the matter needs greater exactness and holding fast to God's commandments.
2- The Holy Bible shows the virtues of the saints and their sins so that we too may be encouraged if we sin and repent, for repentance turns fornicators and sinners into saints.

Concentrate on your aim in life, which is the Kingdom of Heaven, for when Samson neglected his aim, namely the salvation of his people, he was drawn away by the desire for women, and his enemies overpowered him, as will appear later. Remind yourself at the beginning of every day of your aim, so that if you are distracted from it you return to it quickly.

The Philistines in Gaza heard that Samson had come to their city, and the desire to take vengeance on him awoke again in their souls. So they surrounded the house in which he was staying, while another group of them encamped at the gate of the city so that he would not go out by it, and they waited in silence until morning to seize him.

Contrary to the expectation of the people of Gaza, Samson arose in the middle of the night and came to the gate of the city while everyone was asleep, and pulled out the gate with its two leaves, its two posts and its bar, and put the whole on his shoulders and went up to one of the mountains facing the city of Hebron, that is, he headed for a mountain lying between the cities of Gaza and Hebron, and threw the uprooted gate on the mountain and went his way.

If the Philistines boasted of their bodily strength, which appeared afterward in the form of Goliath the giant (1 Sam 17), God sends them a person from His people stronger than all their imaginings, that perhaps they might believe in God and reject their idols.
The valley of Sorek: a valley that begins 21 km west of Jerusalem and extends to the Mediterranean Sea (map 10). Delilah: a name meaning pampered.
For the third time Samson falls into the snare of a pagan woman, whose name was Delilah, a Philistine woman from the valley of Sorek.
The shekel of silver: equal to about 15 grams.
"See wherein his great strength lieth, and by what means we may prevail against him": learn from him the secret of his extraordinary strength and how we can overpower him and overcome him.

The Philistines were waiting for an opportunity to take vengeance on Samson, and when they learned of his attachment to Delilah, and they thought that Samson carried exceptional strength as the result of a magical work which, if annulled, would make him lose his strength and become an ordinary man who could be controlled, five of their chiefs went to Delilah and persuaded her to show him affection and coax him until she learned from him the secret of his strength, and each of them would give her, as a reward for this service of hers, a thousand shekels of silver.
Delilah yielded to the Philistines' demand of her and asked Samson about the source of his strength and with what he could be bound so that he could be controlled.
"Withs" (cords): they were mostly made from the intestines of animals.

Samson told her that his strength would depart and he would become like any ordinary man if he were bound with seven fresh cords. Of course this was a lie, because he knew that Delilah might reveal his secret to the Philistines, for he had been deceived before by his first wife, the Philistine of Timnath, when she revealed the solution of the riddle; so he deceived Delilah and continued with her to enjoy his desire. And this is a great error, for a person to make light of the devil's wars; he should have fled from the passions and so saved himself from what would happen to him when the Philistines seized him.

Sin draws on to other sins, for because Samson submitted to the desire of fornication, he also allowed himself lying. If only you would be careful and cut off sin from its beginning by repentance and keeping away from its sources, lest it draw you on to other sins.

Delilah passed on to the chiefs of the Philistines what Samson had told her, and they prepared for her seven cords with which she bound him tightly, perhaps while he was asleep by the effect of a drug.
"A thread of tow": the weak threads left over after the spinning of flax, which are not fit to be twisted to form strong threads, but can be used in lamps for light.

The Philistines were hiding in Samson's house until Delilah should bind him with the cords, and when she finished binding him she called to him, saying: The Philistines are upon thee, Samson. He awoke from his sleep and broke the cords as a thread of tow is broken, for what Samson had said about the secret of his strength was a deception, so they had not yet arrived at the secret.
"Behold, thou hast mocked me": behold, you have deceived me.
Delilah reproached him for deceiving her and lying to her, and repeated to him the same question, that is, with what he could be bound so that his strength would depart.
When she pressed him for the second time, he told her that his strength would depart if he were bound with new ropes which had not yet been used.

Delilah believed him this time also and bound him with new ropes as he said, and the Philistines were hiding in the house as happened the first time, waiting for the signal to come out of their hiding place and seize him. When Delilah cried out, saying as the previous time, "The Philistines be upon thee, Samson," Samson arose and broke the new ropes as though they were a thin thread.
"The web": the lengthwise threads on the loom, as distinct from the weft, which is the crosswise threads.

The scene was repeated for the third time, for the woman came back again and repeated to him her reproach for deceiving her, and asked him not to repeat what he had done but to be truthful this time and tell her with what and how he might be bound so that his strength would be weakened. So he told her that this would be if she wove the seven locks of his head with the web and fastened them with the pin (v. 14). Samson had braided his hair in seven braids. And the number "7" signifies perfection, and in this he was exact in the outward signs of the vow, but he was careless in what is more important, the evil desires.
"The pin": a piece of wood fixed in the ground to which the ropes of the tent are tied; what is meant by it here may be the lengthwise or horizontal beam of the loom, made of wood.

Delilah did what he told her, and his hair became fixed and interwoven with the threads as though it were of the same fabric, and Delilah was not content with that but, to make the binding firmer still, bound his locks and the threads of the fabric most tightly to the pin of the loom. And when she finished that she cried out, "The Philistines be upon thee, Samson," and Samson awoke from his sleep and pulled the pin from the loom and broke the threads of the fabric.

We marvel here at Samson's continuing in Delilah's hands while knowing that she wanted to reveal his secret to the Philistines, as his wife in Timnath had done, but he submitted because the desire had gained mastery over him, and he kept parleying with her so as not to lose his enjoyment of fornication. Perhaps in pride he trusted in his ability to parley and lie, but unfortunately he fell in the end into the hands of the Philistines because he did not flee for his life from sin but was careless and parleyed with it.

Delilah was angry and told him that he claimed to love her but did not prove it in practice, for he had deceived her three times and had not told her the secret of his strength, so where was that love he claimed ... And Delilah did not despair but continued to press him and kept troubling him with word and deed, until his soul could no longer bear more pressure from her, for his distress reached a great degree, until he was close to death.
"He told her all his heart": he confided his secret to her.
"There hath not come a razor upon mine head": he had not shaved the hair of his head since his birth.

At last Samson weakened before Delilah and was not able to go on keeping the secret, so he revealed to her the secret of his strength, telling her that he was a Nazarite of the Lord (that is, consecrated to the Lord), and one of the conditions of the vow was that no razor come upon his head; if his hair were shaved, his strength would leave him, for by this he would have departed from his vow and turned back from his covenant with God.

We must beware in any special relationship we form with others that it not be a cause of corrupting our spirituality and turning us aside from the path of our salvation. Let us flee for our lives from every relationship that binds us with bonds we may not be able to break free from, so that we remain captives to them, as happened with Samson, whose bodily inclinations gained mastery over his conduct and cast him into perils that could have been avoided if he had been able to free himself from them.
"Lords": chiefs.

Delilah felt that she had succeeded this time in drawing him on to reveal his secret, and that he had been truthful in disclosing it to her, so she sent to the Philistines, assuring them that this time was not like the previous ones and that she had indeed obtained from him the secret of his strength, and they went to her with the reward they had promised her.

Perhaps this was from the effect of an intoxicating drink such as wine that was offered to him, for he slept unconscious on Delilah's knees, and she called a man who cut off the seven locks of his hair. And when he returned to consciousness signs of weakness appeared on him, and Delilah began to mock him and scoff at him, since she realized that his strength had left him.
"Shake myself": rise from the heedlessness of sleep.

She told him, as in the previous times, that the Philistines were upon him; she said it knowing perfectly well that his strength had gone, so Samson awoke from his heedlessness and said to himself, I will rise and face the Philistines, as he had done every time, and he did not realize that the Lord had left him and that he had lost the secret of his strength. So he rose by his own strength and not by the strength of God, and therefore the Philistines seized him easily.

The Philistines were able to seize him easily because he had become weak, and they put out his eyes and led him to their city Gaza and bound him with chains as is done with captives. And to humble him they used him to grind grain at the mill like animals and slaves. Thus the mighty man became humbled, his eyes gouged out, and they treated him like an animal.

With the passing of days while he was in his prison, the hair of his head began to grow little by little, which led him to remember his state as a Nazarite, and he began to realize what his condition had come to as a result of his errors, and he began to return to God in repentance.
Dagon: a pagan god of the Philistines, with the head of a man and the body of a fish.

The Philistines decided to hold a celebration for their god "Dagon" because they believed that it was he who had helped them to seize their enemy Samson, so they sacrificed a sacrifice of thanksgiving to him, expressing their happiness and gratitude to him.

They led Samson in a procession among the people gathered in the temple, a captive bound in chains to the utmost of humiliating him, praising their god and saying that it was he who gave them victory over their enemy Samson who had wronged them, for he had burned their fields and killed many of them, and then they brought him back to the prison attached to the temple.
"When their hearts were merry": they indulged in eating, drinking and revelry.

As is the custom of pagan peoples in their celebrations, they joined them with the drinking of much wine and revelry. When their minds were affected by the wine, an idea occurred to them which they carried out at once, namely to summon Samson into their midst to perform some acrobatic movements, to the utmost of mocking him, and they made him stand between the pillars of the entrance, so that everyone outside the gates of the temple and also those inside it could see him.

Samson asked the boy charged with holding his hand to lead him, to take him to the main pillars on which the temple rests so that he might lean on them, after he showed weariness from much playing, and the boy granted his request.

The temple was full of thousands of men and women of the Philistines, and because the temple was filled with spectators, three thousand of them stood on its roof so as to be able to see Samson as he played like a buffoon. The chiefs of the Philistines were also present at this celebration.

Samson prayed to God and entreated Him, hoping that He would not forsake him because of his sin, and that He would remember him as His son and not leave him because of his thoughtlessness and folly. And he asked God to restore his strength to him, and give it back to him if only once, in which he might take vengeance on the Philistines who had humbled him and put out his eyes, and strike them a blow greater than any previous blow of his against them.
Samson put his hands on the two foundation pillars on which the building of the temple rested, which were near each other, so his right hand was on one pillar and his left on the other pillar.

Samson knew that if he lived after this event of pulling down the temple, the Philistines would make an example of him more and more, and torture him and then kill him; therefore he asked God to help him take vengeance on the Philistines in order to free his people from their occupation and their humbling of them, even if the price were his death with them. Then he leaned on the two pillars with force, as though pushing them apart from each other, and the Lord answered his prayer and accepted his repentance and gave him strength anew, so the pillars of the temple were shaken and it fell on those in it, and a very great number of the Philistines were killed, more than he had killed in his previous battles with them, and their chiefs also fell dead in their midst.

Thus Samson died a martyr in faith in God, sacrificing his life to rescue his people, and the Apostle Paul bore witness of him that he is among the heroes of faith (Heb 11:33). He is a type of Christ, who cast out many demons in His life on earth, but by His death bound all the demons.

His relatives and the sons of his clan came to Gaza and carried his body and returned with it to his birthplace, in his town "Zorah" (ch. 13:2), and buried him in the tomb of his father, lying between Zorah and Eshtaol (ch. 13:25). The period during which he judged the children of Israel was twenty years, during which he broke the power of the Philistines and restrained their domination over his people.

The door of repentance is open to you however much sin has humbled you, for God loves you and is ready to forgive you however grievous your sins, and even restores your strength to you and gives you authority over your enemies the demons.

The miracles of Samson (1) Killing the lion on his way to Timnath (ch. 14:5). (2) Killing thirty of the Philistines at Ashkelon (ch. 14:19). (3) Catching three hundred jackals and burning the fields of the Philistines (ch. 15:4). (4) Breaking the new ropes and killing a thousand men with the jawbone of an ass (ch. 15:13-15). (5) Pulling up the gate of the city of Gaza with its two posts and its leaves, carrying it and going up with it onto the mountain (ch. 16:3). (6) The Lord brings water out of the hollow for him and he drinks (ch. 15:19). (7) Breaking the seven cords, and the new ropes, and pulling out the loom with its pin in Delilah's house (ch. 16:9, 12, 14).

(8) Bringing down the temple of Dagon and killing the Philistines (ch. 16:30). Points of likeness between Samson and the Lord Jesus Christ (1) The birth of each by heavenly good tidings (ch. 13:3, Lk 1:31). (2) The birth of each by a miracle, for Samson was born of a barren woman, and Jesus of a virgin girl (ch. 13:2, Lk 1:27). (3) The Lord declared that Samson would begin to deliver his people (ch. 13:5), and the Lord Jesus' name means Savior, and He saved His people by redeeming them on the Cross (Lk 2:11). (4) The Spirit of the Lord moved Samson (ch. 13:25), and with the Lord Jesus the Spirit led Him (Lk 4:1). But there is a difference in the two cases, for the moving of Samson by the Spirit of the Lord means guiding him, while with the Lord Jesus the Spirit's moving Him means His carrying out the eternal plan that God devised for the redemption of mankind. (5) Samson was able to overcome his enemies, and the Lord Jesus overcame the devil, sin, death and the world by the Cross.
(6) Samson was delivered to his enemies by a group of his own kin and of his tribe Judah (ch. 15:13, 14), and the Lord Jesus was delivered by His disciple Judas to the Jews.
(7) Samson did great deeds alone without the help of soldiers or companions, and Christ accomplished salvation alone.
(8) When Samson fell into the hands of the Philistines they put out his eyes so that he would not see, and when the Jews seized Christ they blindfolded His eyes and struck Him.
(9) Each of them prayed at his death, but Samson's prayer was for vengeance on his enemies, while Christ prayed to forgive those who crucified Him.
(10) With the death of Samson his enemies died with him, and Christ buried sin by His death.

Points of difference between Samson and the Lord Jesus (1) Samson's life was full of human weakness and errors, while Christ is the Holy Lord alone (1 Pet 2:22). (2) Samson's struggle was bodily against the Philistines, while Christ's wrestling was spiritual against the devil and the powers of evil.

(3) Samson declared that he was doing wrong to the Philistines because they had done wrong to him (ch. 15:5), while Christ did not take vengeance on those who opposed Him (1 Pet 2:23). (4) At Samson's death he asked God to take vengeance on his enemies (ch. 16:28), while Christ at His death asked forgiveness for those who opposed Him (Lk 23:34). (5) Samson's deliverance of his people was a material deliverance from the Philistines, while Christ's deliverance is salvation from eternal perdition and the wrath of God.
(6) Samson delivered only his people, while Christ proclaimed salvation to the whole world.

(7) Samson's deliverance of his people was incomplete and temporary, and after him Samuel and David played a part in fighting the Philistines, while Christ completed the free salvation to the full, alone.
Micah's image

This chapter and the next tell the story of Micah's image, which reveals the extent of the spiritual blindness into which the people, and likewise the Levites, had fallen, a blindness shown in idolatrous worship mixed with a mere outward form of worshipping God. This story happened during the period of the judges. It tells of a man named Micah, who lived in the hill country that belonged to the tribe of Ephraim, and who had stolen from his mother a sum of money, eleven hundred shekels of silver (v. 2).
A shekel of silver: equal to about 11-15 grams of silver.
I cursed and also spoke in my ears: You cursed, O mother, and I heard the curse with my ears.

When his mother discovered the theft and did not know who the thief was, she began to curse the thief. The son could not bear to hear the curse with his ears, and he feared that his mother's curse would fall upon him, so he confessed to her that he was the one who had stolen the silver and that it was in his possession. The mother commended her son's confession and blessed him in place of the curse she had pronounced before.

Micah returned to his mother the silver he had stolen. She refused to put it back in her treasury, but vowed to dedicate it to the Lord by making a graven image, that is, one shaped with carving tools, and another made by melting metal and pouring it into a mold in the form of an image, and Micah would place them in his house to worship them. She gave the silver to her son Micah to make the images.

Micah returned the silver to his mother, and she set aside two hundred shekels of it to make the two images and gave it to the craftsman, who made the two required images, one graven and the other molten, and Micah placed them in his house. The mother gave the rest of the sum to her son to spend on the service and worship of the two images.
Ephod: a linen garment worn by the priest.
Teraphim: small images that people kept in their houses for worship and to bring good fortune.
He consecrated one of his sons: he appointed one of his sons and set him apart for the service.
Micah had set apart a place in his house for worship. He placed the two images in it, made an ephod, and consecrated one of his sons to be a priest for the family, performing the priestly service.
What Micah did, many do today, choosing gods for themselves, such as money or honor, and choosing priests after their own desires, to tell them what suits their desires and not the voice of God.

This story reveals the depth of ignorance to which that family had sunk, and it was not an isolated case but an example of the general corruption that prevailed among the people. Among the many errors that this story reveals, into which Micah and his mother fell, was setting up a private shrine in his house, although the one house in which worship was to be offered to the Lord was the house of God in "Shiloh." Micah also made for himself two images and teraphim, which the Law utterly forbade; and he set up his son as a priest, though he was not of the seed of Aaron. This verse fixes the time of what Micah did: it was the age of the judges, before kings were set up over the children of Israel. In this period the people of God sometimes held fast to God's commandments and to His Law given by Moses, as the judges taught it, and at other times they drifted away from it, and the enemies around them humbled them. This is one picture of spiritual ignorance.

All these errors that Micah and his mother committed teach us that a people without a teacher to guide them are exposed to spiritual dangers and perhaps even to eternal spiritual perdition, for the Scripture says, "My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge" (Hos 4:6). Therefore let us pray to God to preserve the shepherds of our Church, that they may "rightly divide for us the word of truth," and let us submit to their teachings and guidance so that we do not go astray.

Bethlehem-judah: it lies nine kilometers south of Jerusalem, and it is the place where Christ was born (Map 10). There was a young man living in Bethlehem in the land of Judah. Though he is said to be of the family of Judah, in truth he was of the tribe of the Levites, of the family of the Gershomites, as is stated in (ch. 18:30), but he was living among the family of Judah. The Levites had cities in which they lived among the tribes. (Ch. 18:30) mentions that the name of this Levite was Jonathan.
Where he could find a place: to any place, seeking a livelihood.
He came on his way: going on his way.

Poverty drove this young man to leave Bethlehem for another place in search of a livelihood. He came to the hill country of Ephraim, and on his way he chanced upon Micah's house and turned aside to it to ask about work. In this the Levite abandoned his work as a teacher of the people and a servant of the house of God and began to seek money and honor. This is a picture of the decline of the Levites in the age of the judges.

Micah asked him where he was from, and he answered that he was from the tribe of Levi, that he had been living in Bethlehem before coming here, and that he had decided to leave his town and go seeking a livelihood in any other place where he might settle.

Micah rejoiced in the young Levite and asked him to stay with him to be a priest to him in place of his son, thinking that by this he would complete the ideal picture of worship: he had the ephod and the teraphim, and here was a true priest from the tribe of Levi to lead the worship in his house, which would be better than his son. He offered him a yearly wage in addition to his clothing and his food, and called him father, that is, one responsible for Micah and his family in praying for them. The Levite found this offer a generous one for him compared with the circumstances in which he had lived before, so he agreed to Micah's offer.

The Levite accepted to stay with Micah, and Micah treated him very well, loving him and honoring him. While the Levite was in effect a spiritual father with regard to the priesthood, Micah treated him as one of his sons.

Micah consecrated the Levite as his priest and gave him all his rights as a priest. So the Levite settled permanently in his house with Micah's family and served in the house that Micah had earlier set apart for worship (v. 5).

Micah was very glad of the Levite, for he knew that the Law prescribes that this tribe is the one set apart for the priesthood, although the priesthood was confined to the seed of Aaron. Yet he saw that the Levite, in any case, belongs to this holy tribe for the service of God and was more entitled than his son to do this spiritual work, believing that it was God who had brought this Levite across his path, and that by this He wished to do him good and bless him. This shows the extent of the spiritual ignorance that prevailed at that time.

Honoring the priests and servants who labor faithfully in the service of God gladdens the heart of God, but with wisdom in this honor toward those you know, so that you encourage them and help them to care for all souls and to complete their service. The tribe of Dan seeks a land to possess

entries.section: (1) The tribe of Dan chooses Laish to possess it

paragraphs.text: The book fixes the time of the events mentioned in this chapter as the age of the judges, that is, before the age of the kings began among the people of God. It makes clear that the portion of the tribe of Dan that it received in the Promised Land was small and lay beside the Mediterranean Sea, west of the tribes of Benjamin and Judah and the western half of the tribe of Manasseh. It appears that the Amorites, the pagan inhabitants of the land, harassed the tribe of Dan and settled beside them in the fertile valleys, so the tribe of Dan was forced to live in the mountains and so did not have a sufficient portion among the tribes. Their zeal and concern appeared in seeking another land to possess that would be wide enough for their growing numbers.

entries.section: (1) The tribe of Dan chooses Laish to possess it

paragraphs.text: As is customary in wars, the tribe of Dan sent a group of strong men from two famous cities in the land of Dan, Zorah and Eshtaol, to spy out the land in order to find a suitable place that the tribe would fight to obtain. In the course of their travels these men came down into the land of the tribe of Ephraim and lodged at the estate that belonged to Micah, which was a place prepared for receiving strangers to stay in.

entries.section: (1) The tribe of Dan chooses Laish to possess it

paragraphs.text: While they were at Micah's house, they heard the voice of the Levite as he was serving in the shrine belonging to Micah's family, and they recognized him because they had seen him before, since he had lived in Bethlehem, which lies in the portion of the tribe of Judah, and there was close association between the tribes of Judah and Dan. So they went toward the place of the voice and asked him what had brought him here and what he was doing in this place.

entries.section: (1) The tribe of Dan chooses Laish to possess it

paragraphs.text: The young man told them what had happened to him: how he had left his town, how Micah had welcomed him, what he had offered him of staying with him, and how he served as a priest for the family in return for a fixed wage, food, and clothing.

entries.section: (1) The tribe of Dan chooses Laish to possess it

paragraphs.text: When the spies of the tribe of Dan learned that the Levite served in the office of priesthood, they asked him to inquire of the Lord concerning what they had resolved to do. Thus the spiritual ignorance of the people of God appears, for they thought that this Levite was able to do what the high priests used to do by means of the Urim and Thummim in the tabernacle of meeting, while this Levite was performing the rites of the worship of idols, the teraphim, and the false gods, which cannot foretell anything to anyone through him. This also shows the extent of the confusion that prevailed in that time and the mixing of the worship of God with the worship of idols.

Therefore God sets up in His Church bishops and elders who govern, to shepherd the people faithfully and to preserve the doctrine without any confusion, and "as they once received it from the saints." The Church has always preserved the ancient faith from the distortion of heretics and those who depart from the faith, so they have been and remain guardians of the right doctrine and the appointed rites, as is prayed in the Litany of the Archpriests and Priests in the Divine Liturgy: "And those who rightly divide with him the word of truth, grant them to Your holy Church, that they may shepherd Your flock in peace."

entries.section: (1) The tribe of Dan chooses Laish to possess it

paragraphs.text: The Levite (the priest) pretended that God was inspiring him, and he told them what they believed to be divine counsel, and prophesied to them that they would be under God's care wherever they went.

entries.section: (1) The tribe of Dan chooses Laish to possess it

paragraphs.text: The Sidonians: the inhabitants of Sidon, which lies on the coast of the Mediterranean Sea, south of the city of Tyre.

There was no magistrate in the land, that might put them to shame in any thing, as an heir of authority: no one to harm them in anything, and no ruler who had inherited rule from those before him lorded it over them.
They had no business with any man: they had no quarrel with anyone, nor any alliances with others.

The five men walked through the land of Canaan until they reached a city in the far northeast near Mount Hermon, the city of Laish. Its inhabitants were Sidonians who had migrated from their original city, and like all Sidonians they were fond of maritime occupations, fishing and trade. They had settled there content with their life and their work, with no enmities or alliances with anyone outside, and no one tyrannized over them from within. They were without a king and completely independent of those around them, even of Sidon, because of the distance between Sidon and Laish, for the first lies in the far northwest and the second in the far northeast.

entries.section: (1) The tribe of Dan chooses Laish to possess it

paragraphs.text: The five men returned from their scouting journey to their city in Zorah and Eshtaol, and the people of their tribe asked them what they had found on this journey and what was the news of the lands and their inhabitants.

entries.section: (1) The tribe of Dan chooses Laish to possess it

paragraphs.text: The five spies advised the men of their tribe not to delay or be slothful, but to go up at once to "Laish" to possess it, for the land was very good and all the circumstances were favorable for taking it.

entries.section: (1) The tribe of Dan chooses Laish to possess it

paragraphs.text: The five men went on recounting the facts they had learned about the land they had spied out. They told their brethren that if they came to Laish they would find a people not expecting anyone to attack them, who made no preparations or fortifications to defend their city. They also told them that the land was wide and far-stretching, that is, able to hold all the sons of their tribe, besides the richness of the land and the abundance of its goods, so that whoever lived in it would need nothing from outside. They also assured them that God would give them the land according to His promise to His people through Moses and Joshua.

The tribe of Dan took courage to carry out God's commands to drive out the pagan inhabitants of the land. So do not hesitate to carry out God's commandments, and you will find your rest and your fullness, and trust in the power of God that supports you, and you will defeat all your enemies, the demons.

entries.section: (2) The theft of Micah's priest and images

paragraphs.text: The men of the tribe were persuaded by what their five messengers told them and decided to invade the city of Laish. So they equipped six hundred warriors from among them, from Zorah and from Eshtaol, supplied them with weapons and fighting equipment, and set out toward Laish.

entries.section: (2) The theft of Micah's priest and images

paragraphs.text: The town of Kirjath-jearim: it lies on the border of Judah and Dan near the city of Zorah, 14.5 km west of Jerusalem. It is one of the four cities of the Gibeonites (Josh 9:17). Behind Kirjath-jearim: west of the town of Kirjath-jearim.

The men of war set out from their cities, Zorah and Eshtaol, and reached one of the cities of Judah near Zorah and stayed some time in that place. Therefore it was called "Mahaneh-dan," and it kept this name until the time this book was written.

entries.section: (2) The theft of Micah's priest and images

paragraphs.text: From there they went north to the hill country of Ephraim until they reached the place where Micah lived.

entries.section: (2) The theft of Micah's priest and images

paragraphs.text: The five spies, who had already seen the region, told them that there was an ephod, teraphim, a graven image, and a molten image in Micah's house, and they encouraged their brethren not to neglect these precious things but to work to take them to be a blessing for their tribe, as they believed. This confirms the spiritual error in which the people of God lived in this period, since they counted the images of idols as something great.

entries.section: (2) The theft of Micah's priest and images

paragraphs.text: The soldiers responded to the call of the five men and decided to seize those things. So they went to the place where they were kept, which was the shrine that Micah had set apart for that purpose. The young Levite was performing the religious rites when they came, and when they arrived they spoke with him.

entries.section: (2) The theft of Micah's priest and images

paragraphs.text: Their conversation with the Levite took place at the door of the house, where the six hundred warriors of the children of Dan stood armed with weapons of war.

entries.section: (2) The theft of Micah's priest and images

paragraphs.text: The priest was startled to find six hundred armed men and was very afraid. Meanwhile the five spies went in and took the two images, the ephod, and the teraphim from the shrine.

entries.section: (2) The theft of Micah's priest and images

paragraphs.text: The priest was astonished at their stealing the images and tried to object to the five men.

entries.section: (2) The theft of Micah's priest and images

paragraphs.text: The men rebuked him and commanded him to be silent and not to open his mouth in any objection or to argue with them about what they had done. Rather, they asked him to go with them to be priest to them and to be a spiritual father to their tribe, for in this he would be priest to a great company, a whole tribe of the tribes of Israel, and this was better for him than being priest to one family. Thus they used violence and rebuke with him, and also enticement: they threatened him with the armed men and at the same time enticed him to become a priest and spiritual father to a whole tribe.

entries.section: (2) The theft of Micah's priest and images

paragraphs.text: The priest's heart was glad: he rejoiced and was delighted.
He went in the midst of the people: he walked among them.

This was a tempting offer for the Levite, for the soldiers of the tribe of Dan succeeded in bringing a spirit of boasting and pride into his heart; no doubt his moral standing would rise by being priest to a tribe instead of priest to a family, and besides, he expected his wage and his share of the offerings of a whole tribe to increase. So he overlooked their taking the ephod, the teraphim, and the images, and walked in the midst of the soldiers, declaring by this his agreement to the offer made to him by the tribe.

The men of Dan made theft lawful for themselves, and they stole what leads astray from God, namely the idols. Do not break the commandment and become occupied with the possessions of the world. They are all vanity, and do not clash with others because of them, but rather possess God in your heart, and He will bless your life, and you will lack nothing.

entries.section: (3) Micah tries to recover his property

paragraphs.text: They put the carriage before them: they put their baggage in front of them.

The soldiers left Micah's house, heading for Laish, and they placed their little ones, their women, their cattle, and their baggage in front, and the men walked behind them to guard them and protect them from any attack that an enemy might make on them.

entries.section: (3) Micah tries to recover his property

paragraphs.text: Some time passed until Micah noticed the Levite's absence and discovered the theft of his sacred things. He gathered his relatives and those working in his house to pursue the men of the tribe of Dan, hoping to recover what they had taken from him, until they overtook them.

entries.section: (3) Micah tries to recover his property

paragraphs.text: Micah and his men cried out, calling the men of the tribe of Dan to pay attention to him and hear his protest. They turned to him in disapproval, asking him scornfully what this crying out was and who these men were that he had brought, and what had happened that he should do all this.

entries.section: (3) Micah tries to recover his property

paragraphs.text: What have I more?: what is left to me after what you have taken from me.

Micah answered them, protesting at what they had done in taking the idols and the teraphim and also his Levite priest, for by this they had deprived him of the most precious thing he owned, leaving him nothing. And after doing all this, they objected to his crying out and protesting.

entries.section: (3) Micah tries to recover his property

paragraphs.text: Let not thy voice be heard among us: do not speak.
Angry fellows: in great distress and ready to strike down whoever opposes them.

The Danite soldiers threatened him that if he did not be silent and stop crying out, they would not bear with him any longer, for they were weary and troubled by the length of the journey and by their thinking about the hard task, the task of the war they were about to undertake, and if he persisted in his crying out and in following them on their march, they would kill him and all who were with him.

entries.section: (3) Micah tries to recover his property

paragraphs.text: The men of Dan disregarded Micah's words and continued on their way toward Laish, and Micah felt that there was no use in protesting and even feared them, so he returned to his house.

Do not become involved in evil, like Micah who made idols, lest you lose much, and if you lose, take heed to return to God by repentance and keep away from evil, and do not do as Micah did, who returned to his house but did not understand God's message to turn away from the worship of idols.

The Danites reached the city of Laish, with the two images, the ephod, and the teraphim, and also the Levite priest who had belonged to Micah. The people of the city did not expect anyone to attack them, so they were surprised by the attack of the Danites, and the surprise was greater than their ability to face it, so their resistance collapsed before the children of Dan, who took the city, burned it, and killed those in it.

Just as it is true to say that unpreparedness to defend the homeland against foreign invasion is the sure prelude to defeat before it, so also unpreparedness and spiritual heedlessness tempt the enemy of good to storm souls and gain control over them. Let us then always be watchful, knowing that our enemy is "a roaring lion, walking about, seeking whom he may devour," and let us prepare with prayers, reading the Holy Bible, repentance, and partaking of the Mysteries.

No one hastened to rescue them, not even the Sidonians, the inhabitants of Sidon, the original homeland of the people of Laish from which they had come. They did not rush to the aid of their brethren because of the distance of the city of Laish from the city of Sidon, and likewise the people of Laish had no alliances with any of the other neighboring peoples to cry to for help. The city of Laish, as the Scripture says, lay in the valley that is in Beth-rehob, a valley which is today in Lebanon, and in this valley there was a city called "Beth-rehob," from which the valley took its name. When the Danites took the city and settled in it, they rebuilt it anew after having burned it in their attack to take it.

They changed the name of the city from its old name "Laish" to a new name, "Dan," the name of their great forefather Dan, the son of Jacob by his wife Bilhah, Rachel's maid (Gen 30:6). Thus the tribe of Dan found a new land to take in its increase in numbers, so part of the tribe remained in their first portion in the southwest of the land of Canaan, and the other part lived in the city of "Laish" in the northeast.

Until the day of the captivity of the land: until the day when the Lord delivered them into the hands of the Philistines, who defeated them and took the ark of the covenant from them to their country, and the glory departed from Israel (1 Sam 4). The tribe set up Micah's graven image as a god for themselves, to worship and to perform rites for, and the people also consecrated the young Levite as priest for this god whom they worshipped. This was one of the signs of the people's spiritual decline and their departure from true worship in order to live according to their own desires.

Thus the Danites continued to worship the graven image, for which they appointed a priest who was not of the seed of Aaron, although the true house of God, the tabernacle of meeting, was still in "Shiloh," where lawful priests served in it. This shows the disunity among the tribes, their not gathering around the place of true worship, and their not submitting to the word of God and His Law.

The establishment of idol worship among the people of God in the age of the judges in the city of Dan perhaps encouraged Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who divided the kingdom after King Solomon and then set up images in Dan and in Bethel to turn them away from the worship of God that was in Jerusalem (1 Kgs 12:19-33). Although the Danites had possessed Laish and driven out the pagans from it, they returned and worshipped idols in the story of Micah. This is like many who begin with God and reject sin and then return to it of their own will a second time.
The Levite and his concubine

entries.section: (1) The Levite brings back his concubine

paragraphs.text: When there was no king: that is, in the age of the judges, before the age of the kings began.
The sides of mount Ephraim: "sides" is the plural of a word meaning a high place, that is, the high places in the hill country of Ephraim.

From this verse to the end of the book, the inspired text tells us another story that also happened in the time of the judges, which gives us a picture of the extent of the spiritual decline and of the spread of fornication among the people of God, so that it almost destroyed an entire tribe, the tribe of Benjamin.

The story here is about a man of the Levites who was living temporarily on one edge of the land of Ephraim, and who had taken a maidservant as a wife, which the ancient Law permitted, and she was from Bethlehem.

entries.section: (1) The Levite brings back his concubine

paragraphs.text: That maidservant fell into the sin of fornication and feared that she would be punished by stoning according to the Law, so she fled to Bethlehem, to her father's home, and stayed with him four months.

entries.section: (1) The Levite brings back his concubine

paragraphs.text: To speak friendly unto her: to speak to her kindly and win her consent.

With the passing of time she repented and was sorry, so her husband forgave her for her fault and went to her father's house to reconcile with her and show her that he had put her deed out of mind. The woman welcomed him and brought him into her father's house, and her father also rejoiced when he learned that he had come to reconcile with his wife.

entries.section: (1) The Levite brings back his concubine

paragraphs.text: To show his welcome to him, her father asked him to accept his hospitality for several days, and he stayed with him three days, during which he honored him.

entries.section: (1) The Levite brings back his concubine

paragraphs.text: A morsel of bread: a humble expression of the host, by which he means eating a meal.

On the morning of the fourth day, since the Levite was about to depart, he rose early in preparation for leaving, taking his wife with him, but her father asked him to wait a little until he could give him enough food to help him with the hardship of the journey so that he would not be weary on the way.

entries.section: (1) The Levite brings back his concubine

paragraphs.text: The Levite accepted his father-in-law's invitation, and the two sat together and ate, and as he was leaving, his father-in-law held on to him and asked him to stay with him another night, so that they might converse in the evening and enjoy being together.

entries.section: (1) The Levite brings back his concubine

paragraphs.text: The Levite had resolved to depart, but his father-in-law held him and urged him to stay another night.

entries.section: (1) The Levite brings back his concubine

paragraphs.text: The guest rose early on the morning of the fifth day to take his wife and leave his father-in-law's house, but his father-in-law again urged him anew to stay and eat, for there was no reason for such haste, and to wait until after noon. The Levite was compelled to accept his father-in-law's invitation, so he sat and ate.

entries.section: (1) The Levite brings back his concubine

paragraphs.text: When the time to depart came again, and the Levite, his wife, and his servant were about to go, his father-in-law said to him that the day was declining and that it was not right to begin their journey at that late hour of the day, so let him stay this night also, lest night fall upon them on the road and they be exposed to dangers, and he promised him that when the night passed he would let him leave early in the morning to return to his dwelling place.

entries.section: (1) The Levite brings back his concubine

paragraphs.text: This time the Levite did not yield to his father-in-law's request and insisted on leaving. He went on his way until he came to a place near Jebus (Jerusalem), and with him were his concubine, his servant, and his two asses with saddles and riding gear.

How good it is to honor our guests so that they feel comfortable and at ease in being with us, knowing that God honors us if we honor others, but let it be done with wisdom, so that we do not hinder them from their work and responsibilities.
Jebus: the city that was afterward called Jerusalem.

The Levite left Bethlehem and went on his way until he came to the city of Jebus, which is about 9 km from Bethlehem. The Jebusites, the original inhabitants of the land, were still living in it. The Levite's servant who worked for him said to his master, "Let us lodge in Jebus, for the night has come."

Gibeah: a city north of Jerusalem (Map 10). The Levite did not agree to his servant's proposal because the people of Jebus were not Israelites, that is, they were strangers to him, and he saw that it was more fitting to go on a little farther until they reached the town of "Gibeah," one of the cities of the tribe of Benjamin.
Ramah: a village 8 km north of Jerusalem.
The Levite urged his servant to continue until they reached a place where the children of Israel lived, such as "Gibeah" or "Ramah," and spend their night there.
They did go on until they reached the town of Gibeah, where the tribe of Benjamin lived, and they arrived after the sun had set and night had come.

They entered the city to spend the night in it and came to a wide square at the entrance of the city. Everyone who passed by the place saw them, but no one invited them to lodge with him. This shows the bad character of the people of the city, for there was no one who cared to take in this stranger, because they were selfish, caring only for their own pleasures.

They stayed in the place until an old man of the town passed by, who was originally of the tribe of Ephraim but was living in Gibeah temporarily. He was returning from his work in the field to his house, and he saw the Levite, his concubine, and his servant sitting in the square, so he came and asked them where they had come from and where they were going.

The Levite answered the old man that they had left Bethlehem for the sides of the hill country of Ephraim, where they lived. He was going to the house of the Lord at "Shiloh," which is about 27 km north of Jerusalem.

The Levite made clear that he would not burden the one who took him in with anything but a place to sleep. They had everything they needed of food and drink and provender for the asses, so their lodging would not be a burden on their host.
The old man said to him, "Do not say so, for I will take care of all your needs of food and drink, for this is the duty of hospitality, so come with me to my house and leave the city square."

They accepted the old man's invitation and came with him to his house, where he honored them and gave provender to their asses, and they washed their feet, and he gave them food and drink, and they ate and drank and rested at his house.

Be reassured if you live or deal with selfish or wicked people, for God will not leave you alone but makes with the temptation a way of escape, sending you someone who cares for you and solves your problems.

entries.section: (3) The rape and death of the concubine

paragraphs.text: As they were making their hearts merry: rejoicing in eating and drinking and rest after the day's weariness.
Men of Belial: wicked men, sons of Satan, for Belial is the name of a pagan god, called the god of the night.
Bring forth the man that came into thine house, that we may know him: bring out the man that we may commit fornication with him.

While they were sitting conversing after the toil of the journey, a group of wicked men of the city gathered before the old man's house, beating hard on his door, demanding that he hand over his guest to them so that they could commit perversion and sin with him.

entries.section: (3) The rape and death of the concubine

paragraphs.text: The master of the house objected to the wicked men gently so that they would not abuse his guest, and offered them to hand over to them his virgin daughter and the man's concubine to commit fornication with them. This is of course a wrong solution, but it seems that at this time the position of woman was low in the eyes of society, and this offer was an attempt by the host to deliver the Levite from their hand.

A similar story happened in the book of Genesis, the story of Lot when the wicked attacked his house to abuse the two men he had taken in, who were the two angels (Gen 19), but the situation here is harder because the wicked are of the people of God and not pagans like the people of Sodom.

entries.section: (3) The rape and death of the concubine

paragraphs.text: The wicked men did not respond to the entreaties of the master of the house and insisted on their demand, so the Levite guest had no choice but to bring his concubine out to them, handing her over to their hand. They took her and committed fornication with her all night long, enjoying their evil desires, and then they let her go in the morning.

entries.section: (3) The rape and death of the concubine

paragraphs.text: The concubine went from the hand of the wicked men and came to the old man's house where her lord the Levite was, and she was in great exhaustion, so she fell down before the house until the sun rose.

entries.section: (3) The rape and death of the concubine

paragraphs.text: The Levite rose in the morning to return to his country, having lost his concubine, since he thought that the men of Gibeah would not give back the concubine, and he was startled to find his concubine fallen at the door of the house with her hands stretched out toward the door, perhaps because she had wanted to knock on it and could not for extreme weariness.

entries.section: (3) The rape and death of the concubine

paragraphs.text: The Levite thought she was asleep and called to her, trying to wake her to continue the journey with him, but she had departed this life. So the man loaded her body on his ass and returned with her to his house on the edges of Ephraim.

This concubine had been living quietly with her lord and husband the Levite, but she was negligent and committed fornication, and God allowed the gravity of fornication to be shown in that those wicked men raped her and were the cause of her death. So do not be negligent with sin, even with a small negligence, lest your immersion in it increase and you bring many evils upon yourself and become a cause of your own destruction.

entries.section: (3) The rape and death of the concubine

paragraphs.text: Shock and grief drove the Levite to a harsh thought, which was to cut the concubine's body into twelve pieces and send them to the twelve tribes, in order to show them how monstrous was what the Gibeonites had done to him, and to ask their judgment and verdict in this matter.

entries.section: (3) The rape and death of the concubine

paragraphs.text: Everyone of the children of Israel who saw and heard was astonished and disgusted at this vile deed, the like of which had not happened since they came out of the land of Egypt to this day. And they considered the matter, how they would face this great evil.
The war between the tribe of Benjamin and the rest of the tribes

The story of the rape of the Levite's concubine shook the conscience of the people, so the men of Israel from all the tribes assembled, from the north where Dan is to the south where Beer-sheba is, and from the east also, where Gilead is. They all gathered before the house of the Lord and the ark of His covenant, which they had moved from Shiloh to Mizpeh. They gathered in the name of the Lord to present their matter to Him.
Footmen: those who walk, that is, a huge company of infantry.
That drew sword: fit to use swords in war.

The chiefs of the people and the leading figures of all the tribes stood in the assembly the people held to consider this vile matter committed by a group of wicked men, and the number of those assembled was four hundred thousand footmen able to bear arms.
Tell us, how was this wickedness?: they asked everyone who knew anything about this dreadful event and this vile deed.

Benjamin learned of the assembly the tribes held at Mizpeh, but they did not try to set right their position. The chiefs of the people who were present asked the Levite and those who knew him to present the vile story to the tribes.
The Levite began to speak, since he was the first concerned in the matter, and he described what had happened from the time he entered the house of his host in Gibeah to spend the night with him.

A company of the people of the city attacked the house and wanted to commit perversion with him, so he handed over his concubine to them, fearing for his life, and they assaulted her in a savage manner until she departed this life from extreme exhaustion.

The Levite was gravely shocked by this barbarous act, so he decided to inform all the children of Israel so that they might judge his case. He cut his concubine's body into 12 pieces and sent them to all the territories of Israel so that they might judge this heinous crime.
"And here you represent all the tribes of the children of Israel; judge in this case of mine and give your opinion on this dreadful tragedy."

If you face a problem, bring it to the priests and servants responsible in the Church to judge it, and do not act by yourself in anger, lest you sin. Lift up your heart in prayer, consult your father of confession, wait for God's guidance to you, and know that your God is just and strong, and no matter escapes Him.

entries.section: (2) Benjamin refuses to hand over the criminals

paragraphs.text: Those assembled decided with one mind that no one should leave his place in this great assembly and that none of them should return to his dwelling place until they had examined the story and judged it, and they decided to ask God and cast lots to choose who would fight against Gibeah and who would provide for the needs of the fighters.

entries.section: (2) Benjamin refuses to hand over the criminals

paragraphs.text: Ten thousand: a myriad.

Those assembled also decided to divide the men of each tribe into ten parts and to choose one part of them, that is, a tenth, to return to its place and bring food and the needs of war, while the rest would remain ready to fight Gibeon if it did not submit to them, and to chastise it for the evil it had done.

entries.section: (2) Benjamin refuses to hand over the criminals

paragraphs.text: The men of the tribes advanced, united in one opinion, to fight Gibeon.

entries.section: (2) Benjamin refuses to hand over the criminals

paragraphs.text: Before fighting Gibeah, they sent to the families of the tribe of Benjamin asking them to hand over the wicked men who had committed the crime, but they refused in pride.

Be understanding if you have erred and confess your error, and even accept the punishment if all agree on it, in order to be reconciled with those you have wronged and to submit to the opinion of the community. Then the just God will be pleased with you, and you will save yourself from many evils and calm the anger of those around you, and you will be able to win them over as time passes.

entries.section: (3) The first and second battles and the defeat of the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: The tribe of Benjamin did not submit to the decision of the tribes, and after their refusal to hand over the wicked men, they prepared to fight them, so all the men of Benjamin gathered at Gibeah. It would have been better for them to apologize for their sin and not rely on their military strength; but their pride and their reliance on their strength caused much trouble and almost wiped out their tribe entirely.

entries.section: (3) The first and second battles and the defeat of the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: The number of Benjamin's men who went into the war from their various cities was 26 thousand, in addition to 700 warriors from the city of Gibeah itself, chosen for their courage in wars and their physical abilities.

entries.section: (3) The first and second battles and the defeat of the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: Lefthanded: men who use their left hand instead of the right.
The sling: a weapon of war like a slingshot for throwing stones to great distances.
At an hair breadth: they hit any target accurately, even if it was a hair.

Among those chosen for the war from the children of Benjamin were seven hundred who used their left hand, yet they hit the most exact targets from a long distance without missing, that is, they were very skilled in war and in using its tools in that time.

entries.section: (3) The first and second battles and the defeat of the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: Against the men of Benjamin, four hundred thousand men of war who drew the sword gathered from the tribes of Israel to fight the tribe of Benjamin.

entries.section: (3) The first and second battles and the defeat of the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: The army of the tribes assembled at Bethel on the border of the tribe of Benjamin, where the ark of the covenant of God and the tabernacle of meeting had been moved (v. 27), and they asked the Lord which of them should be at the head of the army and take the command (they asked by the Urim and Thummim, as was the custom). The Lord answered them that the one to be in front was the tribe of Judah. It would have been better for them to ask God first whether they should fight or not. Then God allowed them to be defeated the first two times to show them that they were all sinners and not only the tribe of Benjamin. And when they were chastened and returned to God, He allowed them victory the third time, in appreciation of their prayers, their consulting God, and their repentance, as will appear in the following verses.

entries.section: (3) The first and second battles and the defeat of the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: On the day after they asked the Lord, the army of the tribes advanced toward Gibeah, the sinful city, and made their camp on the border of the city and made ready to fight the army that the tribe of Benjamin had prepared.

entries.section: (3) The first and second battles and the defeat of the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: The tribe of Benjamin was victorious, and they killed 22 thousand of the tribes.

entries.section: (3) The first and second battles and the defeat of the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: Despite the defeat of the tribes, their resolve and their desire to root out evil did not weaken. They did not despair but returned and organized their ranks anew and drew up for battle in the same place before Gibeah, as they had done the day before.

The believer must not despair if he is defeated some times in his spiritual war against Satan, but must not retreat, rather persevere and strive, and the Lord gives him strength and victory. We must always remember that loss of hope is the great sin that leaves no room for repentance and return to God.

entries.section: (3) The first and second battles and the defeat of the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: The children of Israel turned to the Lord and wept before Him all day in sorrow for those of them who had fallen the day before, and they prayed to Him, seeking His will as to whether He was pleased for them to go back to fight the children of Benjamin again or to stop. They called the tribe of Benjamin "my brother" despite the estrangement and the dispute, because in spite of this it is indeed one of the twelve tribes of Israel. The Lord answered them to go up against him.

entries.section: (3) The first and second battles and the defeat of the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: The soldiers of the children of Israel moved forward to meet the children of Benjamin on the day after their prayer to the Lord.

entries.section: (3) The first and second battles and the defeat of the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: On the same day the army of Benjamin advanced toward them to fight them, and the children of Benjamin were victorious also in this second battle and killed 18 thousand soldiers of the tribes, all bearing the sword.
God allowed the defeat of the tribes twice although they had prayed and He had agreed with them to fight Gibeah, for the following reasons:

1- So that the tribes would not become proud, feeling their strength, and kill their brethren cruelly with hearts full of evil, but He wanted them to be humbled, to know that victory would come from God.
2- Perhaps He wanted to purify the tribes of the evil in them, such as the idol worship, an example of which is what the tribe of Dan did (ch. 18).
3- To give the tribe of Benjamin a chance to repent and turn back from its evil.

entries.section: (4) The defeat of Benjamin and the killing of its men

paragraphs.text: Bethel: a city north of Jerusalem, lying between it and Nablus.

The children of Israel grieved over their defeat twice and over the killing of great numbers of them, so the soldiers and the rest of the people went to Bethel and humbled themselves with fasting and weeping before the ark of the covenant, seeking the mercies of the Lord and His intervention to solve their problem. In atonement for their sins they offered burnt offerings, and to express their thanks to the Lord in all circumstances they offered peace offerings. These sacrifices signify Christ the Redeemer, through whom we gain victory over the demons.

entries.section: (4) The defeat of Benjamin and the killing of its men

paragraphs.text: The ark of the covenant in those days was at Bethel, and the high priest was Phinehas, who ministered before the ark. The children of Israel asked the Lord by way of the high priest, by vision or by the Thummim and Urim, whether they should cease fighting the children of Benjamin or face them a third time. The Lord commanded them to fight the children of Benjamin and promised them that He would give them victory in that battle on the morrow.

entries.section: (4) The defeat of Benjamin and the killing of its men

paragraphs.text: Israel set liers in wait round about Gibeah: that is, he set an ambush around Gibeah.

The children of Israel began to lay a plan for the war, to place an ambush of their men around Gibeah, whose task was to enter the city after the army of Benjamin came out of it to meet the children of Israel, and to burn it with fire, which was in fact carried out, as will come in the rest of the verses.

entries.section: (4) The defeat of Benjamin and the killing of its men

paragraphs.text: For the third time the soldiers of the children of Israel drew up facing Gibeah, as they had done in the first and second confrontations.

entries.section: (4) The defeat of Benjamin and the killing of its men

paragraphs.text: Were drawn away from the city: moved away from the city.

The army of the children of Benjamin came out of the city to meet the army of the children of Israel, and in this was a preparation for what the children of Israel had planned, to draw the army of the children of Benjamin away from the city. Indeed the army of the children of Israel deliberately distributed its companies on several roads so that the army of Benjamin would be scattered behind them, and more than that, they pretended to be defeated in order to encourage the enemy army to go farther and farther from the city, so that the ambush surrounding Gibeah and behind it, of the children of Israel, could enter the city and burn it. Indeed the army of Benjamin came out behind the tribes of Israel on two roads, one leading to Bethel and the other in the wilderness around Gibeah. The total of the men of the army of Israel who were killed in this pursuit was only thirty men.

entries.section: (4) The defeat of Benjamin and the killing of its men

paragraphs.text: The children of Benjamin were deceived by their previous victories and thought that the retreat of the children of Israel was nothing but a third defeat that would strike them. The children of Israel, however, continued to carry out their plans of drawing the army of Benjamin after them away from the city, pretending to flee and be defeated, and their plan was to scatter them more and more until they grew tired and confused, so that the ambush could enter the city without hindrance.

entries.section: (4) The defeat of Benjamin and the killing of its men

paragraphs.text: The soldiers of the army of Israel gathered at "Baal-tamar," a place near Gibeah, and at the same time the ambush came out of its hiding place in the wilderness of Gibeah, entering the city.

entries.section: (4) The defeat of Benjamin and the killing of its men

paragraphs.text: They knew not that evil was near them: they did not feel that they were in danger.

Other fighting companies joined the army of the children of Israel, their number estimated at ten thousand valiant fighters, and a fierce battle took place. The Benjamites thought they were victorious as in the previous times and did not appreciate the weakness of their position and the strength of their enemies.

entries.section: (4) The defeat of Benjamin and the killing of its men

paragraphs.text: The children of Israel were victorious over the Benjamites, and the victory was from the Lord, and in this battle 25,100 soldiers of the children of Benjamin were killed, all of them strong in fighting.

entries.section: (4) The defeat of Benjamin and the killing of its men

paragraphs.text: And the children of Israel gave place to the Benjamites: they fell back before Benjamin to draw them away from Gibeah in order to give the ambush an opportunity according to the plan laid down.

When this great number of the army of Benjamin was killed, they were sure that they had been defeated this time before the army of the tribes, although the children of Israel continued to pretend to fall back in order to draw the children of Benjamin away from the city, to give the ambush the opportunity to carry out the plan laid down.

It was pride that drove the tribe of Benjamin to come out behind the army of the tribes and move away from the city, so God allowed it to be defeated because of its pride. So do not rely on your previous successes and become proud, but give the glory to God and examine your affairs before Him in prayer and humility, and He will guide you and you will remain victorious over the devil, for by humility and holding fast to God you remain steadfast in Him and trample all the powers of evil.

entries.section: (4) The defeat of Benjamin and the killing of its men

paragraphs.text: The way was indeed cleared for the ambush to carry out the plan, for the children of Israel succeeded in drawing the children of Benjamin away from the city and occupied them with pursuing them, so the ambush entered the city and killed everyone in it.

entries.section: (4) The defeat of Benjamin and the killing of its men

paragraphs.text: There was an agreement between the soldiers of Israel and the men of the ambush that when they entered the city and destroyed those in it, they would burn it so that the smoke of the fire would rise, as a sign of the full carrying out and success of the plan.

entries.section: (4) The defeat of Benjamin and the killing of its men

paragraphs.text: Here is a repetition of what was mentioned before in (v. 31), that from the beginning of the battle, when Benjamin saw the (planned) retreat of the children of Israel, they thought they were fleeing, so they pursued them and killed thirty men of them.

entries.section: (4) The defeat of Benjamin and the killing of its men

paragraphs.text: The smoke from the burning of the city rose, which the men of the ambush carried out after entering it, and went up to heaven, and when the children of Benjamin looked behind them, they saw the whole city burning.

entries.section: (4) The defeat of Benjamin and the killing of its men

paragraphs.text: The children of Israel turned to advance toward Gibeah after having pretended to withdraw in the other direction, in application of the plan they had laid. Meanwhile the soldiers of Benjamin began to be terrified by the burning of their city and the attack of the army of Israel upon them, so they began to flee from before the children of Israel, after they were sure that they were defeated this time.

entries.section: (4) The defeat of Benjamin and the killing of its men

paragraphs.text: And them which came out of the cities they destroyed in the midst of them: the soldiers of the children of Israel who had stayed behind from taking part in the war because they were assigned to protective duties inside the cities came out to join their brethren and killed the fleeing soldiers of Benjamin.

The children of Benjamin turned back, but not toward their city because they saw it burning, so they began to flee into the wilderness around it, while the army of the tribes pursued them in every direction, and at the same time the men of the ambush who had taken their city came out against them from the other side, so both parties surrounded them from both directions and they fell dead in their midst, in addition to the soldiers of Israel coming out from their cities and killing those fleeing of the tribe of Benjamin.

entries.section: (4) The defeat of Benjamin and the killing of its men

paragraphs.text: The armies of Israel surrounded the children of Benjamin and pursued them while they were defeated and trying to escape, and the armies overtook them to the east of the city of Gibeah.

entries.section: (4) The defeat of Benjamin and the killing of its men

paragraphs.text: Vast numbers of the men of the children of Benjamin fell in this battle and terrible pursuit, for the number of their dead reached 18 thousand valiant warriors.

entries.section: (4) The defeat of Benjamin and the killing of its men

paragraphs.text: Gidom: a town between Gibeah and the rock of Rimmon.
They pursued hard after them: they chased them.

The children of Benjamin tried to find a gap through which they could escape from the pursuit, so they headed for a fortified place near their town called "the rock of Rimmon," but on the road they took in their flight five thousand of them were killed, whom the men of the tribes picked off easily and killed. And those who tried to escape and went farther on the road of flight, the men of the children of Israel followed them and pursued them zealously and killed two thousand more of them.

entries.section: (4) The defeat of Benjamin and the killing of its men

paragraphs.text: The approximate number of the dead of that battle from the tribe of Benjamin was 25 thousand sword-bearing valiant men.

entries.section: (4) The defeat of Benjamin and the killing of its men

paragraphs.text: Six hundred men of the tribe of Benjamin were able to save themselves by reaching the fortress called "the rock of Rimmon." They hid in it among its caves and remained hidden about four months until what will be mentioned in the next chapter happened.

It is noted that the number of the soldiers of the tribe of Benjamin was 26 thousand soldiers (v. 15), of whom 25,100 were killed (vv. 44-46) and 600 soldiers hid at "the rock of Rimmon," and there remained 300 soldiers who fell in the first and second battles and, because of their small number, were not mentioned, so that by this all the soldiers of Benjamin were killed, approximately.

entries.section: (4) The defeat of Benjamin and the killing of its men

paragraphs.text: After the army of Benjamin collapsed, all the cities in which the families of their tribe lived became a target for the fury of the children of Israel, who entered the land of Benjamin and killed everyone they met, even the beasts, and burned all their cities. By this the tribe almost became extinct entirely, had it not been for the success of the six hundred men who took refuge in "the rock of Rimmon" in saving themselves and remaining alive.
The tribe of Benjamin faces extinction

entries.section: (1) Israel's regret at the extinction of Benjamin

paragraphs.text: After the victory of the tribes, the men of the children of Israel swore that none of the tribes would give his daughter as a wife to any man of the tribe of Benjamin.

entries.section: (1) Israel's regret at the extinction of Benjamin

paragraphs.text: The tribes of Israel gathered before the tent of the Lord at Bethel, and they repented and wept over the loss of so many in this war and because the tribe of Benjamin was nearing extinction, since they had killed most of its men.

entries.section: (1) Israel's regret at the extinction of Benjamin

paragraphs.text: They spent their night at Bethel, and in the morning they built an altar to the Lord and offered burnt offerings on it in atonement for the sins into which the people had fallen and seeking forgiveness, and they also offered peace offerings in thanks to the Lord for giving them the victory.
